title: Taxonomy of Managerial Actions
description: Working taxonomy of the actions, interventions, investments, and choices available to managers seeking to improve a team.
notes: IDs are sequential 1-102. #1-81 are the original taxonomy (former #82, Manager Accessibility / Availability, is now #81). #82-102 were added later.

categories.description: Working with one person at a time through feedback, motivation, reflection, guidance, and coaching tailored to that individual.

examples.quote: I started giving Maya feedback right after her client calls instead of saving it for later. She tried one small change each week, and within a month she was handling tough questions without looking to me for help.

I kept trying to motivate Ben by giving him bigger goals, but he only got quieter. When I asked him to walk me through what was getting in his way, I learned he was confused about who could approve his work, not lacking ambition.

I encouraged Luis to speak up more when he disagreed, and he suddenly challenged nearly every decision in meetings. I told him I had pushed too hard, then worked with him on picking the moments where his concern really needed the room.

target.reason: Individual coaching primarily develops the person's capabilities, motivation, and self-awareness while often improving how they approach their work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager personally engages in feedback, reflection, and guidance while also communicating expectations and encouragement.

temporal.reason: Coaching can be an ongoing practice or a case-specific intervention.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective coaching is a collaborative process in which the manager guides and the individual reflects and acts.

time_horizon.reason: Initial changes may appear within weeks, while deeper capability and behavioral development often take months.

domain.reason: Individual coaching primarily develops a person’s skills, self-awareness, and effectiveness through tailored feedback and guidance, while relying on trust and rapport in the one-to-one relationship.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Tailored one-to-one support helps identify and overcome personal barriers, making the desired behaviour easier to perform.

bcw_functions.name: Training
bcw_functions.reason: Individualized feedback, guidance, and practice build the person’s skills and procedural know-how.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Motivational dialogue and reflection can shift beliefs, confidence, and emotional commitment toward the desired behaviour.

clarifications.for: structured training or practice to build specific skills across individuals or groups
learning from the practices and performance of other organizations
improving collaboration, group dynamics, or team-wide ways of working

observations: One person repeatedly misses the same expectation despite team-wide reminders.
A team member becomes quiet or defensive when receiving feedback.
Someone asks for more guidance, feedback, or opportunities to grow.
A team member’s performance or engagement has changed noticeably from their usual pattern.
The same person raises a sensitive concern only in 1:1 conversations.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is specific to one person’s skills, motivation, confidence, or understanding and requires tailored support.

challenges.what_if: What if the repeated misses, defensiveness, or change in engagement reflect a mismatch between the standard working arrangement and this person’s specific constraints, rather than a coachable performance gap? Explore #66, Individual Accommodation / Personalized Working Arrangements.
What if this person is struggling because the work reaches them through a confusing or burdensome process, and they are simply the first to show the effects? Explore #19, Workflow / Process Design.

What if the sensitive concern raised only in 1:1s is about being asked to cross an ethical line, making the apparent motivation or confidence problem a sign of unresolved ethical tension? Explore #85, Ethical Barriers / Ethical Stance.

categories.description: Demonstrating behaviors through your own conduct, deliberately or incidentally, including everyday habits and actions.

examples.quote: I started owning my mistakes in team meetings instead of quietly fixing them later. Within a few weeks, people brought up problems sooner, and we caught several before they got expensive.

I blocked off quiet work time on my calendar and turned down some meetings, hoping others would do the same. Nobody did, and I learned their calendars were mostly controlled by other teams, which I hadn’t realized before.

I began answering customer questions right away whenever I saw them. The team copied me so closely that customers sometimes got three different replies, so I assigned one person to each issue and stopped jumping in unless they asked.

target.reason: The manager's conduct demonstrates desired ways of working while also shaping informal norms and expectations around the work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager signals expected behavior through visible personal conduct, which inherently involves acting directly.

temporal.reason: Its influence typically comes from consistent, ongoing conduct rather than a single isolated demonstration.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager independently controls and demonstrates their own conduct, even though others decide whether to emulate it.

time_horizon.reason: The signal is noticed immediately, while changes in team habits and norms typically emerge over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The action centers on the manager modeling behavior through their own conduct, while those visible habits help establish and reinforce shared team norms.

bcw_functions.name: Modelling
bcw_functions.reason: The manager demonstrates behaviors through their own conduct, providing an observable example for others to imitate.

clarifications.for: letting a team face natural consequences rather than stepping in to correct the situation

clarifications.category: Managerial Deep Dives / Direct Engagement with Details
clarifications.for: personally examining the substance and details of a specific piece of work
redesigning how you gather feedback, observe work, or investigate team patterns
changing when and how team members can reach you for support or decisions

observations: Team members copy how the manager runs meetings, responds to mistakes, or handles disagreement.
The manager asks for punctuality, preparation, or openness but does not consistently demonstrate it.
People repeat the manager’s phrases and habits when working with others.
Team members look to the manager’s reaction before responding to bad news or conflict.
A behavior the manager displays regularly has started appearing across the team.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the team is taking its behavioral cues from what the manager does rather than from what the manager says.

challenges.what_if: What if the manager and team behave similarly because the same productivity measures reward that behavior, not because people are copying the manager? Explore #38, Productivity Definition / Productivity Measurement.

What if people watch the manager before reacting to bad news because escalation rules and consequences are unclear, so the manager’s reaction functions as an approval signal? Explore #43, Escalation Design / Escalation Response.

What if the manager and team are both reacting to the same unfiltered organizational pressure, with the manager displaying the pattern first rather than causing it? Explore #48, Buffering / Selective Exposure / Organizational Shielding.

categories.description: Explaining strategies, decisions, direction, expectations, or organizational matters through structured communication.

examples.quote: I held a monthly all-hands to explain why we were changing our product priorities and what each group should focus on. People still had questions, but the teams stopped pulling in different directions and we hit the next deadline.

I sent a detailed memo laying out the new approval process, but hardly anyone followed it. The questions afterward showed me that people understood the steps but not which decisions actually needed approval, and I would not have caught that from the silence alone.

I started a weekly update email listing missed targets and upcoming expectations. People unexpectedly treated every item as urgent and began dropping planned work, so I switched to a shorter note that clearly separated immediate actions from things to watch.

target.reason: Formal one-to-many communication primarily clarifies direction, priorities, and expectations while also conveying organizational context and rules.

manager_mode.reason: The manager acts by explicitly communicating and reinforcing strategies, decisions, and expectations.

temporal.reason: Each communication is usually a discrete event tied to a strategy, decision, update, or organizational matter.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager generally controls the message and delivers it to the audience, even when its content reflects wider organizational decisions.

time_horizon.reason: The message can change awareness immediately, while alignment and behavior typically develop over the following weeks.

domain.reason: The category centers on structured one-to-many information flow that clarifies strategy, direction, expectations, and organizational context. Authority-governance is secondary because these communications often convey decisions, mandates, and decision rights.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Structured explanations increase employees’ knowledge and understanding of organizational strategies, decisions, direction, and expectations.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Formal communication can frame priorities and provide rationale that shapes employees’ beliefs, attitudes, and motivation to align with the stated direction.

clarifications.for: subtly signaling priorities through what you mention, emphasize, acknowledge, or ignore
representing the team’s story, status, and needs to the wider organization
connecting the team’s work to its broader customer, organizational, or mission impact

observations: Different team members give different explanations of the current priorities or strategy.
The same questions about a decision or organizational change keep coming up.
People leave meetings unsure about who owns what or what happens next.
Important information is scattered across Slack threads, documents, and separate conversations.
Several people say they did not know about a decision, deadline, or expectation.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is a shared lack of clear, consistent, and accessible information.

challenges.what_if: What if people give different explanations because the strategy has not been translated into concrete choices and tradeoffs for their work, not because it needs another announcement? Explore #97, Strategy Deployment / Translation / Cascade.
What if uncertainty about ownership and next steps persists because authority to decide or approve is unresolved? Explore #16, Decision Rights / Authority Distribution.

What if recurring questions and scattered information reflect a failure to capture and maintain decisions as durable organizational knowledge? Explore #77, Knowledge Stewardship / Institutional Memory.

categories.description: Communicating priorities and values through what you choose to mention, emphasize, share, acknowledge, or ignore.

examples.quote: I started opening our Monday meeting with one customer problem we had solved and calling out the people who helped. Within a few weeks, the team was bringing me fixes before I even asked.

I stopped commenting on every draft because I wanted the team to feel trusted, but the work got more cautious instead. I learned that my silence sounded like I had lost interest, which I would not have guessed without trying it.

I shared a story about someone staying late to rescue a deadline, and suddenly several people started working late to get noticed. I backed off, said clearly that I did not want that, and began calling out people who prevented emergencies during normal hours.

target.reason: Selective attention directs people toward particular priorities while also shaping the team's implicit norms and values.

manager_mode.reason: The manager communicates importance indirectly through what they emphasize, acknowledge, share, or ignore.

temporal.reason: A signal may be sent in a single interaction or reinforced as an ongoing pattern of managerial attention.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager primarily controls what they mention, emphasize, acknowledge, share, or ignore.

time_horizon.reason: People can notice a signal within days, while repeated attention typically shapes priorities and norms over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The action signals priorities through selective communication and attention, while repeated emphasis or omission shapes shared norms about what the team values.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Selective emphasis and attention make certain priorities more salient, shaping employees’ beliefs about what matters.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Repeated mentions, sharing, and omissions alter the social cue environment that guides employees’ behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Incentivisation
bcw_functions.reason: Acknowledging selected actions provides informal recognition that positively reinforces those behaviors.

clarifications.for: formally explaining strategies, decisions, direction, or expectations to a broad audience
shaping how the team is perceived and advocated for outside its boundaries
making the larger purpose and impact of the team’s work tangible

observations: A stated priority rarely comes up in meetings, updates, or the manager’s questions.
Team members focus their updates on topics that receive the manager’s attention and follow-up.
The manager regularly asks about short-term delivery but rarely asks about quality, learning, or customer impact.
Messages or examples shared by the manager repeatedly highlight some work while overlooking other stated priorities.
People change what they discuss after noticing which topics the manager acknowledges or ignores.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the manager’s everyday attention is sending unclear or conflicting signals about what truly matters.

challenges.what_if: What if the manager keeps focusing on short-term delivery because the measurement system makes those results visible and consequential while quality, learning, and customer impact remain invisible? Explore #15, Measurement / Performance Systems.

What if short-term topics dominate because the team has accepted more external commitments than it can reliably meet, forcing attention toward the next deadline? Explore #56, Demand Management / External Commitments.

What if the manager’s attention is being shaped by narrow information channels that surface delivery updates but hide quality risks, learning, and customer impact? Explore #60, Organizational Sensing / Inquiry Design.

categories.description: The manager publicly praising, rewarding, challenging, or discouraging specific behaviors in front of others to signal what is valued or unacceptable.

examples.quote: I called out Maya in our team meeting for admitting a mistake early and asking for help. After that, people started raising problems sooner, and we caught a couple before they grew.

I praised the person who closed the most tickets in front of everyone, hoping it would lift the pace. It did not; people felt I cared more about speed than hard cases, which showed me the number was rewarding the wrong thing.

I told the group that late handoffs had to stop, and people took it more harshly than I expected. They started sending half-finished work just to beat the deadline, so I clarified that complete work mattered more and eased off the public reminders.

target.reason: Public reinforcement shapes team norms and social expectations while also influencing the behavior of the person being praised, rewarded, challenged, or discouraged.

manager_mode.reason: The manager visibly communicates what is valued or unacceptable through direct praise, rewards, challenges, or discouragement.

temporal.reason: It is typically used in response to particular behaviors or moments rather than operating as a standing system.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager generally decides which behavior to highlight and delivers the public response unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: The signal is felt immediately, while resulting changes in behavior and norms may develop over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: Public praise or discouragement shapes shared behavioral norms by signaling what the team values or rejects, while the manager’s use of rewards, challenges, or sanctions reflects positional authority and enforcement.

bcw_functions.name: Incentivisation
bcw_functions.reason: Public praise or rewards create positive social consequences that reinforce desired behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Coercion
bcw_functions.reason: Public challenges or discouragement create social pressure and negative expectancies around unacceptable behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Visible approval and disapproval signal organizational values and shape others’ beliefs about which behaviors matter.

clarifications.for: shaping team identity through stories about its origins, history, and defining moments
improving how mistakes are admitted, discussed, corrected, and handled
using peer behavior, approval, or benchmarks to show what is normal

observations: A useful behavior happens in front of the team but receives no acknowledgment.
The same unhelpful behavior appears repeatedly in group settings without being challenged.
Praise is broad or generic, so people cannot tell which specific actions earned it.
Team members react differently to the same behavior because no public standard has been established.
After one person is publicly recognized or corrected, others quickly adjust similar behavior.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that people need visible social consequences to understand which specific behaviors the group values or rejects.

challenges.what_if: What if the unhelpful behavior keeps recurring because the work is structured in a way that makes it the easiest or fastest response, regardless of public praise or correction? Explore #7, Work Design / Task Structuring.

What if team members react differently because their work styles are colliding without explicit integration, rather than because they need a public signal from the manager? Explore #88, Work Style Differences / Integration.

What if people adjust quickly after public correction because they fear arbitrary or embarrassing treatment, not because they now understand the desired standard? Explore #76, Procedural Fairness / Appeals / Due Process.

categories.description: Changing the format, participants, facilitation, structure, or flow of meetings and organized interactions.

examples.quote: I cut our weekly meeting to 30 minutes and asked everyone to post updates beforehand. We spent the time on the two decisions that actually needed the group, and we stopped running over.

I tried inviting the whole support team to our product review so we could hear more voices. Hardly anyone spoke, but it showed me that the large group made people hold back, which I would not have known from their written feedback.

I started rotating who led our morning check-in, and a few people turned it into a full planning session. When the meetings began taking an hour, I gave each person a simple outline and capped updates at three minutes.

target.reason: Meeting design primarily changes how people coordinate and interact, while also shaping participation conditions and working relationships.

manager_mode.reason: The manager designs meeting structures and rules and may also directly facilitate the resulting interactions.

temporal.reason: A structure can govern recurring meetings or be created for a single organized interaction.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager can set the meeting design unilaterally, though teams are often involved in shaping or refining it.

time_horizon.reason: The effects are felt during the next interaction, with broader coordination benefits emerging over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: Meeting design primarily changes how collaborative work is organized and conducted, while also shaping how information, context, and input flow among participants.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redesigning meeting formats, participants, facilitation, and flow changes the social environment and introduces structures or cues that support desired behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Structured interactions can remove barriers to participation, coordination, decision-making, and follow-through, making desired behaviors easier to perform.

clarifications.for: adjusting how intensely or quickly the team works and how long that pace should continue
embedding guardrails, templates, hard limits, or mandatory steps into the work process

clarifications.category: Unstructured Time / Learning Time / Innovation Time
clarifications.for: reserving self-directed time for learning, exploration, or innovation

observations: The same two people do most of the talking in meetings.
Meetings regularly end without a clear decision, owner, or next step.
People repeat questions that were already discussed in earlier meetings.
Several attendees stay silent during the meeting but raise concerns afterward.
Recurring meetings run over time or drift away from the stated agenda.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the current meeting format, participation, or facilitation is preventing useful discussion and clear decisions.

challenges.what_if: What if people stay silent or revisit concerns later because they do not trust that disagreement and challenges will be handled fairly, not because the meeting format is wrong?
What if meetings end without decisions because the people in the room do not have a clear mandate to decide, regardless of how well the meeting is facilitated?
What if the repetition and agenda drift reflect unresolved strategic choices, so participants keep reopening the same questions because daily priorities have never been settled?

categories.description: Changing tasks, assignments, scope, deliverables, sequencing, or the nature of work people undertake.

examples.quote: I split the client rollout into smaller pieces and gave each person a clear part to own. We caught problems earlier, and the final handoff went much more smoothly.

I moved all the routine reports to one person so the others could focus on bigger projects. It slowed everything down, but it showed me that several reports depended on knowledge spread across the team, which I hadn't realized.

I let two people take a new feature from start to finish instead of passing it between specialists. They started changing more of the product than we expected, so I narrowed the assignment and added a review before any extra changes went ahead.

target.reason: The action primarily changes the content, scope, and outputs of work, while sequencing and task structure can also alter how work is performed.

manager_mode.reason: The manager designs how work is divided and organized, often by directly changing assignments, scope, or deliverables.

temporal.reason: Task structuring can establish an ongoing operating model or address a particular project, workload, or situation.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers often hold authority to allocate and structure work, although effective redesign may involve team input and collaboration.

time_horizon.reason: New assignments or sequencing can affect work within weeks, while broader changes to roles and scope may take months to realize fully.

domain.reason: The category directly concerns structuring tasks, scope, deliverables, sequencing, and assignments. People-talent is secondary because assigning work also involves matching responsibilities and roles to team members.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redesigning assignments, scope, deliverables, or sequencing changes the organizational environment in which behavior occurs.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Structuring work can remove practical barriers, clarify pathways, and make desired performance easier to carry out.

clarifications.for: redistributing limited time, expertise, or bandwidth across competing priorities
slowing, sequencing, or limiting simultaneous organizational changes
accommodating or integrating differences in how people prefer to work

observations: People start work before the deliverable or acceptance criteria are clear.
Large assignments remain in progress for weeks without an intermediate output to review.
Team members frequently stop one task to respond to a newer request.
Work is repeatedly sent back because key steps or dependencies were missed.
Multiple people are doing overlapping work on the same deliverable.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that work is scoped, divided, or sequenced in a way that makes successful execution difficult.

challenges.what_if: What if people start many tasks, switch frequently, and leave work unfinished because the organization rewards visible activity rather than completed outcomes?
What if newer requests keep disrupting assignments because the team accepts more external commitments than it can fulfill, not because individual tasks are poorly structured?
What if missed steps, unclear criteria, and overlapping effort come from critical knowledge being scattered, outdated, or difficult to find?

categories.description: Changing role definitions, responsibilities, and the formal expectations attached to a role.

examples.quote: I rewrote the team lead’s responsibilities so she owned the weekly planning meeting instead of waiting for me to run it. After a few uneven weeks, decisions started getting made faster and fewer things came back to my desk.

I moved customer follow-ups into one person’s job, thinking that would stop them from falling through the cracks. It didn’t, because the workload was too spiky for one person, but it showed me the real problem was coverage during busy weeks, not unclear ownership.

I made senior engineers formally responsible for approving every technical change, and reviews suddenly piled up for days. I hadn’t expected people to treat even tiny fixes as needing approval, so I narrowed the expectation to risky changes and let the rest move without them.

target.reason: Role design primarily changes what work a role owns while also altering the formal structure and expectations surrounding that work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager redesigns a formal role structure and then communicates the resulting responsibilities and expectations.

temporal.reason: The revised responsibilities remain in effect as an ongoing feature of the role.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager usually has formal authority over role design, though effective changes may be developed with the affected individual.

time_horizon.reason: New expectations can alter behavior within weeks, while their full effects on coordination and performance may take months.

domain.reason: Defining roles and responsibilities is primarily a people and organizational design action; formal expectations also establish accountability, decision rights, and mandated boundaries.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing role definitions and responsibilities restructures the social and organizational environment in which behaviour occurs.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Formal expectations constrain which behaviours and decisions are considered appropriate within the role.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Clarifying authority and responsibilities can remove role ambiguity and make expected behaviours easier to perform.

clarifications.for: changing who belongs to the team or how the collective unit is defined
helping individuals enter, integrate into, or transition within the team
creating or changing awards, competitions, privileges, or special recognition programs

clarifications.category: Hiring Process / Hiring Role Definition / Interview Design
clarifications.for: defining a vacancy and designing the interviews, rubrics, and decisions used to fill it

observations: Two people each say the other person owns the same decision or task.
Important responsibilities are repeatedly left unclaimed.
Team members regularly ask who has authority to approve or decide something.
A person is evaluated on an outcome they say they do not control.
Different stakeholders give the same role conflicting instructions.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that responsibilities, decision rights, or formal expectations are unclear, conflicting, or assigned to the wrong role.

challenges.what_if: What if responsibilities are clear enough, but people avoid claiming difficult work and rely on the manager to settle ownership rather than holding one another accountable?
What if disputes over ownership are defensive reactions to a review system that holds people responsible for outcomes they cannot control?
What if stakeholders give conflicting instructions because broader strategic choices have not been translated into consistent priorities, rather than because the role itself is poorly defined?

categories.description: Introducing, purchasing, building, adapting, or retiring technologies and tools that support work.

examples.quote: I bought the field team a simple mobile app so they could log repairs on site instead of writing notes twice. After a few rough days, missing reports dropped and jobs got closed faster.
I built a dashboard for the weekly numbers, but hardly anyone used it. That showed me the real problem wasn't seeing the numbers; people couldn't agree on who was supposed to update them.

I turned on automatic alerts for overdue customer requests, and everyone got flooded with messages. People started ignoring them, so I limited the alerts to urgent cases and sent one daily summary for the rest.

target.reason: Tools primarily change how work is performed while also altering the technical environment surrounding it.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes or changes the team's technical infrastructure and may personally evaluate, purchase, configure, or retire tools.

temporal.reason: Once introduced or adapted, tools generally become an ongoing part of the team's operating system.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective tooling changes commonly incorporate team needs and feedback, although the manager may retain unilateral authority over selection or procurement.

time_horizon.reason: Initial access or relief may arrive within weeks, while adoption, integration, and sustained productivity effects usually develop over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on selecting, creating, adapting, and retiring technology and tools in the work environment. Its secondary relevance is to work design and delivery because those tools enable and shape workflows, processes, quality, and execution.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Introducing, adapting, or retiring tools changes the digital or physical work environment in ways that shape how tasks are performed.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Providing suitable technology removes practical barriers, reduces effort, and makes desired work behaviours easier or possible.

clarifications.for: changing the physical, virtual, spatial, or scheduling conditions of work
redesigning system architecture, boundaries, dependencies, or foundational capabilities

observations: People copy the same information manually between systems or spreadsheets.
Team members maintain separate trackers with different versions of the same data.
Routine tasks require repeated manual steps that consume significant time.
People avoid or work around a tool because it is slow, unreliable, or hard to use.
Work pauses because employees cannot access the information or system they need.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team's tools do not adequately support the work or create avoidable effort and errors.

challenges.what_if: What if duplicate trackers and manual copying persist because teams have never agreed on a shared source of truth, handoffs, or data ownership, and the technology is merely exposing that gap?
What if access delays and workarounds are caused by outdated or inconsistently applied permission policies rather than inadequate tools?
challenges.explore_category: Formal Policies / Handbooks / Codes of Conduct

challenges.what_if: What if repetitive manual work remains because no one is expected or empowered to identify and implement improvements, even though the existing tools could support them?

categories.description: Changing team membership through hiring, removal, transfers, or replacement of individuals.

examples.quote: I hired a support engineer who had dealt with our kind of customers before. Within two months, the rest of us were spending less time on repeat issues, though it took a while to stop routing everything through her.

I transferred one of our strongest developers onto the project, thinking he could get it unstuck. It still slipped, but I learned the real gap was product knowledge, not coding skill, which I couldn't have seen from the backlog alone.

I replaced a team lead who kept missing deadlines, and I didn't expect the rest of the group to worry that more people were about to be pushed out. I paused the other planned moves and met with everyone individually to explain what was and wasn't changing.

target.reason: Staffing changes alter the team's relational and capacity context by changing who is present to perform the work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager directly initiates or executes membership changes, sometimes also redesigning roles or the staffing structure.

temporal.reason: Membership changes are usually discrete decisions made when a staffing need or issue arises.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically drives the staffing decision, although HR, senior leadership, recruiters, or other teams often participate or constrain it.

time_horizon.reason: The team feels a membership change within days or weeks, while its full effects on capability and dynamics often emerge over months.

domain.reason: The category directly concerns staffing and team composition through hiring, removal, transfers, and replacement. It also involves managerial decision rights and authority over who joins, leaves, or moves within the team.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing team membership directly alters the social environment, including available expertise, relationships, norms, and work dynamics.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Hiring, transferring, or replacing people can remove capacity or capability barriers by ensuring the team has the personnel needed to perform effectively.

clarifications.for: addressing an existing team member’s performance or conduct through expectations, warnings, or consequences
deciding who receives stretch assignments, visibility, promotions, or career sponsorship
preventing valued or at-risk employees from leaving through stay conversations and targeted action

observations: Committed work remains unassigned because everyone is already at capacity.
The team repeatedly depends on outside help for the same missing skill.
A vacant position has left recurring responsibilities uncovered.
One team member's missed commitments repeatedly block the rest of the team.
The team's workload has grown while its headcount has stayed the same or decreased.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team has the wrong number or mix of people, or that a current member cannot meet the role's requirements.

challenges.what_if: What if the team looks understaffed because it keeps accepting more commitments than it can reliably deliver, so additional hiring would only provide temporary relief?
What if vacancies, outside help, and blocked work reveal that knowledge and responsibilities are concentrated in too few people rather than that the team has the wrong members?
What if one person's missed commitments block everyone because the technical architecture creates a critical dependency on that person's specialty?

categories.description: Building individual or collective capabilities through training, education, practice, and structured learning opportunities.

examples.quote: I paired two newer analysts with a senior one for a weekly practice session using old client cases. After a couple of months, they were handling the simpler cases on their own, and the senior analyst had fewer basic questions coming her way.

I paid for an online course on presentation skills, but hardly anyone finished it and the meetings did not improve. That showed me the issue was not knowing the basics; people needed practice with our actual reports and honest feedback from colleagues.

I started rotating engineers through support so they could learn how customers used the product. They began spending so much time fixing every request that their main projects slipped, so I limited the rotation to one morning a week and had the support lead choose the cases.

target.reason: Upskilling primarily develops people's knowledge and abilities, which in turn improves how they perform their work.

manager_mode.reason: Managers typically create or arrange learning structures and may also coach, teach, or facilitate practice themselves.

temporal.reason: Upskilling may be an ongoing development system or an episodic intervention addressing a particular capability need.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective development is usually jointly shaped by the manager and learner, with collective programs similarly involving the wider team.

time_horizon.reason: Initial learning can improve performance within weeks, while durable capability generally develops through practice over several months.

domain.reason: The category directly concerns building skills and knowledge through training, education, practice, and structured learning. Its secondary relevance is to people-talent because upskilling supports employee growth, career development, and workforce capability.

bcw_functions.name: Training
bcw_functions.reason: It directly builds skills and procedural know-how through practice and structured learning opportunities.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: It increases the knowledge and understanding needed for stronger individual or collective capability.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Providing organized development opportunities can remove capability barriers that would otherwise prevent effective behavior.

clarifications.for: personalized feedback, reflection, motivation, or guidance for one person
exploring how external organizations operate to identify new approaches
facilitating a team reset, retrospective, launch, or group-dynamics issue

observations: Work is repeatedly sent back because it does not meet the expected technical or quality standard.
Team members frequently ask one person to handle tasks that require a particular skill.
People take much longer than expected when using a new tool, process, or method.
The same mistakes continue to appear after reviews or retrospectives.
Team members explicitly ask for training, examples, or opportunities to practice.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is a gap in the knowledge or skills people need to perform the work well.

challenges.what_if: What if the repeated mistakes and slow work come from people being spread too thin and rushing, not from a lack of skill? Explore whether capacity is concentrated on too many competing demands.
What if reviews are not leading to improvement because people expect mistakes to be blamed or deflected, so the real causes never become discussable?
What if the standard way of working fits some team members poorly, making capable people look unskilled or unusually slow?

categories.description: Changing who works with whom on particular efforts without permanently changing team membership.

examples.quote: I paired Maya with Luis for the customer rollout because their strengths filled different gaps. They caught problems earlier, and we finished with fewer last-minute fixes.

I put two of our fastest engineers together on a short cleanup job, but they kept stepping on each other and barely moved faster. It showed me they both needed clear ownership, which I would not have seen from their individual work.

I brought three extra people onto a late project for a week, and suddenly the lead spent all day answering questions instead of finishing the work. I pulled two people back out and left one to handle testing, which made the help manageable.

target.reason: The action changes working relationships and collaboration arrangements, which also affects how project work is carried out.

manager_mode.reason: The manager designs a temporary staffing structure and may directly assign people to specific efforts.

temporal.reason: The configuration is typically made for a particular project or need rather than as a permanent team structure.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager commonly controls staffing decisions, though team input may shape effective collaboration pairings.

time_horizon.reason: The assignment takes effect quickly, while its collaboration and performance benefits typically emerge over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The action changes temporary staffing and collaborator assignments for specific projects, making personnel deployment the main focus while also reshaping how the work is organized and delivered.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Reconfiguring who collaborates on an effort changes the immediate social environment in which the target behavior occurs.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Assigning collaborators with complementary expertise, capacity, or access can remove practical barriers and make effective performance easier.

clarifications.for: changing pay, bonuses, equity, or other material rewards
tailoring duties, schedules, conditions, or support to one individual’s needs

observations: A project repeatedly stalls while waiting for input from someone outside the project group.
Most of the work on a shared project is being completed by one or two people.
People discover late that another teammate had relevant expertise or prior experience.
Handoffs between project contributors regularly lead to missed details or duplicated work.
The same people are assigned together despite recurring friction or gaps in coverage.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the current mix or pairing of people on the work does not provide the right expertise, capacity, or collaboration.

challenges.what_if: What if projects are waiting on outsiders and leaning on one or two people because decision authority is unclear, not because the project has the wrong mix of contributors?
What if expertise is discovered late and handoffs lose details because knowledge is not captured or findable, regardless of who is assigned to the project?
What if a few people carry most of the work because teammates expect the manager or strongest contributors to enforce commitments rather than holding one another accountable?

categories.description: Adding to or enriching the business, strategic, operational, and historical context the team holds.

examples.quote: I started giving the team a quick rundown of why each customer request mattered before we planned the work. They made better tradeoffs and caught one request that would have caused trouble for our biggest account.

I walked everyone through the history behind our pricing rules, hoping it would clear up the debate. It did not change anyone’s mind, but their questions revealed that the real gap was how our costs had changed this year, which I had not thought to explain.

I shared the full sales forecast so the team could see what might be coming. They treated every possible deal as a firm promise and started reshuffling work, so I followed up with a shorter list that separated likely deals from long shots and asked them to stop planning around the rest.

target.reason: It expands the surrounding business, strategic, operational, and historical context that helps the team understand its direction and priorities.

manager_mode.reason: The manager communicates information and interpretation that broaden the team's understanding.

temporal.reason: Context enrichment may occur through standing communication practices or as episodic updates when relevant information arises.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager usually selects and supplies the context, though team discussion can jointly interpret and enrich it.

time_horizon.reason: New context can change understanding within days, while its effects on alignment and decisions often emerge over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The category primarily concerns improving the flow and visibility of business, strategic, operational, and historical information so the team can understand its work in context. It secondarily develops shared organizational knowledge and better-informed judgment.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Sharing business, strategic, operational, and historical context increases the team’s knowledge and understanding of decisions, priorities, and constraints.

clarifications.for: making work, decisions, dependencies, or outcomes more observable to others
filtering, delaying, translating, or absorbing organizational demands before they reach the team

observations: Team members give different explanations for why a project is important or what success looks like.
Decisions are repeatedly reopened because people are working from different assumptions.
People propose approaches that were previously tried and rejected, without knowing that history.
The team is surprised by dependencies, constraints, or leadership decisions that were known elsewhere.
Questions about customer needs, business priorities, or strategic tradeoffs regularly go unanswered.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team lacks shared business, strategic, operational, or historical context needed to make sound decisions.

challenges.what_if: What if decisions keep reopening because people do not trust how they were made or lack a credible way to challenge them, rather than because they lack context?
What if conflicting explanations and surprise dependencies reflect uncertainty about what the team actually owns and where its boundaries sit?
What if previously rejected approaches keep returning because past mistakes and decisions were never openly acknowledged and learned from, not simply because history was not shared?

categories.description: Exposing the team to outside people, perspectives, experiences, research, writing, and ideas.

examples.quote: I invited two longtime customers to walk us through how they actually used the product. We changed the setup screen based on what they showed us, and support calls dropped the next month.

I had the team try ideas from a book about running shorter meetings, but our meetings still dragged. It revealed that the real problem was people coming in without decisions from their own groups, which I would not have spotted from inside the team.
I shared a competitor’s product demo, and the team suddenly wanted to copy half of it. I paused the new work, talked through what our customers actually needed, and limited us to testing one idea.

target.reason: The action expands the team's external relationships and informational environment while also broadening members' knowledge and perspectives.

manager_mode.reason: The manager typically creates channels or opportunities for external exposure and may also personally invite people or share materials.

temporal.reason: It may be established as a recurring boundary-spanning practice or used as a one-time intervention.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager enables access, the team engages with the input, and outside people or sources contribute the perspectives.

time_horizon.reason: New perspectives can influence thinking within weeks, while sustained exposure may reshape team judgment and practices over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on bringing external people and perspectives into the team, with a secondary emphasis on broadening knowledge and learning through research, writing, experiences, and ideas.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Exposure to external research, writing, experiences, and viewpoints increases the team's knowledge and understanding.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Bringing outside people and ideas into the team's information and social environment creates new cues and broadens the context shaping behavior.

clarifications.for: helping the team understand customer needs and the real-world impact of its work through customer stories and outcomes
building sustained relationships with outside peers, mentors, or professional communities
giving team members direct, frequent interaction with customers or involving customers in the work

observations: Planning discussions rely almost entirely on internal opinions and examples.
The team is surprised by customer, partner, competitor, or industry developments.
People repeatedly use the same approaches even when those approaches are not producing better results.
Team members ask how other organizations or experts handle a similar problem.
Research, customer conversations, or outside expertise rarely appear in proposals or decisions.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team’s thinking is too limited by its internal experience and lacks useful outside perspectives.

challenges.what_if: What if people rely on familiar internal approaches because delivery pressure leaves no protected time to research, learn, or test alternatives?
challenges.explore_category: Unstructured Time / Learning Time / Innovation Time

challenges.what_if: What if the team knows outside evidence exists but current rewards favor predictable activity and low-risk conformity over trying better approaches?
What if the team is surprised by external developments because organizational pressure and information are being filtered too heavily before reaching them?

categories.description: Changing which inputs, outputs, KPIs, outcomes, guardrails, and feedback signals are tracked to assess performance.

examples.quote: I stopped judging the support team on tickets closed and started tracking how many issues stayed fixed after a week. Repeat contacts dropped, and customers were less frustrated, even though the daily ticket count looked worse.

I added a weekly count of sales calls because I thought low activity was the problem, but sales did not improve. It showed me the reps were already making plenty of calls; the real gap was that our list had too many bad leads.

I started posting each crew's error rate every morning, and people got so cautious that orders began backing up. I switched to a weekly team-level number and added a limit for acceptable delays, which eased the slowdown without hiding the mistakes.

target.reason: Performance systems change the evaluative context and signals around work while also influencing which results and priorities receive attention.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or modifies a measurement structure whose selected indicators also signal what matters.

temporal.reason: Once established, performance measures generally operate as an ongoing assessment and feedback system.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers often hold authority over performance measures, although team participation can improve metric relevance and legitimacy.

time_horizon.reason: New measures can alter attention within weeks, but meaningful behavioral and performance effects usually emerge over months.

domain.reason: Performance measures define how work, quality, outcomes, and constraints are evaluated, while KPIs and feedback signals determine what performance information is made visible and communicated.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing KPIs, guardrails, and feedback signals reshapes the informational environment that directs attention and guides behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Relevant and timely performance measures make it easier to identify gaps, self-correct, and sustain desired behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Tracking inputs, outputs, and outcomes increases understanding of current performance and the effects of actions.

clarifications.for: negotiating responsibilities, dependencies, handoffs, or commitments with other teams
designing leave, breaks, disconnection practices, or other protections for recovery

observations: The dashboard shows strong performance while customers or stakeholders continue to report poor results.
Different meetings use conflicting numbers for the same outcome.
Problems are discovered late because no tracked signal shows that work is drifting off course.
People focus on hitting a visible target while ignoring quality, risk, or downstream effects.
The team tracks activity completed but cannot say whether the intended outcome improved.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that current measures and feedback signals do not accurately guide behavior or reveal whether performance is improving.

challenges.what_if: What if people ignore quality and downstream effects because material rewards are tied to hitting the visible target, even though everyone knows the metric is incomplete?
What if the dashboard looks healthy because the team has too little direct contact with customers to notice that its internal signals no longer reflect what customers need?
What if problems appear late because people hide, soften, or deflect early signs of failure rather than because the right signal is not being tracked?

categories.description: Changing who makes, influences, participates in, approves, or is excluded from a particular decision.

examples.quote: I let the support leads approve customer refunds under $500 without coming to me. They cleared the backlog in a week, and I only had to step in on two unusual cases.

I asked the whole engineering team to weigh in on which database we should use. We still missed the deadline, but the debate showed me that the real disagreement was about who would be stuck maintaining it, which I hadn’t known before.

I gave each store manager full say over weekly promotions, and a few of them started discounting almost everything. I hadn’t expected sales to jump while margins fell that fast, so I added a discount limit and required a quick check for anything beyond it.

target.reason: Decision rights alter the governance context around work and secondarily shape how decisions are made.

manager_mode.reason: The manager primarily designs or changes decision structures, while sometimes assigning authority directly for a specific decision.

temporal.reason: Authority distribution can be a standing governance arrangement or a one-time choice for a particular decision.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers often have the authority to allocate decision rights, although they may develop the arrangement collaboratively with the team.

time_horizon.reason: The new authority can apply immediately, while its effects on decision quality, speed, and ownership typically emerge over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The category directly concerns allocation of decision authority, participation, approval, and exclusion. Information flow is the next most relevant angle because influence and effective participation depend on who receives context and has visibility into the decision.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redistributing decision roles changes the organization’s social structure, workflows, and authority relationships around the decision.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Granting participation or approval authority removes governance barriers and makes timely, autonomous action possible for designated people.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Defining who may decide, approve, or participate limits decision-making options for those outside the assigned authority.

clarifications.for: defining when problems must be escalated, where they go, and how managers respond
changing reporting lines, management layers, or organizational units
adjusting the amount or types of risk the team may take
creating a fair process to challenge decisions or request impartial review

observations: Decisions are revisited because people disagree about who had the final say.
Work waits in queues for approval from the same senior person.
Several people give conflicting instructions on the same issue.
Team members regularly ask, "Who owns this decision?"
People learn about decisions that affect their work only after they have been made.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is unclear or poorly distributed authority over who decides, contributes, approves, or must be consulted.

challenges.what_if: What if people keep revisiting decisions because they lacked the business context to understand the original choice, not because final authority was unclear? Explore #13 Context Sharing / Context Enrichment.

What if approvals pile up with one senior person because they are too hard to reach when work needs input, rather than because approval authority is assigned incorrectly? Explore #81 Manager Accessibility / Availability.
What if conflicting instructions persist because the manager’s attention and reactions signal different priorities from the stated ones? Explore #4 Informal Signaling / Selective Attention.

categories.description: Changing the general systems by which disagreements, tensions, and problematic situations are surfaced and resolved.

examples.quote: I started a weekly half-hour where anyone could bring up a snag with another team, and we agreed who would handle it before leaving. A few old arguments finally got settled, and people stopped letting new ones sit for weeks.

I set up an anonymous form for people to report tensions, but almost nobody used it. When I asked around, I learned they were worried that written complaints would be traced back to them, so we needed a way to talk things through without creating a record first.

I told everyone they could bring unresolved problems straight to me, and suddenly I was pulled into every small disagreement. I was becoming the judge for things people could settle themselves, so I added a first step where they talked directly or asked a neutral teammate to sit in before coming to me.

target.reason: The action changes the rules, channels, and relational conditions for surfacing and resolving conflict, as well as the processes used to do so.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or modifies recurring structures and procedures for handling disagreements and problematic situations.

temporal.reason: The category concerns general systems intended to operate across conflicts rather than a single intervention.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective conflict systems are commonly shaped with team input, although a manager may also establish them unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: New procedures can guide cases within weeks, but their broader effects on trust and conflict patterns typically emerge over months.

domain.reason: Conflict and remediation systems define formal pathways, decision rights, escalation, fairness, and resolution procedures, while also determining how concerns are surfaced and communicated.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redesigning how conflicts are surfaced and resolved changes the organization’s social structures, processes, and cues around handling problems.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Clear remediation pathways, forums, and escalation mechanisms remove barriers to raising concerns and reaching workable resolutions.

clarifications.for: giving team members more autonomy or a greater role in designing how the team operates
clarifying the team’s purpose, remit, responsibilities, or organizational boundaries
changing the evidence, timing, or approvals required to obtain funding or hire staff

observations: The same disagreement resurfaces across multiple meetings without a resolution.
Team members avoid raising concerns in group discussions but bring them up privately afterward.
Slack threads about disagreements become personal, heated, or abruptly go silent.
Two people route routine communication through their manager instead of speaking directly.
Agreed actions after a conflict are not documented or followed up.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is the absence of a safe, reliable, and effective way to surface and resolve conflict.

challenges.what_if: What if the disagreements keep returning because people are rewarded for competing outcomes, so resolving the tension would require someone to lose against their goals? Explore #15 Measurement / Performance Systems.
What if people avoid direct disagreement because they have watched the manager become defensive, personal, or dismissive when challenged? Explore #2 Behavioral Modeling.

What if heated messages, silence, and missed follow-up are signs that the team is operating at an unsustainable intensity, leaving little capacity for thoughtful repair? Explore #84 Work Pace / Intensity Modulation.

aliases: Keeping Others Informed About Your Team
categories.description: Shaping how the team is represented to the wider organization and how its story, status, and needs are carried outward.

examples.quote: I sent a short Friday note to the directors showing what we had finished and where another group was holding us up. After a few weeks, they helped clear a dependency that had been stuck for months.

I asked for two more people by walking through our backlog, but the request went nowhere. The pushback revealed that leadership thought half our work belonged to another team, which I would not have known otherwise.

I invited a few senior leaders to our product demo so they could see what the team was capable of. They got excited and started sending us extra requests directly, so I followed up with a clear list of our current commitments and asked them to route new ideas through me.

target.reason: The action primarily shapes the team's organizational context, relationships, and standing, while sometimes influencing priorities through how its needs are framed.

manager_mode.reason: The manager communicates and frames the team's story while personally carrying its status and needs across organizational boundaries.

temporal.reason: Managers may broker context continuously or intervene around specific decisions, issues, and opportunities.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager commonly serves as the team's representative, though the narrative and needs may be developed collaboratively with team members.

time_horizon.reason: Stakeholder understanding and support can shift within weeks, while reputation and organizational standing generally develop over months.

domain.reason: The core action is carrying the team's context, status, needs, and narrative across organizational boundaries. It also depends on building effective upward and cross-functional relationships with stakeholders who receive and act on that representation.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: It frames the team’s story, status, and needs to influence how organizational stakeholders perceive and respond to the team.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It advocates for the team in ways that can remove organizational barriers and secure the support, access, or resources needed for effective action.

clarifications.for: delivering structured communication about strategy, decisions, direction, or expectations
conveying priorities indirectly through selective attention, emphasis, and acknowledgment
helping team members feel how their work contributes to customers, the organization, or the mission

observations: Other teams describe the team's role or priorities differently from how team members describe them.
Requests from outside the team arrive without the context needed to prioritize them.
Leaders make plans that depend on the team without involving or informing it.
Team members repeatedly say that stakeholders do not understand their work, constraints, or impact.
Updates to senior leaders focus on activity but omit the team's needs, risks, or outcomes.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team's work, needs, status, or constraints are not being represented clearly across organizational boundaries.

challenges.what_if: What if the team is represented through activity because it lacks credible measures that show outcomes, risks, and constraints in terms leaders can use? Explore #15 Measurement / Performance Systems.

What if leaders plan around the team and outside requests arrive without context because the formal structure separates the team from the groups that shape its work? Explore #50 Formal Organizational Structure / Reporting Relationships.

What if different groups describe the team’s priorities differently because the broader strategy has never been translated into clear choices for this team? Explore #97 Strategy Deployment / Translation / Cascade.

categories.description: Introducing, adapting, formalizing, simplifying, removing, or allowing processes and workflows to emerge.

examples.quote: I cut our approval chain from four people to two for routine requests. Work moved faster, and we still caught the few mistakes that mattered.

I gave everyone a detailed checklist for handing off client work, but people kept skipping half of it. That showed me the real problem was that two teams used different information, so I rebuilt the handoff around what each side actually needed.

I let the team create its own way of sorting incoming requests, and they built far more rules than anyone could remember. When small jobs started getting stuck, I stepped in and cut the system back to three simple lanes.

target.reason: The action changes the methods, processes, and workflows through which work is performed.

manager_mode.reason: Managers primarily create or modify operating systems, while sometimes deliberately allowing effective processes to emerge.

temporal.reason: A workflow generally becomes an ongoing way of coordinating and completing work.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective process design commonly involves team participation, though managers may also impose or remove workflows unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: Workflow effects often appear within weeks, while adoption and broader performance effects may take months.

domain.reason: The category directly concerns designing and changing how work flows and is executed. Its secondary governance angle involves deciding which processes are formalized, mandated, simplified, removed, or left to emerge.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Designing or adapting workflows changes the organizational environment, cues, and pathways through which work is performed.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Simplifying, removing, or allowing processes to emerge can reduce barriers and make desired behavior easier or more feasible.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Formalizing workflows can limit available options and discourage competing or inconsistent ways of working.

clarifications.for: adopting, replacing, or retiring a specific professional or collaborative practice
changing the timing, frequency, duration, or synchronization of team activities
defining what productivity means or how it should be measured and discussed
setting quality expectations or reinforcing them through reviews and feedback
changing how the team estimates, forecasts, plans, or commits to work

observations: Work regularly stalls between handoffs because the next step or owner is unclear.
Different team members follow different steps to complete the same recurring task.
The team spends substantial time updating trackers, duplicating information, or waiting for routine reviews.
Tasks are frequently reopened because required checks happened too late or were skipped.
Team members rely on one person to explain how work moves from request to completion.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is a workflow that is unclear, inconsistent, overly burdensome, or poorly matched to the work.

challenges.what_if: What if handoffs stall and routine reviews accumulate because the team has accepted more work than its capacity can support, not because the process itself is poorly designed? Explore #56 Demand Management / External Commitments.

What if people follow different steps and depend on one expert because essential operating knowledge lives in that person’s head rather than being reliably captured and transferred? Explore #77 Knowledge Stewardship / Institutional Memory.

What if tasks are reopened and checks vary because the team has no shared definition of acceptable quality, so each person applies a different threshold? Explore #62 Quality Standards / Quality Reinforcement.

categories.description: Introducing, encouraging, adapting, replacing, or retiring specific professional and collaborative practices.

examples.quote: I started having the team write down decisions at the end of each planning meeting. After a few weeks, we had fewer repeat arguments and people who missed the meeting could catch up quickly.

I asked everyone to switch from code reviews over email to our review tool, but several people kept going back to email. That showed me the tool was too awkward for quick comments, so I stopped pushing a full switch and kept email for small changes.

I retired our daily status spreadsheet because nobody seemed to read it, and suddenly people started asking for updates in three different chat channels. The noise was worse than the spreadsheet, so I brought back a shorter version twice a week and asked everyone to use one channel for follow-ups.

target.reason: The action changes the methods, routines, and collaborative practices used to perform work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes or modifies working practices while also encouraging adoption or communicating deprecation.

temporal.reason: Adopted, replaced, or retired practices generally alter the team's ongoing way of working.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective practice change commonly involves team participation and adaptation, although a manager may sometimes mandate it unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: A practice change can begin affecting work within weeks, while full adoption and stabilization often take months.

domain.reason: Adopting or retiring professional practices primarily changes how work is performed and delivered; it also requires teams to learn, adapt, and apply new methods.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Introducing, replacing, or retiring shared practices changes the procedural and social environment that guides how work is performed.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Adapting or adopting practices can remove workflow barriers and make desired professional or collaborative behaviours easier to carry out.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Deprecating practices limits access to obsolete or undesirable ways of working, reducing competing behaviours.

clarifications.for: redesigning or simplifying an end-to-end workflow or formal process
changing when or how often recurring team activities happen
redefining productivity or choosing individual versus collective productivity measures
establishing quality standards and mechanisms that reinforce them
changing planning horizons, estimation methods, forecasts, or commitment practices

observations: Team members use an agreed practice inconsistently or stop using it after a few weeks.
A recurring practice continues even though people routinely skip it or say it adds no value.
New hires learn key ways of working through informal tips rather than shared guidance.
Different people use incompatible methods or tools for the same type of work.
The team repeats avoidable mistakes that an established professional practice is meant to catch.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that a specific way of working has not been adopted effectively, no longer fits the team's needs, or should be replaced or retired.

challenges.what_if: What if people abandon new practices because they are absorbing too many changes at once, rather than because the practices are unsuitable or poorly introduced? Explore #74 Change Pacing / Change Saturation Management.
What if the agreed practice fades because managers and influential peers visibly bypass it, teaching everyone that it is optional? Explore #2 Behavioral Modeling.

What if people skip the practice because performance measures reward immediate output while ignoring the errors or coordination costs the practice prevents? Explore #15 Measurement / Performance Systems.

categories.description: Personally acting to resolve impediments, unblock work, secure decisions, or change a situation directly.

examples.quote: I called the finance lead myself and got the budget decision that had been sitting for two weeks. The team ordered the equipment the next day and made up most of the lost time.

I took over a stalled vendor issue and pushed for a quick fix, but it failed again a few days later. That showed me the real problem was our own messy setup, which I would not have seen from the team’s updates alone.

I joined a project meeting to settle one open question, and suddenly everyone started bringing every small decision to me. I told them which calls they could make without me and stopped attending the daily meetings.

target.reason: The manager primarily changes conditions or constraints surrounding the work, sometimes also altering how the work proceeds.

manager_mode.reason: The defining feature is the manager personally taking action to resolve the issue.

temporal.reason: The manager intervenes case by case when a particular obstacle or blocked decision arises.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager is the principal actor who personally drives the resolution, even when engaging others for approval or support.

time_horizon.reason: Successful intervention is generally intended to unblock work within days, though full effects can take several weeks.

domain.reason: The action focuses on removing constraints and unblocking execution, while emphasizing the manager’s personal, hands-on intervention.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Directly removing impediments or securing needed decisions makes the desired work possible or easier to carry out.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing the surrounding situation or workflow alters the work environment so progress can continue with less friction.

clarifications.for: shifting which team objectives take priority or redefining what counts as progress
limiting, declining, or renegotiating work requested by external stakeholders

observations: Work is stalled while the team waits for a decision from another group.
The same blocker is raised in several stand-ups without a clear owner or resolution date.
Team members repeatedly ask the manager to escalate an access, approval, or dependency issue.
A critical task cannot start because a needed resource, permission, or commitment has not been secured.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is a specific impediment that requires the manager's authority, access, or direct action to remove.

challenges.what_if: What if repeated escalation is teaching the team to hand blockers to you rather than own the follow-through and consequences?
What if the blocker keeps returning because the teams involved never made a clear, enforceable agreement about handoffs, approvals, or response times?
What if the apparent access or dependency issue is really a structural limitation in the underlying systems, so each manual unblock only treats the symptom?

categories.description: Changing which collective objectives receive attention and what counts as meaningful progress.

examples.quote: I put the reliability target at the top of every weekly review instead of letting new features take over. Within a month, the team cleared most of the old failures, and customer complaints dropped.

I tried counting tickets closed as our main sign of progress, but people just picked off the easy ones and the bigger problems sat there. That showed me the count was hiding the work that actually mattered, so I switched to tracking whether the worst issues were resolved.

I told everyone that cutting response time was our only goal for the quarter, and people started rushing replies that were incomplete. I hadn’t expected them to take it that literally, so I added a basic quality check and stopped praising speed by itself.

target.reason: The action changes which collective objectives matter most and how progress toward them is defined.

manager_mode.reason: The manager emphasizes certain objectives and progress indicators, potentially embedding that framing in planning or measurement systems.

temporal.reason: The framing may be a standing prioritization system or an episodic adjustment prompted by changing circumstances.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager commonly establishes or emphasizes priorities, though the team may participate in defining meaningful progress.

time_horizon.reason: The shift can redirect attention within days, while changes in execution and reported progress usually emerge over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The category centers on setting collective priorities and defining progress in the delivery of work, while also shaping how objectives and progress are framed and made salient to the team.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
