bcw_functions.reason: Framing certain objectives and indicators as meaningful shifts their salience and influences how employees interpret and value progress.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Reordering collective priorities changes the social and organizational cues that direct attention and day-to-day effort.

clarifications.for: personally removing a specific obstacle, securing a decision, or directly unblocking work
changing the commitments or promises the team makes to stakeholders

observations: People are working on many tasks, but the most important objective is not moving.
Team members give different answers when asked what the top priority is.
Status updates emphasize activity and completed tasks without showing progress toward a shared outcome.
New requests repeatedly displace previously agreed work without an explicit priority decision.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is unclear or misaligned priorities and an unhelpful definition of meaningful progress.

challenges.what_if: What if people understand the priority but their pay, bonuses, or other material rewards still favor task volume, responsiveness, or local targets?
What if priorities keep shifting because organizational demands are reaching the team without enough filtering, rather than because the team cannot choose what matters?
What if people give different answers because they disagree about what the team actually owns, not because the objectives themselves are unclear?

categories.description: Changing expectations and boundaries around team autonomy and participation in designing how the team operates.

examples.quote: I asked the team to set its own rules for running our weekly planning meeting. They dropped two steps I had always insisted on, and the meeting got shorter without things falling through the cracks.

I let everyone choose which tasks they would take instead of assigning them. It left a few important jobs untouched, but it showed me that nobody understood why those jobs mattered, which I would not have learned from simply handing them out.

I told the team they could change any of our day-to-day working rules, and they came back with so many changes that people were confused about what still applied. I paused the rollout and asked them to test one change at a time for two weeks.

target.reason: The action changes autonomy, decision rights, and participation conditions while also shaping how the team designs its operating practices.

manager_mode.reason: The manager redesigns participation and autonomy structures and communicates the resulting expectations and boundaries.

temporal.reason: The action establishes ongoing expectations for how the team participates in designing its operations.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager sets or negotiates boundaries with the team while enabling team members to drive the design within them.

time_horizon.reason: Participation may change within weeks, while durable autonomy and co-design norms usually develop over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on decision rights, autonomy, and boundaries for team participation, with a secondary focus on jointly designing operating processes and ways of working.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Expanding autonomy and participation removes organizational barriers and gives team members the authority to shape how work is done.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redefining expectations, decision boundaries, and co-design processes changes the team’s social and organizational environment to support participation.

clarifications.for: redesigning how disagreements, tensions, and problematic situations are surfaced and resolved
defining the team’s core mandate, scope, responsibilities, or reason for existing
changing how the team justifies and secures funding, investments, or new hires

observations: Team members wait for the manager to decide routine matters they could handle themselves.
Decisions about team processes are announced with little or no team input.
People say they do not know what they are allowed to change without approval.
Only the manager or a few vocal people contribute when the team discusses how work should be organized.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is an ineffective balance between managerial control, team autonomy, and participation in designing how the team works.

challenges.what_if: What if people wait for approval because past mistakes were punished or hidden, making independent decisions feel unsafe?
What if the team has formal freedom but lacks the skills or knowledge to make routine decisions confidently?
What if low participation is driven by conversational norms that let a few people dominate or make disagreement costly?

categories.category: Sponsorship / Air Cover for Individual Initiatives
categories.description: Protecting, legitimizing, supporting, or amplifying efforts initiated by individuals or small groups.

examples.quote: I gave Maya two afternoons a week to build the scheduling tool she had been pushing for, and I kept other requests off her plate. Her team started using it, and missed handoffs dropped within a month.

I backed two reps who wanted to rewrite our customer guide and got them time with the support team, but hardly anyone used the new version. That showed us the real problem was that people could not find the guide during calls, which we would not have learned if they had not tried.

I praised a small group's buddy system in our managers' meeting, and suddenly every team thought they were expected to copy it. People got paired up without asking, so I clarified that it was optional and asked the original group to keep it small until we knew where it actually helped.

target.reason: Sponsorship primarily changes the political, relational, and organizational support around an initiative while also helping its content gain attention or priority.

manager_mode.reason: The manager chiefly signals legitimacy and backing, sometimes intervening directly to protect or amplify the initiative.

temporal.reason: Air cover is generally provided case by case in support of a particular initiative or at critical moments.

locus_of_agency.reason: The individual or small group originates the effort while the manager collaborates by legitimizing, protecting, or amplifying it.

time_horizon.reason: Legitimacy and protection can be felt within days, while broader traction and support usually develop over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: Air cover and sponsorship use managerial authority to legitimize, protect, and authorize employee-led efforts; they also enable those initiatives to proceed through delivery despite organizational constraints or resistance.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Sponsorship and air cover remove organizational, political, and resource barriers that might otherwise prevent individuals or small groups from advancing their initiatives.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Managerial legitimization and visible support reshape the social environment by creating permission, protection, and stakeholder backing for the initiative.

clarifications.for: setting or defending ethical limits when demands conflict with the team's values

observations: Someone has proposed an improvement but cannot get time, attention, or permission to test it.
A small group is making progress on an initiative, but other stakeholders question whether the work is legitimate.
An employee's idea is overlooked until someone more senior repeats it.
People hesitate to lead new efforts because they expect criticism or competing demands to shut them down.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is a promising employee-led initiative lacking legitimacy, visibility, protection, or senior support.

challenges.what_if: What if the initiative is not short of legitimacy, but everyone involved is already spread across too many demands to give it real attention?
What if stakeholders are unconvinced because the idea is based on internal assumptions and lacks direct customer evidence?
What if people avoid leading improvements because the reward system favors immediate delivery and makes experimentation personally costly?

categories.description: Changing the physical, virtual, spatial, or temporal conditions in which people work.

examples.quote: I turned an unused office into a quiet room where anyone could do heads-down work. People actually used it, and the complaints about constant interruptions dropped within a few weeks.

I tried making every morning meeting-free, but support and sales kept having to break the rule for customer calls. It showed me that one shared schedule would never fit the whole team, so I stopped forcing it.
I set up separate chat rooms for each project so people could find things more easily. Instead, everyone started checking ten places all day, so I cut it back to three rooms and archived the rest.

target.reason: Workplace design primarily changes the conditions surrounding work and can secondarily shape how people collaborate and perform tasks.

manager_mode.reason: The manager primarily creates or modifies workplace arrangements, while sometimes directly moving resources, configuring tools, or adjusting schedules.

temporal.reason: Changes to physical, virtual, spatial, or temporal arrangements generally persist as ongoing working conditions.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers often control workplace arrangements directly, although effective design may involve team input and joint experimentation.

time_horizon.reason: People experience changed working conditions as soon as they are implemented, while behavioral and performance effects may emerge over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The category centers on shaping physical, virtual, and spatial work environments; temporal conditions also influence workflows, cadence, and how work is organized and delivered.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing physical, virtual, spatial, or temporal workplace conditions directly restructures the environment to cue, support, or facilitate desired behaviours.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Workplace design can remove practical barriers and make desired behaviours easier or more feasible to perform.

clarifications.for: introducing, purchasing, adapting, or retiring tools that support work
changing technical system boundaries, dependencies, or underlying architecture

observations: Meetings regularly fall outside people's working hours or interrupt their main focus time.
Team members report difficulty finding quiet space, suitable equipment, or reliable access to shared tools.
Remote participants struggle to hear, see, or contribute during hybrid meetings.
People lose time switching between offices, platforms, time zones, or fragmented schedules.
The workspace or schedule makes confidential, collaborative, or focused work visibly difficult.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team's physical, virtual, spatial, or scheduling environment is making effective work harder.

challenges.what_if: What if off-hours meetings and lost focus are symptoms of the team carrying more commitments than can fit into normal working time?
What if the real problem is not where people work, but unclear choices about which channels to use and when responses are expected?
What if the standard environment works for most people but creates a serious mismatch with particular individuals' needs or constraints?

categories.description: Creating opportunities for informal, non-work interaction, familiarity, and relationship development among team members.

examples.quote: I started a Friday team lunch where nobody brought laptops or talked through project updates. After a few weeks, people who barely spoke before were joking together and reaching out to each other more easily.

I paired people up for random virtual coffee chats, but most of the meetings never happened. I learned that our time-zone gaps and school pickup schedules made one-on-one calls much harder than I had realized.

I set up an evening game night, and it got so popular that people started planning one every week and some teammates felt pressured to join. I moved it to once a month and made it clear that skipping it was completely fine.

target.reason: The action improves the relational and social context surrounding the team's work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates recurring or ad hoc opportunities for connection and may also participate personally.

temporal.reason: It can be established as an ongoing team practice or used as an occasional event.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager enables the opportunity, while team members jointly create the relationships through participation.

time_horizon.reason: Initial familiarity can grow within weeks, while deeper trust and durable relationships usually develop over months.

domain.reason: The category primarily builds rapport, familiarity, and social bonds among team members; secondarily, it reinforces norms of connection, belonging, and interpersonal cohesion within the team culture.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Creates a social environment and dedicated opportunities that make informal interaction and relationship development more likely.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Reduces practical and social barriers to building familiarity, trust, and supportive connections among team members.

clarifications.for: building cross-organizational alliances and political support for the team's priorities
personally mediating a specific dispute between team members
engaging directly with employees multiple levels away from you

observations: Team conversations are almost entirely about tasks and deadlines.
People rarely talk before or after meetings unless they already know each other well.
Team members who do not work together directly struggle to recall basic details about one another.
New team members are left out of informal chats, lunches, or social plans.
In 1:1s, people say they do not feel comfortable reaching out to certain teammates.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that weak personal familiarity is making trust, communication, or collaboration harder.

challenges.what_if: What if people stay task-focused because workloads and schedules leave no room for informal contact, not because they lack interest in one another? Explore #25 Working Environment / Workplace Design.
What if individual targets and rewards make relationship-building feel like time taken away from the work that counts? Explore #63 Compensation / Material Incentives.

What if the apparent social distance reflects an in-group formed around who gets visible assignments and access, leaving others—especially newcomers—on the margins? Explore #55 Opportunity Distribution / Career Sponsorship.

categories.description: Sharing customer stories, experiences, needs, and outcomes with the team so it can see the real-world effect of its work.

examples.quote: I played a short recording of a customer using the feature we had just shipped. The team heard where she got excited and where she stumbled, and we fixed the confusing step that week. Her next session went much more smoothly.

I started forwarding customer emails to the team, but most people skimmed them and nothing changed. It showed me that raw messages were too scattered to be useful, and that the team needed more context about who the customers were and what they were trying to do.

I invited an upset customer to tell the team about a bad rollout, and people reacted by trying to fix every complaint at once. I paused the follow-up work, separated the urgent issue from the smaller frustrations, and asked the team to tackle only the biggest problem first.

target.reason: Customer stories connect the team to its external context and may also influence its understanding of priorities and desired outcomes.

manager_mode.reason: The manager communicates customer experiences, needs, and outcomes to make their importance and relevance visible.

temporal.reason: Sharing may occur as an ongoing practice or as an episodic response to a notable customer experience or outcome.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically selects and shares the material, while customers or other external parties provide the underlying experiences and feedback.

time_horizon.reason: The team can gain awareness within days, while changes in motivation, judgment, or priorities may emerge over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The category centers on connecting the team to customer experiences, needs, outcomes, and real-world impact, while the mechanism is sharing that information and making it visible.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Customer stories make the consequences and purpose of the team’s work emotionally salient, strengthening motivation to act in customers’ interests.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Sharing customer needs, experiences, and outcomes increases the team’s understanding of how its work affects customers in practice.

clarifications.for: introducing broader outside perspectives, research, experiences, or ideas beyond customer feedback
developing ongoing peer, mentor, advisory, or professional-community relationships
enabling team members to engage with customers directly rather than receiving customer stories secondhand

observations: Team members cannot name a recent customer outcome connected to their work.
Planning discussions focus on outputs and deadlines without mentioning customer needs.
Customer feedback reaches only managers or customer-facing roles.
The team rarely hears what happened after a feature, service, or project was delivered.
People ask whether their work makes any real difference to customers.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team cannot see or feel the real-world customer impact of its work.

challenges.what_if: What if the team talks about outputs and deadlines because its definition of productivity rewards completed activity rather than customer outcomes? Explore #38 Productivity Definition / Productivity Measurement.

What if people cannot connect their work to customers because the organization’s strategy has never been translated into concrete customer choices for the team? Explore #97 Strategy Deployment / Translation / Cascade.
What if customer outcomes are available but are not being captured, maintained, and passed back to the people who did the work? Explore #77 Knowledge Stewardship / Institutional Memory.

categories.description: Creating, adapting, legitimizing, restricting, or closing channels for expressing ideas, concerns, frustrations, needs, and dissent.

examples.quote: I started a weekly drop-in hour where anyone could bring me concerns without their lead there. People raised a scheduling problem we had missed, and we changed the handoff so fewer shifts started short-staffed.
I tried an anonymous form for warehouse concerns, but almost nobody used it. When I asked around privately, I learned the link required a company login, so people did not believe it was anonymous.

I opened a team chat thread for frustrations, and it quickly turned into people piling onto one coworker. I locked the thread, spoke with that person, and moved future complaints into short meetings with one issue discussed at a time.

target.reason: Voice forums primarily change the communication context and norms around work while also shaping how concerns and ideas enter team processes.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes or changes communication channels and also signals which forms of expression are legitimate or welcome.

temporal.reason: A forum for expression is typically an ongoing channel or norm rather than a single intervention.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective voice forums depend on team members using and shaping them, although managers may unilaterally create, restrict, or close the channels.

time_horizon.reason: New channels can affect expression within weeks, while durable changes in trust, candor, and participation typically develop over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on channels through which ideas, concerns, needs, and dissent are voiced, while their legitimization, restriction, or closure reflects rules and power over who may speak and how.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It changes the social and organizational environment by establishing, modifying, or removing channels through which people can voice ideas and concerns.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Creating or legitimizing forums removes practical and social barriers to speaking up, making employee expression easier and safer.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Restricting or closing forums limits available opportunities for expressing dissent, concerns, or other forms of voice.

clarifications.for: creating or revising a document, diagram, prototype, shared board, or plan
establishing common terms, labels, metaphors, or concepts for the work
capturing, maintaining, retrieving, transferring, or retiring collective knowledge
choosing communication media or setting synchronous and asynchronous channel norms
translating strategy into team choices and connecting daily work to strategic priorities

observations: The same few people speak in meetings while others remain silent.
Concerns appear in private messages or after meetings rather than in the room.
People say they do not know where to raise an idea, complaint, or disagreement.
Questions submitted through existing channels receive no visible response.
Team members repeatedly raise topics in forums that cannot address them.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that people lack a safe, credible, or effective channel for expressing what they think and need.

challenges.what_if: What if people have channels to speak but have learned from the manager’s reactions that disagreement is unwelcome or risky? Explore #47 Self-Reflection / Personal Awareness.
What if concerns keep landing in the wrong places because no one is clear about who can decide, approve, or act on them? Explore #16 Decision Rights / Authority Distribution.
What if silence in meetings reflects an unsustainable pace that leaves people no time to form, test, or articulate concerns until afterward? Explore #84 Work Pace / Intensity Modulation.

categories.description: Choosing not to rescue, stabilize, resolve, or correct situations so learning, accountability, or reorganization can emerge.

examples.quote: I stopped reminding the shift leads to place the weekly supply order. We ran short once, and after that they set up their own checks and never missed it again.

I left two senior developers to sort out their disagreement instead of settling it for them. They stayed stuck and the release slipped, but it showed me the real problem was that neither one knew who had the final say.

I stopped filling open weekend shifts myself and let the team work out the gaps. I was surprised when people started volunteering for too much overtime, so I capped the extra hours and covered one shift while we reset the schedule.

target.reason: The manager changes the surrounding conditions by withholding support so people experience consequences that may build learning and accountability.

manager_mode.reason: The defining managerial action is deliberately choosing not to rescue, stabilize, resolve, or correct the situation.

temporal.reason: The manager generally chooses nonintervention case by case when a particular situation arises.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager unilaterally steps back so the team or affected people must drive the response, learning, or reorganization.

time_horizon.reason: Immediate consequences often appear within weeks, while deeper learning, accountability, or reorganization may take months.

domain.reason: The core action is the manager deliberately withholding intervention, while the intended secondary effect is learning and growth through experiencing consequences.

bcw_functions.name: Coercion
bcw_functions.reason: Allowing natural negative consequences to occur creates accountability and discourages repetition of ineffective or undesirable behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Experiencing the uncorrected outcome helps people understand causal relationships and learn from the consequences of their choices.

clarifications.for: demonstrating the expected habits or standards through your own conduct

clarifications.category: Managerial Deep Dives / Direct Engagement with Details
clarifications.for: entering the details of the work yourself to diagnose or address an issue
gathering better information about team dynamics before deciding how to respond
making your attention, advice, or decision-making authority easier to access

observations: The manager repeatedly steps in to finish work when deadlines slip.
Team members escalate routine disagreements before trying to resolve them directly.
The same preventable mistake recurs after the manager quietly fixes its consequences.
Owners wait for the manager to make decisions that fall within their roles.
When a plan starts failing, the manager immediately reorganizes the work or takes control.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that repeated managerial rescue is preventing people from experiencing consequences, taking accountability, and adapting.

challenges.what_if: What if the manager keeps taking over because the team genuinely lacks enough people or the right mix of capabilities to meet its commitments? Explore #10 Team Composition / Staffing Changes.

What if plans repeatedly fail because technical dependencies and system constraints make ownership unusually difficult, rather than because people are being rescued too quickly? Explore #68 Technical Architecture / System Design.
What if people wait for the manager and escalate routine disputes because their responsibilities and decision expectations are genuinely unclear? Explore #8 Role Design / Formal Expectations.

categories.description: Changing which work, decisions, behaviors, dependencies, challenges, and outcomes are made more or less observable.

examples.quote: I put our launch tasks and outside dependencies on one shared board. People spotted two blocked handoffs early, and we fixed them before they pushed the date.

I started posting weekly decision notes, but hardly anyone opened them. When I asked why, I learned the night shift couldn’t access that folder from their work computers, which I wouldn’t have found out otherwise.

I made each engineer’s daily bug count visible, and people started avoiding the hard bugs and rushing easy ones closed. I took down the names and switched to a weekly team total, which calmed things down.

target.reason: The action changes the information environment surrounding work and may also alter practices for documenting and sharing it.

manager_mode.reason: Managers commonly establish mechanisms, access rules, or routines for visibility while also communicating what should be surfaced.

temporal.reason: Visibility may be embedded as an ongoing practice or changed temporarily for a particular issue or decision.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager often controls access and reporting expectations, although the team may jointly shape what is shared and how.

time_horizon.reason: Changes in access or observability can take effect within days, while their coordination and behavioral effects often emerge over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The category primarily concerns what information is visible and how broadly it is exposed. Its secondary relevance is to delivery because visibility into work, dependencies, challenges, and outcomes affects coordination, planning, and execution.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing what is visible restructures the informational and social environment by introducing or removing cues, transparency, and feedback.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Making work, decisions, dependencies, challenges, and outcomes observable increases people's knowledge and understanding of what is happening.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Greater visibility can remove information barriers that otherwise hinder coordination, decision-making, and effective action.

clarifications.for: giving the team additional business, strategic, operational, or historical background
shielding the team from disruptive pressures or selectively limiting what reaches them

observations: Two people give different accounts of who owns the same piece of work.
Decisions are announced without the reasoning or tradeoffs behind them.
Blocked work becomes visible only when a deadline is missed.
Teams discover dependencies late in the project.
Progress updates report activity but do not show outcomes, risks, or unresolved issues.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that important work, decisions, dependencies, or risks are not visible to the people who need to act on them.

challenges.what_if: What if people hide blocks and report activity because rewards favor looking busy and on track, even when surfacing risk would be more useful? Explore #63 Compensation / Material Incentives.
What if dependencies appear late because the technical architecture contains hidden coupling that ordinary status visibility cannot reveal early? Explore #68 Technical Architecture / System Design.

What if conflicting ownership, late dependencies, and surprise risks come from weak planning and commitment practices rather than missing visibility? Explore #99 Planning / Forecasting / Commitment Practices.

categories.description: Introducing, changing, encouraging, or retiring documents, diagrams, prototypes, shared boards, plans, and other artifacts.

examples.quote: I put up a simple shared board showing who was handling each customer issue. People stopped chasing updates in chat, and we caught two stuck cases before they got worse.

I made a clickable prototype before we started building, but the team barely used it. That showed me they needed real customer examples to judge the idea, which I would not have known from our planning talks.
I introduced a detailed weekly plan, and people started spending hours making every line look perfect. I cut it back to three sections and told everyone rough notes were enough.

target.reason: Artifacts primarily shape how work is represented, coordinated, and performed while also influencing the team's shared informational context.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes or changes tools and structures for work, often by personally creating, introducing, or retiring an artifact.

temporal.reason: An artifact may become a standing part of the workflow or be created temporarily for a specific situation.

locus_of_agency.reason: Artifacts are often developed and adopted collaboratively, although a manager can also introduce or retire them unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: Artifacts can affect communication immediately, while consistent workflow benefits usually emerge over several weeks.

domain.reason: Artifacts primarily structure, preserve, and make information visible; they also guide planning, coordination, workflows, and execution.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Introducing or changing shared artifacts alters the work environment by adding cues, structures, and coordination tools that shape behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Well-designed documents, boards, plans, or prototypes reduce practical barriers by making information, decisions, and next steps easier to access and act on.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Artifacts such as diagrams, plans, and prototypes can increase understanding by making concepts, expectations, or processes explicit.

clarifications.for: creating or protecting a forum where people can raise ideas, concerns, frustrations, or dissent
changing the vocabulary, labels, metaphors, or concepts people use to describe work
managing how organizational knowledge is preserved, updated, retrieved, transferred, or retired
deciding which communication channel or medium suits a purpose and how it should be used
cascading strategy, negotiating its interpretation, or translating it into team-level decisions

observations: People ask where the latest plan, decision, or design can be found.
Different team members bring conflicting versions of the same document to meetings.
The same workflow or system is explained from scratch in multiple conversations.
A shared board or plan is rarely updated and no longer matches the work underway.
Reviews stay abstract because there is no draft, diagram, or prototype to react to.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is the lack of a useful, trusted artifact that makes the work, decisions, or progress visible.

challenges.what_if: What if the competing documents and stale boards exist because no one has clear authority to declare a version final or require updates? Explore #16 Decision Rights / Authority Distribution.
What if people know which artifact to maintain but constant external commitments keep pushing that work aside? Explore #56 Demand Management / External Commitments.
What if reviews stay abstract and records remain vague because people expect mistakes or contested decisions to be used against them? Explore #71 Error Acknowledgment / Mistake Response.

categories.description: Changing the timing, frequency, duration, synchronization, and cycles through which team activities occur.

examples.quote: I moved our daily check-in from first thing in the morning to just after lunch. People came in with real updates, and we stopped wasting half the meeting guessing what the day might bring.

I tried switching our weekly planning meeting to every other week, but small decisions piled up and people started working from different assumptions. It showed me that the meeting was doing more to keep us aligned than I’d realized, so I put it back on the calendar each week.

I set aside every Friday afternoon for uninterrupted work, and people took it so seriously that urgent questions sat unanswered until Monday. I kept the block but added one rotating person to watch for anything that truly couldn’t wait.

target.reason: Temporal design primarily changes how work is coordinated and performed while also shaping the conditions surrounding it.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or modifies recurring schedules, cycles, and timing structures.

temporal.reason: A cadence is typically an ongoing temporal structure rather than a one-time intervention.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective cadence design commonly incorporates team needs and feedback, although a manager may also impose scheduling changes unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: A new rhythm changes schedules within days, while its broader coordination and performance effects usually emerge over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: Timing, frequency, duration, synchronization, and cycles are core elements of workflow and operating cadence. Repeated rhythms also shape team rituals and shared expectations about how work happens.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redesigning schedules, cycles, and synchronization changes the team’s operating environment and creates temporal cues for desired behaviours.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Establishing an effective cadence reduces coordination barriers and makes timely participation, follow-through, and collaboration easier.

clarifications.for: redesigning the steps, handoffs, or structure of a workflow
introducing, encouraging, replacing, or retiring a specific professional practice
changing how productivity is defined, understood, or measured
defining quality or strengthening quality through reviews, feedback, and standards
changing how work is planned, estimated, forecast, or committed

observations: Meetings regularly run out of time before key decisions are made.
Team members repeatedly say that requests or reviews arrive too late for them to respond well.
Status meetings repeat information that has barely changed since the previous meeting.
Dependencies are discovered only after one team has already missed a handoff.
Long stretches pass without feedback, followed by urgent rounds of review and rework.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is a mismatch between the team's operating rhythm and the timing needed for coordination, decisions, and feedback.

challenges.what_if: What if late reviews, rushed decisions, and unchanged status updates reflect more commitments than the team can realistically service, not a poorly chosen rhythm? Explore #56 Demand Management / External Commitments.
What if dependencies surface late because the systems themselves are tightly coupled in ways the teams cannot easily anticipate or control? Explore #68 Technical Architecture / System Design.
What if meetings drag and feedback arrives in urgent bursts because people are unsure who can decide without waiting for approval? Explore #16 Decision Rights / Authority Distribution.

categories.description: Introducing, changing, reinforcing, or retiring the terms, metaphors, labels, and concepts used to describe work.

examples.quote: I started calling last-minute customer requests “interrupt work” instead of “small favors.” People got more honest about the time they took, and we finally planned some room for them each week.

I tried replacing “handoff” with “shared finish,” but nobody used it after the first few days. That showed me the problem was not the word—the two groups genuinely disagreed about where one team’s job ended.

I introduced “red flag” for blocked tasks, and suddenly people used it for every minor delay. It made the morning check-in feel like a crisis, so I set a narrower meaning for the term and asked people to call smaller issues “snags” instead.

target.reason: Shared vocabulary changes the team’s communicative context and, secondarily, how members coordinate and make sense of work.

manager_mode.reason: Managers establish language mainly by communicating and modeling it, sometimes codifying it in glossaries, templates, or standards.

temporal.reason: Once adopted, shared terms generally become an ongoing part of how the team discusses work.

locus_of_agency.reason: A manager can propose terminology, but the team’s collective use and interpretation determine whether it becomes shared.

time_horizon.reason: New terms can clarify discussion within weeks, while consistent adoption and cultural embedding often take months.

domain.reason: Shared vocabulary directly shapes how work and concepts are communicated, while reinforced terms and metaphors also influence collective meaning, expectations, and team identity.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Establishing or retiring shared terminology changes the social and informational environment in which employees interpret and discuss work.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Introducing vocabulary and concepts increases employees’ understanding of work practices, distinctions, and expectations.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Labels and metaphors frame issues in ways that can shift beliefs, emotions, and motivation toward particular behaviours.

clarifications.for: providing a legitimate channel for people to express concerns, needs, ideas, or dissent
introducing or changing a concrete document, diagram, prototype, board, or plan
ensuring important knowledge is captured, maintained, discoverable, transferred, and eventually retired
selecting communication media or defining written, verbal, synchronous, and asynchronous norms
explaining strategic priorities and translating them into choices the team can act on

observations: People use the same word to mean different things during discussions.
Meetings stall while participants debate what a label, status, or priority means.
The same type of work has different names across teams, documents, or tools.
Team members frequently ask for clarification when goals or concepts are discussed.
Two groups describe the same issue in ways that make their work sound unrelated.

I began answering every message right away so people would know I was available. I was surprised when they started messaging late at night and waiting for my reply before making small decisions, so I set clearer hours and asked them to call only when something truly could not wait.

categories.description: Setting standing, organization-wide rules about what leadership mandates, what teams determine, and what individuals control.

examples.quote: I set one rule for the whole company: leadership picked the quarterly goals, but each team decided how to reach them and each person organized their own daily work. Teams stopped waiting for approval on small choices, and we hit more of our targets.

I told every team they could set their own release schedule. It fell apart when two teams changed the same system at once, but that showed me shared systems needed company-level scheduling while everything else could stay with the teams.

I gave individuals full control over which meetings they attended. People dropped nearly every optional invite, and some teams suddenly could not make decisions because nobody had the same context. I pulled it back by requiring attendance for decision meetings while leaving the rest up to each person.

categories.description: Changing what productivity means: how it is defined, understood, and discussed, including individual versus collective productivity.

examples.quote: I stopped talking about productivity as how many tasks each person finished and started asking what the whole team got over the line. People helped each other more, and we cleared a stubborn backlog by the end of the month.

I tried defining productivity by the number of requests each person closed, but the count pushed people toward the easy ones. It failed, but it showed me that the hard requests were taking most of our time and had been almost invisible before.

I started praising the team for time spent helping other groups, and people unexpectedly began saying yes to nearly every request. Our own work slipped, so I narrowed the definition to help that removed a real blocker and asked people to check with me before taking on anything large.

I kept retelling the story of the weekend we rescued a broken release, and people started treating late-night heroics like something to aim for. I stopped praising the all-nighter and retold it with more focus on the mistakes that caused it and the safeguards we added afterward.

examples.quote: I sat with the support team and read through a week of customer tickets instead of relying on the summary. I spotted a confusing setup step we had all missed, and fixing it cut repeat complaints pretty quickly.

categories.description: Changing what warrants escalation, how issues are raised, who receives them, and how the manager responds.

I started responding to raised issues within an hour, and people began sending me every small decision because they knew I would jump in. Feedback to the manager points to a recurring skill gap, such as delegation, conflict handling, or prioritization.
The manager avoids tasks or situations that require an unfamiliar management skill.
The manager relies on one approach even when it repeatedly fails to produce the desired result.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is a gap in the manager's own knowledge, skill, or range of approaches.

challenges.what_if: What if the manager keeps defaulting to one approach because competing demands leave no capacity to prepare, reflect, or try something different? Explore #49 Capacity Allocation / Capacity Balancing.

What if difficult conversations and coaching attempts fail because employees do not trust the manager enough to share what is really happening? Explore #36 Direct Relationship Building / Managing Down.

What if the manager appears weak at delegation or prioritization because authority boundaries are inconsistent and their decisions are routinely overridden? Explore #37 Governance Boundaries / Mandate Levels.

categories.description: Studying how other companies, teams, and organizations operate to broaden one's perspective and options.

examples.quote: I asked two managers at other companies to walk me through how they ran weekly planning. We borrowed their idea of limiting the meeting to unresolved issues, and ours dropped from an hour to about twenty minutes.

I had the team copy a support handoff process I saw at a larger company, but it slowed us down. It showed me that their setup depended on specialists we didn't have, so I learned we needed a simpler version built around generalists.

I shared a competitor's project dashboard as an example, and the team suddenly started tracking every tiny task. The extra updates ate up more time than they saved, so I cut the dashboard back to three measures and told everyone to stop logging minor work.

target.reason: External learning primarily broadens the learner's knowledge and perspective, often informing changes to team methods and practices.

manager_mode.reason: The manager directly researches, observes, or engages with practices used by other organizations.

temporal.reason: It can be a one-time investigation or an ongoing organizational learning practice.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager often initiates and conducts the learning, though the team may participate in gathering and interpreting external practices.

time_horizon.reason: New perspectives can emerge within weeks, while translating benchmarks into meaningful operational improvements usually takes months.

domain.reason: The core action is learning through benchmarking and studying others’ operating methods to expand organizational knowledge and available approaches. Its secondary angle is outward-facing engagement with external companies, teams, and organizations as sources of perspective.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Studying other organizations increases knowledge and understanding of alternative practices, structures, and approaches.

bcw_functions.name: Modelling
bcw_functions.reason: External organizations provide observable examples of effective behavior and operating patterns that managers can adapt or imitate.

clarifications.for: helping one person improve through tailored coaching and feedback
building skills through structured education, training, and practice
helping a whole team improve its internal processes and working relationships

observations: The team repeatedly debates how to solve a common problem without looking at how others handle it.
People say, "We have to invent this ourselves," even though similar work exists elsewhere.
Competitors or peer teams achieve noticeably better results with comparable resources.
The team's processes have changed little despite recurring delays or quality issues.
Planning discussions rely mostly on internal experience and contain few outside examples or reference points.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is an overly narrow view of available practices and options because the team has not learned from other organizations.

challenges.what_if: What if the team already has enough examples but does not treat testing and implementing improvements as part of its regular work? Explore #75 Continuous Improvement Culture / Improvement Participation.
What if the team keeps reinventing solutions because previous experiments, decisions, and lessons were never captured or made findable? Explore #77 Knowledge Stewardship / Institutional Memory.
What if better practices are known but remain unused because the team cannot obtain timely funding or approval for the required investment? Explore #67 Team Funding / Investment Authorization.

categories.description: Developing relationships with outside peers, mentors, professional communities, and informal advisory networks.

examples.quote: I started meeting monthly with two managers from other companies who faced similar problems. One of them shared a simple on-call setup we adapted, and our weekend escalations dropped within a couple of months.

I asked a former boss to mentor me, but our talks stayed too general to help with the decisions I was facing. It showed me that I needed someone closer to my current kind of work, which I could not have known from his experience alone.

I invited a few outside contacts into a group chat for quick advice, and it unexpectedly turned into nonstop debate that distracted my team. I limited the chat to one question a week and moved longer discussions to a monthly call.

target.reason: External relationships expand the team's professional context, access to advice, and support while also developing participants' knowledge and perspective.

manager_mode.reason: Managers usually participate personally in networking and relationship-building, though they may also create recurring channels for external engagement.

temporal.reason: Professional communities and advisory relationships generally create ongoing sources of connection rather than isolated interventions.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically initiates and maintains the connections, but outside peers, mentors, and communities must reciprocate for the relationships to function.

time_horizon.reason: Useful advice and connections may emerge within months, while trust, reputation, and a durable professional network accumulate over longer periods.

domain.reason: The category centers on engaging external peers, mentors, communities, and advisory networks, with relationship-building as the main mechanism.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: External peers, mentors, and advisors provide support, expertise, and connections that help managers overcome barriers and act effectively.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Building these relationships creates a supportive social environment with new sources of guidance, feedback, and opportunity.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Professional communities and advisory networks increase managers’ knowledge and understanding through shared insights and experience.

clarifications.for: exposing the team to diverse external ideas, research, speakers, or experiences without prioritizing ongoing relationships
showing the team how its work affects customers through their stories, needs, and outcomes
increasing direct customer contact or customer participation in the team's work

observations: The same internal people are consulted whenever an unfamiliar problem comes up.
The team spends time building solutions that peers in other organizations may have already tried.
No one can name an outside peer or expert they could call for advice.
Questions about industry practices or how other teams operate regularly go unanswered.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is limited access to outside perspectives, experience, and trusted advice.

challenges.what_if: What if the team keeps reinventing solutions because earlier decisions, experiments, and lessons are not captured or easy to find—not because outside advice is unavailable? Explore #77, Knowledge Stewardship / Institutional Memory.

What if no one has external relationships because immediate delivery consumes every available hour, leaving no protected time to build or maintain them? Explore #92, Unstructured Time / Learning Time / Innovation Time.
challenges.explore_category: Unstructured Time / Learning Time / Innovation Time

challenges.what_if: What if unfamiliar questions go unanswered because the team lacks a consistent way to frame problems and evaluate possible approaches, so it defaults to asking the same familiar people? Explore #89, Thinking Frameworks / Selection / Mandate.

categories.description: Examining one's own assumptions, emotional responses, motivations, habits, blind spots, and impact on others.

examples.quote: I listened back to a few meeting recordings and noticed I cut people off whenever I thought we were running late. I started leaving more space, and two quieter people began speaking up regularly.
I kept a note of every time I got defensive, hoping that alone would stop it, but it didn’t. It did show me that I reacted most sharply when I hadn’t prepared, which I hadn’t connected before.

I realized I was taking over too many discussions, so I swung too far the other way and barely spoke. The team thought I was upset with them, so I explained what I was doing and started contributing again without dominating.

target.reason: The action primarily develops the manager's own awareness of their internal patterns, blind spots, and interpersonal impact.

manager_mode.reason: The manager personally engages in reflection, observation, or self-assessment.

temporal.reason: Reflection can be an ongoing practice or an episodic response to a particular experience or outcome.

locus_of_agency.reason: Although others may provide feedback, the manager must personally undertake and drive the examination of self.

time_horizon.reason: Insights may arise immediately, but meaningful changes in habits, judgment, and impact usually emerge over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on a manager examining their own assumptions, emotions, habits, blind spots, and interpersonal impact. This is primarily self-reflection and self-awareness, with capability development as the secondary angle because reflection supports learning and improved leadership skills.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Self-reflection increases the manager’s understanding of their own assumptions, emotions, habits, blind spots, and effects on others.

clarifications.for: building managerial knowledge or developing a specific professional skill

observations: People become quiet or guarded after the manager reacts strongly in meetings.
The same feedback about the manager's communication or behavior appears in multiple 1:1s or surveys.
The manager's stated intent differs from how team members describe the impact.
Certain people, topics, or setbacks repeatedly trigger defensiveness, impatience, or avoidance from the manager.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is the manager's unexamined habits, reactions, or blind spots affecting the team.

challenges.what_if: What if the manager's impatience and defensiveness are signs of an unsustainable work pace that is eroding their ability to respond calmly, rather than an unexamined personal habit? Explore #84, Work Pace / Intensity Modulation.
What if the manager reacts strongly because problems surface late and as high-stakes surprises, with no reliable path for raising them earlier? Explore #43, Escalation Design / Escalation Response.

What if people become guarded because they have no trusted way to question the manager or recover after a difficult exchange, making every reaction carry extra weight? Explore #28, Forums for Expression / Voice.

categories.description: Filtering, absorbing, delaying, translating, or blocking organizational pressures, demands, and information before they reach the team.

examples.quote: I took the stream of last-minute requests from senior leaders and made them come through me first. I pushed back on the vague ones and bundled the rest into one weekly list, which gave the team enough quiet time to finish a difficult release.

I held back news about a possible budget cut because I did not want everyone worrying over something that might not happen. When they finally heard, they were more upset about being kept in the dark, and I learned they preferred early context even when the answer was uncertain.

I started rewriting every urgent message from our director before passing it along so the team would not feel constantly pressured. People unexpectedly stopped taking any deadline seriously, so I began forwarding the truly urgent messages as they were and only softened the routine ones.

target.reason: Shielding primarily changes the team's organizational context and can also alter which demands, priorities, or information reach its work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager personally filters or absorbs pressures, sometimes supported by standing intake, escalation, or communication structures.

temporal.reason: Buffering is typically an ongoing boundary-management function, even though individual interventions occur case by case.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager generally decides what to absorb, delay, translate, block, or pass through at the team's boundary.

time_horizon.reason: Filtering can reduce disruption within days, while sustained shielding may improve focus over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The core action controls how organizational demands and information flow to the team through filtering, delay, translation, or blocking. It also involves exercising decision rights over which pressures reach the team and when.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It alters the team’s informational and social environment by filtering, translating, or delaying external demands before they reach employees.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It removes organizational distractions and pressures that could impede the team’s ability to perform the desired work.

clarifications.for: helping the team understand decisions or priorities through richer background and rationale
changing who can observe work, decisions, challenges, dependencies, or results

observations: New requests from senior leaders reach the team several times a week and interrupt planned work.
Different stakeholders send the team conflicting instructions or priorities.
Team members spend significant meeting time interpreting organizational messages and deciding which requests are real priorities.
Stakeholders regularly bypass the manager and assign work directly to team members.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is excessive or poorly translated organizational pressure reaching the team without enough filtering.

challenges.what_if: What if senior leaders are sending conflicting requests because the organization's strategy has never been translated into clear choices, so each stakeholder is applying a different interpretation? Explore #97, Strategy Deployment / Translation / Cascade.

What if stakeholders bypass the manager because the team lacks enough political backing for others to respect its priorities and operating boundaries? Explore #70, Organizational Advocacy / Coalition Building.

What if the team treats every incoming request as urgent because its risks are highly concentrated and it does not feel able to delay or decline anything consequential? Explore #53, Risk Exposure / Risk Balancing.

categories.description: Changing how time, attention, energy, expertise, availability, and bandwidth are divided across competing demands.

examples.quote: I moved our strongest troubleshooter off routine updates for two weeks and paired her with the team chasing a nasty outage. They found the cause in three days, and the updates still went out a little late but without much fuss.

I blocked every Friday afternoon for the team to clear small customer requests, but the backlog barely moved. It showed me that the real holdup was waiting for answers from our legal team, not a lack of hours on our side.

I gave the launch project nearly all of our meeting time for a month, and I was surprised when two quieter projects started making conflicting decisions without us. I cut the launch check-ins to twice a week and set aside one hour for each of the other project leads.

target.reason: Capacity allocation primarily changes which demands receive effort and priority, while often also changing how work is staffed or organized.

manager_mode.reason: Managers commonly establish allocation mechanisms or staffing arrangements and may also directly reassign work in specific cases.

temporal.reason: Allocation may operate as a standing capacity-management practice or as an episodic response to competing demands.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective balancing often combines managerial authority with team input, although managers may sometimes make allocation decisions unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: Reallocation can change availability and workload within days, with fuller effects on delivery and balance emerging over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: Capacity balancing primarily concerns planning and prioritizing how work and bandwidth are distributed across competing demands; it secondarily involves matching staffing, roles, availability, and expertise to those demands.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Reallocating time, expertise, attention, and bandwidth removes resource constraints and makes priority behaviours more feasible.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Balancing capacity changes the organizational and social conditions under which work occurs, reducing friction and aligning available resources with demands.

clarifications.for: redesigning task scope, assignments, deliverables, or workflow sequencing
managing the pace, disruption, or cumulative saturation of change initiatives
pairing people or resolving friction caused by differing work styles

observations: Some team members regularly work late while others ask for more work.
Several high-priority commitments are assigned to the same person or specialist.
Planned work repeatedly slips because urgent requests consume the available week.
Calendars are filled with meetings, leaving little uninterrupted time for core work.
The team has more active priorities than it can staff at the same time.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is available capacity being spread unevenly or across too many competing demands.

challenges.what_if: What if the overloaded specialists are not an allocation problem but a sign that critical knowledge and responsibilities have no credible backups? Explore #65, Continuity / Redundancy / Succession Design.

What if meeting-heavy calendars and constant interruptions come from unclear channel and response norms that turn routine coordination into synchronous work? Explore #94, Communication Channels / Media / Async Norms.
What if apparent capacity shortages are actually avoidable effort created by slow, fragmented, or unreliable tools? Explore #9, Tooling / Technology Enablement.

categories.description: Changing reporting lines, management layers, organizational units, structural dependencies, and formal authority relationships.

examples.quote: I moved the support team under the product lead they worked with every day. Decisions stopped bouncing between two bosses, and customer fixes started going out faster, though the handoff took a few weeks.

I added a team lead between me and the six supervisors, hoping it would free me up. It only slowed decisions down, but it showed me that the supervisors needed clearer authority, not another boss, so I removed the role.

I split one large group into two separate units so each could focus on its own work. They unexpectedly started guarding people and information from each other, so I kept the split but gave one manager authority over the shared staff and required a weekly joint review.

target.reason: It changes the formal authority, coordination context, and structural dependencies within which work is performed.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or modifies durable organizational structures, roles, and authority rules.

temporal.reason: Structural changes establish ongoing arrangements rather than case-by-case interventions.

locus_of_agency.reason: The responsible manager typically initiates or decides the design, though senior leaders, HR, or other organizational authorities may need to approve or drive it.

time_horizon.reason: Formal changes may take effect quickly, but their operational benefits and lasting organizational consequences usually emerge over months or longer.

domain.reason: Reporting lines, management layers, and formal authority relationships primarily define decision rights and accountability; they secondarily shape roles, staffing arrangements, and team composition.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing reporting lines, units, layers, and authority relationships restructures the social and organizational environment in which behavior occurs.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Clarifying authority, accountability, and structural dependencies can remove coordination barriers and make desired actions easier to carry out.

clarifications.for: changing decision authority without altering reporting relationships
designing routes and triggers for raising issues to higher authority
changing the risks the team is expected or permitted to bear
providing mechanisms to contest decisions or obtain impartial reconsideration

observations: People receive conflicting direction from two managers or organizational units.
Decisions stall because no one is sure who has final authority.
Work repeatedly crosses team boundaries and gets delayed at the same handoffs.
A manager has too many direct reports to hold regular 1:1s or provide timely decisions.
Employees routinely escalate routine issues because their reporting lines do not match how the work gets done.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is formal reporting lines, authority, or organizational boundaries obstructing effective work.

challenges.what_if: What if conflicting direction and repeated handoff friction persist because peer leaders do not trust one another or resolve disagreements directly, regardless of where the reporting lines sit? Explore #34, Peer Relationship Building / Lateral Influence.

What if routine decisions escalate because people lack clear criteria for when they may depart from standard rules, rather than because authority sits in the wrong part of the org chart? Explore #73, Exception Management / Discretionary Overrides.

What if the manager is overloaded because team members habitually route coordination and accountability through them instead of resolving routine commitments with one another? Explore #80, Peer Accountability / Collective Responsibility Culture.

categories.description: Addressing performance or behavioral issues through explicit expectations, confrontation, consequences, warnings, or formal corrective measures.

examples.quote: I pulled him aside and told him the missed handoffs had to stop, then spelled out what I expected each day. He started sending updates before anyone had to chase him, and the next two releases went much more smoothly.

I gave her a written warning after she kept arriving late, but it did not change anything. When we talked again, I learned the start time conflicted with a caregiving problem she had never mentioned, so I finally understood why my warning had missed the real issue.

I told the team lead there would be consequences if he kept snapping at people in meetings. He became so cautious that he barely spoke, so I met with him again and made clear that I wanted disagreement without the personal shots, not silence.

target.reason: Corrective action primarily seeks to change an individual's performance or behavior, often by reinforcing expectations, rules, and consequences.

manager_mode.reason: The manager directly confronts the issue while clearly communicating expectations, warnings, or consequences.

temporal.reason: It is typically initiated case by case when a particular performance or behavioral issue arises.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically addresses the issue with the individual, while retaining unilateral authority to set consequences or initiate formal measures.

time_horizon.reason: Expectations and consequences are communicated immediately, while sustained improvement is usually assessed over the following weeks.

domain.reason: Corrective action is primarily a performance-management practice involving feedback, warnings, consequences, and potentially formal employment measures. It also relies on managerial authority, clear rules, consistent enforcement, and fair procedures.

bcw_functions.name: Coercion
bcw_functions.reason: Warnings, confrontation, and formal consequences create pressure and negative expectancies to discourage unacceptable performance or behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Explicitly clarifying expectations and identifying performance or behavioral gaps increases understanding of what must change.

clarifications.for: changing team membership by hiring, transferring, replacing, or removing people
allocating development opportunities, high-visibility work, promotions, or sponsorship
understanding and addressing why a valued employee may leave before they resign

observations: A team member repeatedly misses agreed deadlines without raising concerns in advance.
The same behavior problem continues after it has been discussed informally.
Colleagues complain that one person is not meeting the standards others are held to.
A team member dismisses or argues about clear feedback rather than changing the behavior.
Work has to be reassigned or redone because one person repeatedly fails to deliver.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is an individual's repeated failure to meet clear performance or behavior expectations and that direct accountability or consequences are now needed.

challenges.what_if: What if the missed deadlines and rework are not defiance, but the result of brittle systems or technical dependencies that affect this person’s work more than others’?
What if the person is responding rationally to a definition of productivity that rewards visible activity or speed over the delivery standard you are trying to enforce?
What if an unaddressed personal constraint or mismatch in the standard working arrangement is making commitments unreliable, and the defensiveness comes from feeling unable to discuss it?

categories.description: Negotiating or changing agreements with other groups about responsibilities, dependencies, commitments, handoffs, and expectations.

examples.quote: I sat down with the support lead and agreed on which customer issues my team would take and what details had to come with them. The back-and-forth dropped, and urgent cases started reaching the right person much faster.

I asked the data team to promise a two-day turnaround on every request, but they couldn't keep it up. When we went through the misses, I learned that some of our requests depended on a finance check I hadn't known about, so we set different timelines for different types of work.

I arranged for engineering to join every product handoff so fewer details would get lost. They started getting pulled into far too many meetings and stopped doing deeper work, so I cut it back to only risky launches and used a written checklist for the rest.

target.reason: Cross-team agreements primarily change responsibilities, relationships, and operating conditions while also shaping handoffs and coordination processes.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes or revises cross-team arrangements through direct negotiation with counterparts.

temporal.reason: Although negotiation is episodic, the resulting responsibilities, commitments, and handoff expectations generally persist.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically represents the team directly, but agreement requires participation and commitment from people outside the team.

time_horizon.reason: Clarified expectations can improve coordination within weeks, while durable effects emerge over months as teams operate under the agreement.

domain.reason: The category centers on coordinating cross-team workflows, dependencies, commitments, and handoffs, while also clarifying responsibility boundaries and mutual decision rights.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It changes the social and organizational environment by redefining roles, handoffs, dependencies, and mutual expectations across teams.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It removes coordination barriers and ambiguity, making reliable cross-team execution easier and more feasible.

clarifications.for: changing the KPIs, outcomes, guardrails, or feedback signals used to assess performance
protecting employee recovery through vacation, leave, breaks, or disconnection policies

observations: Work regularly stalls while the team waits for another group to act.
Two teams give different answers about who owns the same task or decision.
Handoffs arrive late, incomplete, or in a format the receiving team cannot use.
Another group repeatedly changes priorities or commitments without notifying the team.
Cross-team meetings revisit the same disputes about scope, deadlines, or responsibilities.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is unclear, unrealistic, or unenforced agreements between teams about ownership, dependencies, handoffs, or commitments.

challenges.what_if: What if the recurring ownership disputes reflect reporting lines that give both teams legitimate but conflicting mandates, so no agreement between them can hold for long?
What if each team is translating the organization’s strategy into different priorities, making their changing commitments locally reasonable even when they disrupt one another?
What if the late and unusable handoffs are being created by tightly coupled system boundaries that force awkward sequencing and formats, rather than by weak agreements?

categories.description: Changing the types, magnitude, distribution, and consequences of risks the team is expected or permitted to take.

examples.quote: I split one big product bet into three smaller trials and capped what we could spend on each. Two went nowhere, but the third brought in enough new customers to cover the others without putting the whole quarter at stake.

I let a newer team handle a small client launch on their own, and it slipped by a week. That showed me the real trouble was our messy customer data, not their lack of experience, which I would not have seen if I had kept giving launches to the same senior people.

I stopped requiring review for very small production fixes so people could move faster. I did not expect folks to split larger changes into tiny pieces to avoid review, so I added a limit on the total change and checked the first few batches myself.

target.reason: The action primarily changes the rules, constraints, and consequences surrounding risk-taking while potentially shifting which opportunities the team pursues.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes risk boundaries, safeguards, and accountability structures while communicating the desired risk appetite.

temporal.reason: Risk balancing can involve standing guardrails or case-by-case adjustments for particular initiatives.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically holds authority for acceptable risk levels but may involve the team in identifying, assessing, and distributing risks.

time_horizon.reason: New risk boundaries can influence decisions within weeks, while their full effects on outcomes and resilience often emerge over months.

domain.reason: Risk appetite and permission define decision boundaries, mandates, and accountability; balancing the type, scale, and distribution of risk also shapes how work is planned and delivered.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Setting which risks are permitted and limiting their type or magnitude constrains competing or excessively risky behaviours.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redistributing risk and altering its consequences changes the organizational conditions in which team decisions are made.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Reducing or sharing downside exposure can remove barriers that prevent team members from taking appropriate risks.

clarifications.for: deciding who may authorize, influence, or veto risk-related choices
setting triggers and response paths for escalating emerging risks
reorganizing reporting lines or units to address structural dependencies
allowing people to appeal risk decisions or challenge unfair consequences

observations: The team avoids reversible experiments because members fear being blamed if they fail.
Several critical projects depend on the same person, system, vendor, or deadline.
The team repeatedly makes large commitments before testing key assumptions.
Small failures regularly create outsized customer, financial, or operational consequences.
People disagree in planning meetings about what level of risk they are allowed to take.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team's risks are too concentrated, too consequential, or poorly matched to its authority and tolerance for failure.

challenges.what_if: What if people avoid experiments because past mistakes were blamed, hidden, or handled inconsistently, rather than because the permitted level of risk is unclear?
What if large commitments and reluctance to test assumptions are rational responses to incentives that reward ambitious promises and punish visible failures?
What if small failures have outsized consequences because the underlying systems have fragile dependencies and a large blast radius, not because the team is choosing the wrong risks?

categories.description: Changing how individuals enter, integrate into, and move within the team, including knowledge transfer.

examples.quote: I paired our new designer with one teammate for her first two weeks and gave them a short list of people and projects to cover. She was contributing in the second week instead of spending a month figuring out who knew what.

I moved an engineer onto the billing work and had him shadow the person leaving for three days. It wasn’t enough, and he got stuck almost immediately, but that showed us the old setup depended on a bunch of steps nobody had written down.

I started having every new hire sit in on all our team meetings for their first month. They got overwhelmed and stopped asking questions, so I cut it back to the two meetings tied to their work and added the others gradually.
