target.reason: The action changes the processes for joining, integrating, transferring knowledge, and transitioning while also shaping relationships and working conditions.

manager_mode.reason: Managers typically establish onboarding and transition processes while also providing direct guidance and coordination in individual cases.

temporal.reason: Onboarding and transition practices are usually maintained as repeatable systems for successive personnel changes.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager usually coordinates with the transitioning individual while involving teammates in support, relationship building, and knowledge transfer.

time_horizon.reason: Initial integration effects emerge within weeks, while full effectiveness, relationships, and knowledge transfer often take months.

domain.reason: Onboarding and internal transitions primarily concern how people enter, change roles, and integrate into the team; knowledge transfer and ramp-up make capability development the next most relevant domain.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Structured onboarding and transition support removes practical and social barriers that could prevent individuals from functioning effectively in a new role or team.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Knowledge transfer increases individuals’ understanding of their responsibilities, team practices, and organizational context.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing entry, integration, and internal-movement processes reshapes the social and organizational environment around the individual.

clarifications.for: redesigning a role's ongoing responsibilities and formal expectations
deciding who or what formally constitutes the team or workgroup
introducing prizes, awards, competitions, or special recognition beyond normal compensation

clarifications.category: Hiring Process / Hiring Role Definition / Interview Design
clarifications.for: designing how candidates are recruited, interviewed, evaluated, and selected

observations: New hires repeatedly ask where basic information, tools, or decisions can be found.
People joining the team wait days or weeks for access, context, or meaningful work.
Different new team members receive inconsistent explanations of their role and priorities.
Work is disrupted when someone changes roles or leaves because key knowledge was not transferred.
Recently transferred employees continue using processes or assumptions from their former teams.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is an inconsistent or incomplete transition process that leaves people without the access, context, relationships, or knowledge needed to contribute.

challenges.what_if: What if new people wait for access, context, and useful work because experienced team members have no capacity to support them, not because the transition process itself is missing?
What if new hires receive inconsistent explanations because responsibilities and authority are genuinely unresolved for the whole team, rather than poorly explained during onboarding?
What if newcomers are simply exposing that basic information, decisions, and dependencies are invisible to anyone who was not already in the room?

categories.description: Changing who receives development opportunities, stretch assignments, visibility, promotions, and career-enhancing support.

examples.quote: I gave the next big client presentation to Maya instead of the usual senior lead, and I coached her through the prep. She handled the tough questions well, and afterward two directors asked to involve her in their projects.

I put Devon in charge of a rushed product launch because I thought it would help him grow, but he struggled and the launch slipped. It showed me he needed experience managing smaller deadlines first, which I would not have learned from his regular work.

I started rotating people into meetings with senior leaders so more of the team could be seen. Some people suddenly spent hours polishing slides and competing for airtime, so I limited the rotation to one meeting a month and set clearer roles.

target.reason: The action changes access to career-enhancing conditions and relationships while also affecting who receives particular assignments and responsibilities.

manager_mode.reason: Managers directly allocate assignments, advocate for promotions, and provide visibility, and may also establish processes for distributing these opportunities.

temporal.reason: A manager may make case-by-case sponsorship decisions or maintain an ongoing system for equitable opportunity distribution.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager often controls allocation and advocacy decisions, though effective career support may be shaped collaboratively with the individual.

time_horizon.reason: Development and visibility gains often emerge over months, while promotion and broader career effects may take quarters or years.

domain.reason: This category centers on career advancement, promotions, stretch roles, and sponsorship, while also addressing how managers allocate access to these opportunities and ensure fair distribution.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Providing sponsorship, stretch assignments, and advancement opportunities removes access barriers and makes career development more achievable.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing how opportunities, visibility, and promotions are allocated alters the organizational and social conditions shaping advancement.

bcw_functions.name: Incentivisation
bcw_functions.reason: Promotions, recognition, and career-enhancing opportunities can act as positive consequences that reinforce valued behavior and performance.

clarifications.for: changing the team’s membership or staffing mix through hiring, transfers, replacement, or removal
correcting an individual’s performance or behavior through explicit expectations, warnings, or consequences
actively retaining specific employees by identifying flight risks and responding to what would keep them

observations: The same few people repeatedly receive high-visibility assignments or leadership opportunities.
Some team members say they learn about stretch assignments only after someone has been selected.
Promotion-ready work is distributed through informal invitations rather than an open process.
Certain employees regularly present to senior leaders while others doing comparable work remain unseen.
Development goals discussed in 1:1s are not followed by relevant assignments, introductions, or advocacy.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that career-building opportunities, visibility, and sponsorship are being distributed unevenly or through processes that overlook qualified people.

challenges.what_if: What if the same people keep getting opportunities because the manager’s information channels repeatedly surface their readiness and interests while leaving other qualified people out of view?
What if less-visible employees are already carrying essential work that cannot easily be dropped, so stretch assignments keep going to whoever appears to have available capacity?
What if the team’s definition of valuable performance favors presentations and visible individual ownership, while comparable enabling or collective work is not counted?

categories.description: Changing what the team agrees to take on, declines, promises, or renegotiates with stakeholders and other groups.

examples.quote: I told the sales lead we couldn't squeeze in two late customer requests without dropping something else. They picked the one that mattered most, and we delivered it on time without another weekend push.
I tried to move a deadline by two weeks, but the client wouldn't budge. That showed me their launch was tied to a contract date nobody had mentioned, so we cut two less important pieces instead.

I started rejecting any request that hadn't come through our monthly planning meeting. People got so cautious that they held back a couple of real emergencies, so I added a simple urgent path and reviewed those requests myself.

target.reason: The action changes the work the team commits to while also reshaping expectations and agreements with stakeholders.

manager_mode.reason: Managers directly accept, decline, or renegotiate requests and may also establish rules for handling future demand.

temporal.reason: Demand can be managed through standing intake and prioritization systems or through case-by-case negotiations.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager commonly represents the team in commitment decisions, sometimes involving the team to assess capacity and tradeoffs.

time_horizon.reason: Accepting, declining, or renegotiating work can alter workload immediately, with planning and delivery effects unfolding over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: Managing incoming demand and renegotiating commitments directly shapes workload, priorities, capacity, and delivery plans, while also defining who can accept, decline, or alter promises to stakeholders.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Declining or narrowing external commitments limits competing demands and reduces work that can displace priority behaviours.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Renegotiating promises and workload removes capacity and coordination barriers that prevent the team from carrying out priority work.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing agreements with stakeholders reshapes the team's social and organisational environment, including expectations, deadlines, and dependencies.

clarifications.for: directly resolving an impediment instead of renegotiating the team's commitments
reprioritizing collective objectives or reframing how meaningful progress is measured

observations: The team repeatedly misses dates promised to stakeholders.
New requests are accepted without anyone identifying what will be delayed or dropped.
Team members work late or switch priorities frequently to meet external commitments.
Stakeholders cite different expectations about what the team agreed to deliver.
Previously accepted work is quietly postponed rather than explicitly renegotiated.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team is accepting or maintaining more external commitments than it can reliably fulfill.

challenges.what_if: What if the missed dates, late work, and constant reprioritization are caused by critical work depending on one or two people, rather than by too many commitments overall?
What if stakeholders disagree about what was promised because the team and its partners use key terms like “done,” “priority,” or “delivery” differently?
What if the team keeps accepting requests because organizational pressure reaches them unfiltered and they do not feel protected when they push back?

categories.description: Introducing whole management philosophies and named schools of thought from other organizations, such as Lean, Agile, or sociocracy, as overall approaches to managing.

examples.quote: I brought Lean into our warehouse and had the supervisors use it for the whole daily routine, not just one project. After a rough first month, picking errors dropped and the team started fixing small problems without waiting for me.

I tried running the design group on Agile because it had worked well at another company. It never really took hold, but it showed me that our biggest problem was not how we planned the work; it was that two directors kept changing the brief.

I introduced sociocracy across our nonprofit so decisions would not all land on me. People unexpectedly started forming circles for every minor issue, and meetings multiplied fast. I limited the approach to major policy decisions and put routine calls back with the team leads.

target.reason: Management philosophies primarily reshape how work is organized and performed while also changing decision rules, roles, and relationships.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes a new operating system of practices and structures while communicating commitment to its principles.

temporal.reason: Named management approaches are generally intended to become ongoing systems rather than isolated interventions.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager may initiate the philosophy, but effective implementation normally requires the team to interpret and enact it together.

time_horizon.reason: New practices can affect operations within months, while deeper cultural and structural effects often take quarters or years.

domain.reason: Importing named management schools primarily introduces new frameworks and methods for managing; secondarily, these philosophies reshape shared values, expectations, and ways of working.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Adopting a management philosophy typically changes organizational routines, roles, decision processes, and social norms to support new behaviours.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Introducing the philosophy increases employees’ and managers’ understanding of its principles, rationale, and expected practices.

bcw_functions.name: Training
bcw_functions.reason: Implementation often builds procedural know-how in the philosophy’s specific methods, such as Agile ceremonies or Lean improvement techniques.

clarifications.for: choosing or mandating specific tools for decision making, prioritization, or problem solving

clarifications.category: Mentorship Design / Buddy Systems / Peer Guidance
clarifications.for: designing mentorship, buddy, peer-guidance, or reverse-mentoring arrangements

observations: Teams use different routines and rules for planning, decisions, and improvement.
The same workflow problems recur despite isolated process changes.
Managers repeatedly debate how work should be organized without reaching a shared approach.
Employees explicitly ask to adopt practices such as Agile, Lean, or sociocracy.
Process changes are introduced as disconnected techniques and then fade away.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is the absence of a coherent management approach that people can apply consistently across recurring situations.

challenges.what_if: What if new practices fade because the team is already absorbing too many changes, not because it lacks a coherent management philosophy?
What if teams keep reverting to different routines because current metrics and rewards reinforce the old behaviors, regardless of which management approach is introduced?
What if recurring problems and disconnected experiments reflect a failure to capture and transfer what teams have already learned?

categories.description: Setting the standing balance between developing and promoting existing employees and recruiting talent externally.

examples.quote: I started filling most supervisor openings from the team while still looking outside for skills we didn’t have. People saw a real path upward, and the outside hires brought in a few useful new ideas.

I tried giving every open role to someone already here before advertising it. A couple of people struggled badly, and it showed me we hadn’t prepared anyone for the more technical jobs, so now I know where training has to start.

We hired several experienced people from outside at once, and I didn’t expect the existing team to take it as a sign they had no future here. Two good people started looking elsewhere, so I paused the remaining searches and set aside the next few openings for people already on the team.

target.reason: The action changes the staffing and advancement system around the work, with secondary effects on employee development and career progression.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes an ongoing approach or policy for filling roles through promotion and external recruitment.

temporal.reason: The category explicitly concerns a continuing balance that guides staffing decisions over time.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically sets or advocates the balance, often subject to input or constraints from HR and organizational leadership outside the team.

time_horizon.reason: The balance affects hiring and promotion outcomes over months and shapes the organization's talent pipeline over quarters or years.

domain.reason: The category centers on staffing, career mobility, promotion, and external recruitment, while also involving the development of internal employees to build a promotion pipeline.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It shapes the organizational and social environment by determining whether roles are filled through internal career pathways or external talent inflows.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It makes effective performance easier by ensuring needed capabilities are available through employee development and promotion or external recruitment.

bcw_functions.name: Incentivisation
bcw_functions.reason: A meaningful emphasis on internal promotion provides career advancement as a positive consequence for employee performance and development.

clarifications.for: redesigning performance reviews, feedback cycles, documentation, or calibration practices
deciding whether work should be performed by employees or by contractors, vendors, partners, or temporary staff
creating backups, reducing key-person dependencies, and preparing successors for critical roles
defining career levels, advancement paths, and promotion criteria

observations: Open roles remain unfilled while existing employees ask about advancement opportunities.
Promotions repeatedly go to external hires rather than current employees.
Managers report having no internal candidates ready for key roles.
New external hires regularly struggle to learn the organization or leave soon after joining.
Employees cite limited career paths or promotion prospects in 1:1s and exit interviews.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the current balance between developing internal talent and hiring externally does not meet the organization’s capability and career needs.

challenges.what_if: What if internal candidates appear unready because organizational boundaries hide their experience and make cross-unit advancement difficult, rather than because the promotion-versus-hiring balance is wrong?
What if external hires struggle because essential organizational knowledge is undocumented and held informally by long-tenured employees?
What if roles remain open and employees see little reason to pursue them because the compensation or material rewards do not match the demands of the jobs?

categories.description: Changing or locally adapting how individual performance is reviewed, discussed, documented, calibrated, and managed over time.

examples.quote: I replaced the yearly review with short monthly check-ins and kept a running note of what we agreed. People fixed small problems sooner, and the year-end conversations had fewer surprises.

I tried using the same rating guide across two very different roles, and the scores still felt inconsistent. It showed me that we needed concrete examples for each role, which I wouldn’t have known from the ratings alone.

I asked everyone to gather peer comments before each review, and some people came back with pages of conflicting feedback. I limited it to three coworkers and asked for one specific example from each, which made it manageable again.

target.reason: The action changes the evaluative rules and conditions surrounding work, as well as the processes used to review and manage performance.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or adapts a recurring structure for reviewing, documenting, calibrating, and managing performance.

temporal.reason: The design establishes an ongoing process used across repeated review and performance-management cycles.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager commonly owns local system adaptations, though team input may inform how the process is designed and implemented.

time_horizon.reason: Process changes may be noticed within weeks, but their main effects emerge over several review and performance-management cycles.

domain.reason: Performance review systems primarily concern employee evaluation and talent management; their design also establishes decision rules, documentation standards, calibration, and fairness.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redesigning review workflows, documentation, discussion routines, and calibration processes changes the organizational environment and cues that shape how performance is managed.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Adapting the system can remove procedural and coordination barriers, making consistent feedback, tracking, and follow-up easier for managers and employees.

clarifications.for: setting the overall balance between promoting current employees and hiring new employees externally
shifting capabilities or activities between internal teams and external providers
building role coverage, knowledge redundancy, and succession plans
designing career ladders, level definitions, or eligibility standards for promotion

observations: Employees receive performance feedback only during formal review periods.
People are surprised by ratings or performance decisions.
Different managers use visibly different standards for similar work.
Review documents are late, incomplete, or treated as a paperwork exercise.
Calibration meetings reveal large disagreements about what ratings mean.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the current review system does not produce timely, consistent, well-supported performance judgments and conversations.

challenges.what_if: What if managers disagree on ratings because there is no shared definition of acceptable quality for the work, rather than because the review process itself is flawed?
What if feedback arrives only at review time because managers lack the skill or confidence to hold timely performance conversations?
What if ratings are surprising and poorly supported because employees’ work and contributions are not visible to the people evaluating them?

aliases: Keeping a Pulse on the Team
categories.description: Changing how the manager observes work, gathers information, solicits feedback, investigates patterns, and understands team dynamics.

examples.quote: I sat in on three shift handoffs instead of relying on the weekly report. I spotted where details kept getting lost, and the missed follow-ups dropped once we started checking that point.

I sent a short anonymous survey about why our meetings dragged, but hardly anyone filled it out. When I asked people one-on-one, I learned they did not trust that the survey was truly anonymous, which I would not have known otherwise.
I started asking for feedback after every client call, and people began picking apart every tiny mistake. I cut it back to a weekly review and asked them to bring only issues they saw more than once.

target.reason: The action changes the methods used to observe and understand work while also shaping feedback and information flows around the team.

manager_mode.reason: The manager designs channels and routines for sensing while also personally observing, asking questions, and investigating patterns.

temporal.reason: Organizational sensing is typically most useful as an ongoing practice or feedback system rather than a single inquiry.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically chooses and operates the inquiry approach, though effective feedback gathering often requires team participation.

time_horizon.reason: New information can emerge within weeks, while reliable understanding of recurring patterns and dynamics often develops over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on the manager’s own practices for observing, investigating, learning, and diagnosing team dynamics. Its secondary focus is designing feedback and information-gathering channels that improve what becomes visible to the manager.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Systematic observation, inquiry, and feedback increase the manager’s knowledge and understanding of work patterns and team dynamics.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redesigning feedback channels and information-gathering routines changes the social and organizational environment so relevant signals are easier to detect.

clarifications.for: setting an example through your everyday behavior and personal habits
intentionally declining to rescue or stabilize a situation so learning can occur

clarifications.category: Managerial Deep Dives / Direct Engagement with Details
clarifications.for: personally working through the detailed substance of a particular task or problem
changing access to your attention, support, advice, or approvals

observations: The manager first learns about problems after a deadline is missed or someone escalates.
Team surveys, 1:1s, and project reports give conflicting pictures of how work is going.
The same few people provide most of the feedback in meetings and retrospectives.
Team members say they raised an issue earlier, but the manager has no record or recollection of it.
The manager cannot answer basic questions about where work is getting stuck without asking for a new report.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the manager’s current information channels are too narrow, delayed, or unreliable to reveal important patterns in the team.

challenges.what_if: What if people see problems early but do not believe there is a safe or credible way to raise them, so issues surface only after failure or escalation?
What if issues reach the manager late because people cannot get their attention or decisions when needed, rather than because the manager lacks information channels?
What if surveys, reports, and conversations conflict because people use the same words to mean different things and are therefore reporting against different definitions?

categories.description: Defining or changing the team's purpose, remit, responsibilities, boundaries, and reason for existing.

examples.quote: I wrote down the three problems our team was responsible for and, just as importantly, what belonged elsewhere. People stopped picking up every stray request, and we finally finished the backlog we had promised to clear.

I tried giving our group ownership of customer onboarding from start to finish, but the handoffs got worse because we did not control billing setup. It failed, but it showed me that our responsibility could not be wider than the decisions we were actually allowed to make.

I told the team they could say no to any work outside our main purpose, and they started rejecting even small requests that would have prevented trouble for other teams. I narrowed the rule, set a few exceptions, and asked them to check with me before turning down anything urgent.

target.reason: A team charter primarily defines what the team exists to accomplish while also setting contextual boundaries, responsibilities, and interfaces.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes a durable framework for the team's purpose and scope and communicates the resulting direction to stakeholders.

temporal.reason: The charter serves as an ongoing reference for the team's purpose, responsibilities, and boundaries.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective charters are often developed with team input, although the manager may retain authority to define or approve the final mandate.

time_horizon.reason: The charter can improve clarity within weeks, while its larger effects on coordination, ownership, and performance usually emerge over months.

domain.reason: A team charter establishes the team’s formal mandate, scope, responsibilities, and decision boundaries, while also shaping what work the team owns and delivers.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Formalizing the team's purpose, roles, and remit changes the organizational and social structure that guides behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Clear responsibilities and boundaries reduce role ambiguity and coordination barriers, making effective team action easier.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Defining the team's remit and boundaries limits out-of-scope activities and competing behaviors.

clarifications.for: improving the systems used to address conflicts, tensions, and recurring problems
changing team autonomy, decision rights, or participation in designing operating practices
establishing the approval process or business case needed to fund capacity and hiring

observations: Team members give different answers when asked what the team owns.
The team repeatedly takes on work that falls outside its stated responsibilities.
Requests bounce between this team and other teams because ownership is unclear.
Planning meetings include recurring debates about which goals should take priority.
Some expected work is left undone because each group assumes another group owns it.
categories.assumption: The team's purpose, responsibilities, or boundaries are unclear or no longer fit what the organization needs.

challenges.what_if: What if the team keeps taking on out-of-scope work because external commitments are being accepted faster than they can be evaluated or refused, not because the mandate is unclear? Explore whether demand is being controlled at the point of intake.
What if teams argue over ownership because their performance measures reward visible local output and make shared or less visible work unattractive?
What if the recurring priority debates reflect an organizational strategy that has never been translated into concrete choices for this team, rather than a poorly defined charter?

categories.description: Changing what constitutes quality and the behaviors, practices, reviews, and feedback mechanisms that reinforce it.

examples.quote: I started requiring a second person to check every customer report before it went out. We caught a lot of small errors, and within a month the complaints dropped noticeably.

I gave the team a checklist for finished work, but the same mistakes kept showing up. It revealed that people understood “accurate” in very different ways, so I knew we needed real examples instead of another list.

I began reviewing every piece of work in detail, and people got so cautious that deadlines started slipping. I hadn’t expected that, so I limited the deep reviews to higher-risk work and used quick spot checks for the rest.

target.reason: The action primarily changes practices, reviews, and feedback processes while also redefining the quality outcomes the team should pursue.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes mechanisms that produce and assess quality while repeatedly communicating and modeling the expected standard.

temporal.reason: Standards and their reinforcement mechanisms generally operate as ongoing expectations and practices.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective quality standards are often developed and reinforced with the team, although managers may sometimes set them unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: New expectations can affect reviews within weeks, but consistent quality improvement usually emerges over months.

domain.reason: Quality standards directly shape how work is performed, reviewed, and improved, while reinforcement mechanisms establish shared expectations and norms around what good work looks like.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing standards, review practices, and feedback mechanisms restructures the work environment so that quality is consistently prompted and reinforced.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Defining what constitutes quality increases employees’ understanding of expected outcomes and behaviors.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Providing structured reviews and feedback helps employees identify and overcome gaps that prevent them from meeting quality expectations.

clarifications.for: designing or simplifying the workflow through which work moves
adopting or retiring a professional practice not specifically focused on quality
changing the timing, frequency, duration, or synchronization of activities
redefining productivity or deciding how individual and team productivity should be measured
changing estimation, forecasting, planning horizons, or commitment methods

observations: Work is frequently returned for corrections after it has been marked complete.
Team members apply different standards to similar pieces of work.
Reviews catch the same types of errors repeatedly.
People disagree in meetings about what 'good enough' means.
Deadlines are met, but customers or downstream teams regularly report defects or rework.
categories.assumption: The team lacks a shared, consistently reinforced definition of acceptable quality.

challenges.what_if: What if people broadly agree on quality, but the pace and deadline pressure cause them to knowingly ship work before it meets that standard?
What if the repeated defects come from tools that make errors easy to introduce and difficult to detect, rather than inconsistent ideas about what good work looks like?
What if the variation in completed work is concentrated among people who never received the context, examples, or access they needed when joining or changing roles?

categories.description: Changing pay, bonuses, equity, financial rewards, and other material benefits, including how they are determined and distributed.

examples.quote: I added a small bonus for weekend coverage because the same two people kept getting stuck with it. More people volunteered, and the schedule stopped being a weekly fight.

I offered gift cards for closing the most support tickets, but people rushed easy cases and left the hard ones sitting. It showed me that rewarding the raw count pushed the wrong behavior, which I would not have seen from our usual reports.

I gave a few key people extra equity, and word spread faster than I expected. Everyone started asking what they were worth, so I paused the grants and explained the criteria before making any more offers.

target.reason: Compensation changes the material conditions surrounding work and can secondarily affect individual motivation and retention.

manager_mode.reason: Managers primarily establish or modify reward structures and criteria, while also making specific compensation or bonus decisions.

temporal.reason: Compensation can involve standing salary and incentive systems or episodic awards, bonuses, and adjustments.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers often initiate or allocate rewards, but HR, senior leadership, compensation committees, or market constraints commonly shape and approve them.

time_horizon.reason: Compensation changes are noticed as soon as they are announced or paid, with motivational and retention effects often emerging over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: Compensation, bonuses, equity, and benefits are core people-management mechanisms, while the rules, decision rights, and fairness governing how rewards are determined and distributed are a governance concern.

bcw_functions.name: Incentivisation
bcw_functions.reason: Pay, bonuses, equity, and material benefits create positive consequences that reinforce and motivate desired behaviours.

clarifications.for: changing who collaborates on a specific project without altering permanent team membership
personalizing responsibilities, expectations, schedules, or support for an individual

observations: Employees ask how bonuses, raises, or equity decisions are made.
People receive the same financial rewards despite visibly different results or responsibilities.
High-value work is repeatedly avoided while rewarded activities receive attention.
Candidates or employees cite pay or benefits when declining offers or leaving.
Team members compare compensation and point out unexplained differences.
categories.assumption: Current pay or material rewards are insufficient, perceived as unfair, or encouraging the wrong behaviors.

challenges.what_if: What if people are leaving over an unsustainable workload or lack of recovery time, but cite compensation because it is easier and safer to discuss?
What if people favor low-value activities because those are what the organization measures and labels as productive, regardless of how bonuses are structured?
What if compensation comparisons are a proxy for a broader concern that visible assignments, sponsorship, and career-building opportunities are distributed unevenly?

categories.description: Changing which capabilities and activities are performed internally versus through contractors, vendors, consultants, partners, or temporary staff.

examples.quote: I hired a freelance designer to redo our mobile checkout instead of squeezing it into the product team’s week. Sales picked up, and the team only had to fix a few small things after launch.

I paid a consultant to interview our oldest customers, but most of them gave short, guarded answers. It showed me they would only speak openly with people they already knew, which I would not have learned from our usual surveys.

I brought in six temporary support agents to clear the ticket backlog, and they closed cases so fast that repeat complaints jumped. I cut the group to three and had our own agents review their replies until things settled down.

target.reason: External sourcing changes the team's staffing, resource, and partnership context while also altering how activities are delivered.

manager_mode.reason: The manager redesigns sourcing and delivery arrangements and may directly select, contract with, or onboard external providers.

temporal.reason: External sourcing may establish a standing delivery model or provide temporary, case-specific staff augmentation.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically initiates and governs the sourcing choice, while outside providers participate in defining and delivering the arrangement.

time_horizon.reason: Establishing an effective external arrangement often takes months, although temporary staff augmentation can add capacity within weeks.

domain.reason: This primarily changes staffing and workforce composition by using contractors, consultants, vendors, or temporary personnel. It secondarily concerns relationships with external partners that supply capabilities or perform activities.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It changes the organizational and social environment by introducing external people, expertise, and delivery arrangements.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It removes internal capacity or capability barriers by providing access to skills, resources, and labor needed to perform the work.

clarifications.for: balancing internal promotions against external recruitment into employee roles
changing how employee performance is reviewed, discussed, documented, or calibrated
protecting continuity through backups, cross-training, distributed knowledge, or designated successors
establishing employee career levels, advancement paths, and promotion criteria

observations: Important work remains in the backlog because the team lacks available capacity or a needed specialty.
The team spends substantial time learning a capability required only for a short-term project.
A vendor repeatedly misses agreed deadlines or delivers work that needs extensive correction.
Internal employees are doing routine work that an external provider could handle while higher-priority work waits.
Demand rises and falls sharply, leaving the team overloaded in some periods and underused in others.
categories.assumption: The current division of work between internal staff and external providers does not provide the right capacity, expertise, flexibility, or quality.

challenges.what_if: What if the backlog reflects too many commitments being accepted, meaning added external capacity would simply allow demand to keep expanding?
What if the need for scarce specialists and repeated vendor corrections is being created by an overly complex or tightly coupled technical system?
What if the swings between overload and underuse come from weak forecasting and unrealistic commitments rather than the internal-versus-external staffing mix?

categories.description: Reducing single points of failure, developing backups, distributing knowledge, building redundancy, and preparing successors.

examples.quote: I had our only billing expert train two teammates and write down the month-end steps. When she got sick during close, the others finished the run with only a few minor errors.

I asked a senior engineer to hand off one of his systems before he left, but the new owner still got stuck in the first outage. That showed me the notes covered normal work but not the odd fixes he carried in his head.

I started rotating people through customer support so more of us could cover it, but too many new faces made replies slower and customers had to repeat themselves. I cut the rotation to one person at a time and paired each newcomer with someone experienced.

target.reason: The action changes staffing resilience, knowledge access, and succession conditions while also shaping how work and expertise are shared.

manager_mode.reason: The manager primarily creates structures for coverage, knowledge distribution, and succession, while sometimes directly coaching or cross-training people.

temporal.reason: Effective redundancy and succession require ongoing structures and practices rather than a single intervention.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically coordinates team-wide coverage while working individually with backups, experts, and potential successors.

time_horizon.reason: Cross-training and redundancy usually take months to become effective, while successor development may require quarters or years.

domain.reason: Succession planning and backup coverage center on staffing continuity and preparing people for critical roles, while distributing knowledge and developing successors requires deliberate skill and knowledge development.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Redesigns roles, knowledge flows, and staffing arrangements so work does not depend on a single person.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Removes continuity barriers by ensuring backup capacity, access to knowledge, and available successors.

bcw_functions.name: Training
bcw_functions.reason: Builds the skills and procedural know-how needed for backups and successors to perform critical responsibilities.

clarifications.for: setting a general policy on developing and promoting employees versus recruiting externally
redesigning recurring performance reviews, feedback discussions, ratings, or calibration
deciding to use contractors, vendors, consultants, partners, or temporary staff instead of internal capacity
defining organization-wide career ladders, job levels, and advancement requirements

observations: Work stops when one particular person is absent.
Only one team member knows how to operate a critical system or complete a key process.
Important procedures or decisions exist only in one person's notes or memory.
No one can name who would take over a key role if its current owner left.
The same person is always pulled into incidents, approvals, or customer escalations.
categories.assumption: Critical work depends too heavily on specific individuals, without adequate backups, shared knowledge, or prepared successors.

challenges.what_if: What if work stops because only one person has formal approval authority, not because others lack the knowledge to take over?
What if the same expert is always pulled in because escalation rules automatically route every difficult issue to them instead of directing issues by type and severity?
What if the dependency persists because the expert repeatedly rescues the work, preventing others from experiencing responsibility, consequences, and learning?

categories.description: Adapting responsibilities, expectations, working conditions, schedules, or support to accommodate individuals' needs, strengths, and constraints.

examples.quote: I shifted one developer’s start time later because mornings were difficult for him. He stopped missing check-ins, and his work became more consistent, even though we still had to catch him up now and then.

I took client calls off Maya’s plate because she said they were draining her, but the replacement work left her just as frustrated. It showed me the real problem was handling angry clients without backup, not the calls themselves.

I let one of our strongest people focus only on the complex jobs she was good at, and everyone else started sending her anything remotely difficult. She got swamped within two weeks, so I narrowed what counted as a complex job and rotated some of it back through the team.

target.reason: The action primarily changes working conditions, schedules, expectations, and support, while sometimes also adjusting responsibilities or task content.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes a personalized working arrangement and may also directly adjust assignments, schedules, or support.

temporal.reason: An accommodation may be an ongoing arrangement or a temporary, case-specific adjustment.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective personalized arrangements are typically negotiated collaboratively between the manager and the affected individual.

time_horizon.reason: Adjusted conditions can affect the individual within days, while their fuller impact on performance and sustainability may emerge over months.

domain.reason: Personalized arrangements center on fitting roles, expectations, and support to an individual’s needs and retention, while also changing how their tasks, schedules, workload, and working conditions are designed.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Personalized adjustments remove individual barriers and provide tailored support that makes effective performance possible or easier.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing schedules, responsibilities, expectations, or working conditions modifies the social and organizational environment to support the desired behavior.

clarifications.for: reconfiguring project collaborators rather than accommodating a particular individual
changing compensation, financial incentives, equity, or material benefits

observations: A team member repeatedly misses scheduled meetings because of a documented schedule constraint.
One person consistently struggles with a responsibility that does not use their strengths, while performing strongly in other work.
A team member asks more than once for different hours, equipment, workload, or communication methods.
The same working condition causes one individual to miss deadlines or require frequent last-minute adjustments.
A person raises a health, accessibility, caregiving, location, or personal constraint in a 1:1.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is a mismatch between the standard working arrangement and an individual's specific needs, strengths, or constraints.

challenges.what_if: What if this person’s constraint is exposing an overreliance on synchronous meetings and urgent communication, rather than a need for a one-off arrangement? Explore #94, Communication Channels / Media / Async Norms.

What if the responsibility is difficult because essential know-how is undocumented or held by a few insiders, making one person look poorly matched while others compensate from experience? Explore #77, Knowledge Stewardship / Institutional Memory.

What if the repeated last-minute adjustments come from plans that ignore real capacity and uncertainty, with this individual’s visible constraint simply revealing the flaw? Explore #99, Planning / Forecasting / Commitment Practices.

categories.description: Changing how funding is obtained, investments and new hires are justified, and the evidence, timing, or approvals required to secure capacity.

examples.quote: I asked for two new hires using a short breakdown of missed deadlines and customer demand instead of a long headcount pitch. My boss approved one role right away, and that was enough to clear most of the backlog within two months.

I tried to get budget for a new testing tool by showing how many hours it could save us, but the request was turned down. The review made it clear that finance cared more about reducing release failures than saving time, which I would not have known without putting the numbers in front of them.

I let team leads submit small purchase requests without waiting for my approval, and spending jumped faster than I expected because several people bought overlapping tools. I paused new requests, set a lower limit, and added a quick check for anything we might already own.

target.reason: The action changes the funding, approval, and capacity conditions surrounding the team as well as the process used to justify investments.

manager_mode.reason: The manager primarily changes authorization structures and evidence requirements, while also potentially preparing and pursuing specific requests.

temporal.reason: The category concerns changing the recurring system by which capacity requests are justified and authorized.

locus_of_agency.reason: Organizational stakeholders outside the team usually control final authorization, although the manager shapes and advances the request.

time_horizon.reason: Approval changes may be noticed within weeks, but funded investments and added capacity usually materialize over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on approval rights, authorization criteria, and rules for allocating funding. Its secondary impact is on delivery capacity, planning, and the timing of resources needed to execute work.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Authorizing funding, investments, or hires provides the capacity and resources needed for teams to perform the target behaviour.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing evidence, timing, and approval processes alters the organizational environment through which resources are secured.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Requiring specific justifications or approvals limits which investments and staffing actions can proceed.

clarifications.for: redesigning how interpersonal or operational conflicts are reported, mediated, and resolved
expanding team self-management or involving members in co-designing how work is organized
defining or revising the team’s purpose, remit, responsibilities, and boundaries

observations: Hiring or purchasing requests sit unapproved while the team continues operating below planned capacity.
Funding proposals are repeatedly returned with requests for different evidence, estimates, or business justification.
The team delays committed work because it cannot secure budget, headcount, or tools in time.
Managers spend multiple planning cycles rebuilding the same investment case for different approvers.
Approvers say they support the work but will not release resources under the current process or timing.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is the way capacity investments are justified, timed, funded, or approved rather than the team's ability to use those resources.

challenges.what_if: What if funding keeps stalling because the request is not clearly tied to the organization’s strategic choices, so approvers cannot tell what should take priority? Explore #97, Strategy Deployment / Translation / Cascade.

What if the apparent resource shortage is actually the result of accepting too many commitments, and approvers are reluctant to fund a pattern of chronic overextension? Explore #56, Demand Management / External Commitments.

What if proposals keep coming back because the organization’s measures cannot credibly show the expected value or whether added capacity would improve outcomes? Explore #15, Measurement / Performance Systems.

categories.description: Changing technical architecture, system boundaries, dependencies, and underlying capabilities to enable different ways of working.

examples.quote: I split the billing code out of our main app so that team could release without waiting on everyone else. After a rough first month, they went from shipping every few weeks to shipping small fixes twice a week.

I tried replacing our shared database with separate ones for each service, but the reporting jobs became slow and unreliable. It showed me that several teams depended on cross-table queries nobody had documented, so we mapped those uses before trying again.

I added automatic scaling to handle traffic spikes, and it reacted so aggressively that our cloud bill jumped in two days. I capped the extra servers and slowed the trigger down while we figured out which requests were causing the surge.

target.reason: Architecture changes how the team builds and operates systems while also reshaping the technical constraints and capabilities surrounding its work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager primarily enables or establishes a new technical structure, sometimes participating directly in design decisions.

temporal.reason: The resulting architecture becomes an ongoing structure that shapes future development and operations.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers typically sponsor and coordinate architecture work with the team, often involving platform groups or other dependent teams.

time_horizon.reason: Architectural changes usually take months to implement and can influence the team's capabilities for quarters or years.

domain.reason: The category centers on technical architecture, system boundaries, dependencies, and platform capabilities, with a secondary impact on workflows and how work is organized and delivered.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing architecture, dependencies, and system boundaries reshapes the technical environment in which work occurs.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Providing new underlying capabilities and removing technical constraints makes desired ways of working possible or easier.

clarifications.for: selecting, building, deploying, or retiring specific work tools
redesigning where, when, or under what physical or virtual conditions people work

observations: A small change requires coordinated updates across several systems or teams.
Engineers regularly wait on another service, platform, or repository before they can complete work.
Deployments frequently cause failures in unrelated parts of the product.
The team relies on repeated manual steps because the system does not support the desired workflow.
Planning discussions repeatedly end with someone saying the current platform or architecture cannot support the proposed approach.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that current system boundaries, dependencies, or technical capabilities prevent the team from working effectively.

challenges.what_if: What if cross-system delays come less from technical coupling and more from unclear authority among the people who own those systems? Explore #16, Decision Rights / Authority Distribution.

What if deployment failures keep recurring because incidents are handled defensively or superficially, preventing the team from learning and fixing underlying patterns? Explore #71, Error Acknowledgment / Mistake Response.
What if the platform seems incapable because knowledge about its capabilities, workarounds, and prior decisions is fragmented or lost? Explore #77, Knowledge Stewardship / Institutional Memory.

categories.description: Introducing, changing, or retiring prizes, awards, competitions, privileges, and recognition mechanisms beyond ordinary compensation.

examples.quote: I started giving one person each month a paid day to work on any project they chose. People took it seriously, and two of those side projects ended up fixing problems the whole team had complained about.
I tried a prize for whoever closed the most customer requests in a month, but it barely changed the total. It showed me that our slow handoffs, not a lack of effort, were holding people back.

I let our weekly standout pick their next assignment, and people started chasing visible jobs while avoiding routine work. I limited the perk to a short list of choices and rotated the routine tasks so the scramble settled down.

target.reason: Recognition programs primarily alter the incentive and status environment around work while also influencing individual motivation and behavior.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or changes a recognition mechanism that also signals which contributions and behaviors are valued.

temporal.reason: Recognition programs are usually recurring structures even when prizes are awarded at particular times.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers commonly authorize and structure recognition programs, though teams may help define criteria or select recipients.

time_horizon.reason: Recognition can affect motivation within weeks, while repeated use can shape norms and behavior over several months.

domain.reason: Awards and recognition programs are talent and reward mechanisms that acknowledge performance or contribution beyond normal compensation, while also reinforcing the behaviors and values the team celebrates.

bcw_functions.name: Incentivisation
bcw_functions.reason: Awards, prizes, privileges, and recognition create positive consequences that reinforce and motivate desired behaviour.

bcw_functions.name: Modelling
bcw_functions.reason: Recognizing winners or exemplary performers highlights visible examples of the behaviour others are encouraged to imitate.

clarifications.for: changing the duties, authority, or formal expectations attached to a role
changing team membership boundaries or the identity of the collective unit
supporting entry, knowledge transfer, integration, or internal transitions

clarifications.category: Hiring Process / Hiring Role Definition / Interview Design
clarifications.for: structuring a hire and its role definition, interviews, evaluation rubrics, and decision criteria

observations: The same visible people receive most public praise while less visible contributions go unmentioned.
Team members say they do not know what kinds of contributions the organization values.
Participation in an existing award or recognition program is low or has declined.
An award program repeatedly produces complaints about unclear criteria, favoritism, or unhealthy competition.
Important efforts such as mentoring, reliability work, or cross-team support receive little public recognition.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that current recognition mechanisms do not visibly and credibly reinforce the contributions and behaviors the organization wants.

challenges.what_if: What if mentoring, reliability, and cross-team support go unrecognized because the organization defines productivity around visible individual output? Explore #38, Productivity Definition / Productivity Measurement.

What if complaints about favoritism persist because people do not trust how recognition decisions are made or challenged, regardless of the award criteria? Explore #76, Procedural Fairness / Appeals / Due Process.
What if the same people receive praise because less visible work is not captured or exposed to decision-makers in the first place? Explore #30, Visibility / Information Exposure.

categories.description: Building alliances, mobilizing support, and developing political backing for the team's initiatives, interests, and needs across the organization.

examples.quote: I brought the support and sales leads into our planning early and asked them to back the new customer-tracking tool. They spoke up for it when the budget was reviewed, and we got enough money to run a pilot. It was not the full rollout we wanted, but it got us moving.

I asked several department heads to support an extra hire for my team, but the request still got turned down. Their comments revealed that the real concern was our rising contractor costs, which nobody had mentioned to me before. I went back and rebuilt the request around reducing those costs.

I asked a few friendly managers to push for our deadline change with senior leaders. More people joined in than I expected, and it started to look like we were trying to corner them. I asked everyone to stop sending messages and had just two of us explain the problem in one meeting.

target.reason: Advocacy primarily changes the team's political and relational context while also influencing which initiatives and needs receive organizational priority.

manager_mode.reason: The manager personally builds alliances and mobilizes stakeholders, often while communicating the team's value and priorities.

temporal.reason: Managers may maintain standing alliances or assemble coalitions for a specific initiative or need.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically leads cross-organizational advocacy, though team members may help cultivate support or present the case.

time_horizon.reason: Political backing and durable alliances usually develop over months, although support for a specific request can sometimes be secured within weeks.

domain.reason: Coalition building primarily relies on cross-organizational relationships and alliances, while its purpose is to influence decisions, secure backing, and advance the team’s interests within organizational power structures.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Securing allies and political backing removes organizational barriers and makes it easier for the team to advance its initiatives and obtain needed support.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Building coalitions reshapes the team's social and organizational environment by creating supportive relationships and networks.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Advocacy uses framing and argument to influence stakeholders' beliefs and motivate them to support the team's interests.

clarifications.for: creating informal opportunities for team members to socialize and build personal familiarity
intervening as a neutral third party to resolve a specific interpersonal conflict
holding direct conversations with people beyond the usual reporting chain

observations: A team initiative stalls because other departments will not commit people, approvals, or resources.
Different senior stakeholders give conflicting directions about the team's proposal.
The team repeatedly has to re-explain the value of its work to each new decision-maker.
A proposal receives support in private conversations but little backing in decision meetings.
Other teams resist a change because they were not consulted or do not see how it helps them.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is insufficient organizational support and political backing for the team's initiative or needs.

challenges.what_if: What if other teams resist because the change was introduced as a finished proposal rather than through consultation, piloting, or shared learning? Explore #91, Change Introduction Approach / Pilots / Mandates.

What if stakeholders privately support the idea but withhold public backing because the proposal concentrates risk on them without matching authority or protection? Explore #53, Risk Exposure / Risk Balancing.

What if conflicting directions and repeated value explanations reflect an unresolved strategy that has never been translated into shared organizational choices? Explore #97, Strategy Deployment / Translation / Cascade.

categories.description: Changing how mistakes and failures are acknowledged, owned, discussed, corrected, and responded to, including the manager's own errors.

examples.quote: I told the team I had rushed the rollout and missed a warning sign. I apologized, reset the schedule, and fixed the review step; after that, people started flagging problems earlier instead of hiding them.

I tried discussing a botched handoff with everyone in the room, but nobody said much. Later, two people told me they still remembered how sharply I had reacted to an earlier mistake, which showed me why they did not trust the discussion yet.

I started calling out every small mistake I made, hoping people would see that errors were safe to admit. The team copied me so thoroughly that minor slips took over our meetings, so I limited the discussion to mistakes that needed a fix or could affect someone else.

target.reason: The action primarily changes norms and conditions around psychological safety and accountability, while also shaping practices for discussing and correcting errors.

manager_mode.reason: Managers chiefly model and communicate constructive error ownership, sometimes reinforcing it through formal review or correction processes.

temporal.reason: Although activated by particular mistakes, the intended change is usually an ongoing norm or practice for handling errors.

locus_of_agency.reason: Durable change depends on the manager and team jointly adopting new norms, though the manager can unilaterally model ownership and change their own response.

time_horizon.reason: Individual responses affect people immediately, but building durable trust and constructive error norms typically takes months.

domain.reason: How a team acknowledges, owns, and responds to mistakes establishes shared norms around accountability, learning, and psychological safety; the manager’s handling of their own errors is also a key form of reflection and modeling.

bcw_functions.name: Modelling
bcw_functions.reason: By openly owning and correcting their own errors, managers demonstrate the mistake-response behaviour they expect others to imitate.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing how mistakes are discussed and handled reshapes social norms and creates a safer environment for reporting, learning from, and correcting failures.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: A constructive response to errors reduces fear, blame, and other barriers that can prevent employees from acknowledging and addressing mistakes.

clarifications.for: signaling valued or unacceptable behavior through public recognition or discouragement
building collective identity by retelling the team's history and defining moments
showing how peers or high-performing teams behave to establish a norm

observations: Errors are discovered late because no one mentioned them when they first occurred.
People use blame-focused language such as “Who caused this?” when discussing a failure.
The same mistakes recur without a clear correction or follow-up.
Team members become quiet or defensive when mistakes are discussed.
The manager corrects others publicly but rarely acknowledges their own errors.
categories.assumption: mistakes are being hidden, deflected, or repeated because the way they are handled makes open ownership and learning difficult.

challenges.what_if: What if people hide errors or become defensive because performance measures punish visible mistakes and reward looking error-free? Explore whether the signals built into the performance system are creating the blame response.
What if mistakes recur because the team is working at an intensity that leaves no time to investigate causes or apply corrections, rather than because people resist ownership?
What if errors are discussed but the lessons and corrective actions are not captured or made easy to find, so the team repeatedly relearns the same lesson?

aliases: Getting Teams Face Time with Customers
categories.description: Changing how directly and frequently team members interact with customers themselves, and how much customers participate in the team's work.

examples.quote: I had each engineer join one customer call a month instead of hearing everything through sales. They started catching small usability problems earlier, and one fix cut our support emails noticeably.

I invited three customers to our weekly planning meeting, but they barely spoke and stopped coming after two weeks. It showed me they were comfortable reacting to a demo, not sitting through how we chose the work.

I opened a shared chat channel where customers could message the team directly. A few people jumped on every request immediately and our planned work started slipping, so I limited replies to two set times a day and took urgent issues myself.

target.reason: The action changes the team's access to and relationship with customers while also altering how customer input is incorporated into working practices.

manager_mode.reason: Managers typically establish channels, routines, and permissions for customer interaction and may personally arrange or facilitate that access.

temporal.reason: The category usually concerns an ongoing arrangement governing how directly and frequently the team engages customers.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager and team shape how engagement works, but meaningful involvement also depends on customers choosing and being able to participate.

time_horizon.reason: Teams can receive customer feedback within weeks, while deeper effects on decisions, products, and customer understanding usually emerge over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on direct customer contact and customer participation, making customer-external the strongest fit. It also changes how the team’s work is conducted and how customer input is integrated into workflows, so work-design-delivery is secondary.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing customer contact and participation reshapes the team's social environment and creates direct feedback cues.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Greater customer access removes barriers to obtaining timely input, clarification, and validation during the team's work.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Direct interaction with customers increases team members' understanding of customer needs, experiences, and priorities.

clarifications.for: bringing in broader external perspectives, research, writing, and ideas beyond customers
making customer impact visible through shared stories and outcomes without requiring direct customer interaction
cultivating lasting relationships with external peers, mentors, advisers, or professional communities

observations: Team members rely on the manager or another group to relay customer feedback.
Customers raise needs or concerns late in the work, after key decisions have been made.
Team discussions include guesses about what customers want without direct customer input.
Only a small number of team members regularly speak with customers.
Customers see the work mainly at final reviews or delivery.
categories.assumption: the team’s understanding of customer needs is too filtered, indirect, or infrequent to guide the work effectively.

challenges.what_if: What if the team’s distance from customers is built into reporting lines and organizational boundaries, with another group formally positioned as the customer interface?
What if customer input already exists, but most team members lack the interviewing, listening, or synthesis skills needed to use it confidently, leaving contact concentrated among a few people?
What if the guessing is less about missing customer contact and more about an organizational strategy that has not been translated into clear choices about which customers and needs matter most?

categories.description: Defining when, where, and under what conditions exceptions to existing rules, standards, policies, and processes are legitimate.

examples.quote: I told the support leads they could waive late fees when an outage lasted more than two hours, as long as they noted the outage number. Customers stopped waiting days for my approval, and the credits stayed within reason.
I allowed rush orders to skip the usual review if a customer faced a shutdown. It did not speed things up because shipping still held them, but it revealed that the review was not the real delay.

I let store managers accept returns without receipts for damaged goods, and some started using that freedom for almost any return. I narrowed it to store-brand items under $50 and asked them to flag repeat customers, which brought the numbers back down.

target.reason: This action changes the governance conditions around existing rules while also shaping how processes may be legitimately adapted.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes a decision framework for exceptions and communicates what kinds of discretion are acceptable.

temporal.reason: The action creates an ongoing framework for handling exceptions as cases arise.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically holds authority to define or approve exception boundaries, though team input can help make them practical.

time_horizon.reason: The framework can guide decisions within weeks, while its broader effects on consistency and judgment emerge over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on governance of rules and decision rights for approving legitimate exceptions. Its secondary relevance is operational, since overrides affect how established processes, standards, and workflows are executed.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: It limits discretionary overrides to specified circumstances, reducing unauthorized departures from established rules and processes.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It creates a legitimate pathway for bypassing rules when those rules would otherwise obstruct appropriate action.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It reshapes the organizational governance environment by embedding clear conditions and procedures for exceptions.

clarifications.for: setting standing organization-wide boundaries on what leaders, teams, and individuals may decide
selecting the rollout or adoption method for a proposed change

clarifications.category: Formal Policies / Handbooks / Codes of Conduct
clarifications.for: creating, revising, interpreting, or retiring the formal rule from which exceptions may be sought

observations: Similar requests receive different answers depending on who handles them.
People follow a rule even when they can clearly show it will produce a poor outcome.
Exception requests stall while employees search for someone willing to approve them.
Team members repeatedly debate whether a particular policy applies to unusual cases.
People use unofficial workarounds because the formal process offers no clear exception path.
categories.assumption: people lack clear criteria and authority for deciding when it is legitimate to override standard rules or processes.

challenges.what_if: What if people are applying the same policy language differently because key terms such as “urgent,” “material,” or “eligible” do not have shared meanings?
What if exception requests stall mainly because the person with authority is unavailable or difficult to reach when a timely decision is needed?
What if inconsistent answers and unofficial workarounds are rational responses to targets that reward either rigid compliance or speed, without measuring the quality of the final outcome?

categories.description: Changing how much organizational change occurs, how quickly, how disruptively, and whether changes are introduced simultaneously or incrementally.

examples.quote: I spread the new scheduling process over three months instead of switching every team at once. The first group found a few rough spots, and the later groups had a much smoother start.

I delayed two other updates while we rolled out the new reporting system, but people still struggled. That showed me the problem was not the number of changes; even on its own, the system needed more time to learn than I had allowed.

I announced several small changes in one meeting because I thought that would feel less disruptive than dragging them out. People treated the whole list as urgent and started dropping regular work, so I paused most of it and gave them one change to handle first.

target.reason: The action primarily changes the surrounding conditions and disruption load while also altering how changes are sequenced and implemented.

manager_mode.reason: The manager structures the cadence, sequencing, and concurrency of change initiatives and may directly delay, stage, or accelerate them.

temporal.reason: It can operate as an ongoing change-governance practice or as a case-specific response to overload.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager often makes pacing and sequencing decisions but may involve the team in assessing capacity and disruption.

time_horizon.reason: Relief or disruption can be felt within weeks, while the broader effects on adoption capacity and change fatigue emerge over months.

domain.reason: This primarily concerns planning, sequencing, cadence, and disruption of organizational changes to manage delivery capacity. Secondarily, it involves governance over which changes are approved, prioritized, delayed, or introduced together.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Adjusting the timing, sequencing, and volume of change reshapes the organizational environment in which employees work and adapt.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Pacing changes and avoiding saturation reduce overload, disruption, and competing demands that can prevent employees from adopting new behaviors.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Limiting simultaneous initiatives or the rate of change constrains competing organizational demands that could undermine successful adoption.

clarifications.for: changing the structure, scope, sequence, or ownership of tasks
rebalancing team availability, attention, or expertise across current demands
deciding whether and how to accommodate contrasting work styles

observations: Several new tools, processes, or priorities are being introduced at the same time.
People ask which version of a process or priority is currently in effect.
Deadlines slip because the team is attending training, migrating systems, or reworking recently changed procedures.
Employees say they have not had time to absorb one change before the next arrives.
Adoption of recent changes is uneven, with people reverting to older ways of working.
categories.assumption: the volume and speed of change exceed the team’s capacity to absorb and apply it reliably.

challenges.what_if: What if the team is not facing too much change overall, but leadership has failed to choose which changes take precedence, so everything is treated as simultaneous and urgent?
What if people revert to old tools and processes because the replacements are unreliable or add effort, not because they have had too little time to adapt?
