What if version confusion and uneven adoption persist because guidance, decisions, and training materials are scattered or outdated rather than because changes are arriving too quickly?

categories.description: Shaping the expectation that people identify problems, challenge existing practices, experiment with improvements, and participate in evolving how work gets done.

examples.quote: I started ending our Friday meeting by asking everyone to name one thing that made the week harder than it needed to be. We picked one small fix to try, and within a month the team had cleared out several annoying handoffs that kept slowing us down.

I asked everyone to test a new way of reviewing orders, but it created more back-and-forth and we dropped it after two weeks. The trial showed us that the real problem was missing information from sales, which we would not have spotted by debating the review steps.

I told the team they could challenge any routine that seemed pointless, and suddenly people wanted to change half our process at once. Work started getting inconsistent, so I limited us to two experiments at a time and had everyone write down what they were testing.

target.reason: The action primarily changes how work is examined and improved while also shaping norms that support participation and experimentation.

manager_mode.reason: Managers establish routines and mechanisms for improvement while communicating and modeling that challenging current practices is valued.

temporal.reason: A continuous improvement culture is an ongoing expectation rather than a one-time intervention.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager enables and reinforces participation, while team members actively identify problems and drive improvements.

time_horizon.reason: New participation patterns may emerge over months, while a durable improvement culture develops over quarters or years.

domain.reason: The category primarily establishes shared expectations and norms around speaking up, experimentation, and continuous improvement. Its secondary relevance is to work design and delivery because participation is directed at changing processes and how work gets done.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It changes the social environment by establishing continuous improvement, experimentation, and participation as expected norms of work.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: It encourages people to view questioning current practices and proposing improvements as valuable, legitimate, and motivating behaviours.

clarifications.for: creating collective rituals to celebrate accomplishments, milestones, and meaningful events
establishing behavioral agreements about how colleagues communicate, disagree, and treat one another

clarifications.category: Treatment of Departing Employees / Exit Culture
clarifications.for: shaping communication, acknowledgment, and treatment when an employee leaves the team
shifting accountability for standards and collective effectiveness from managers to peers

observations: The same workflow problems appear in multiple retrospectives or team meetings.
People complain about inefficient practices but rarely propose or test alternatives.
Improvement actions are recorded but remain unfinished from one review to the next.
Team members continue using recurring workarounds without trying to fix the underlying process.
Most suggestions for changing how the team works come from the manager rather than team members.
categories.assumption: the team does not consistently see identifying, testing, and implementing improvements as part of everyone’s work.

challenges.what_if: What if people see improvement as part of their job but have no capacity left after delivery commitments, so actions and experiments repeatedly lose out to urgent work?
What if team members identify useful changes but do not know what they are authorized to alter, causing suggestions to wait for the manager or remain unfinished?
What if people avoid testing improvements because failures would create risks they personally cannot absorb, making workarounds safer than experiments?

categories.description: Changing how individuals can challenge decisions, raise concerns about unfair treatment, request reconsideration, and obtain impartial review.

examples.quote: I added a simple way for people to ask for a second look at shift assignments, with another supervisor making the call. We caught two mistakes in the first month, and people stopped assuming the schedule was fixed no matter what.

I offered private office hours for anyone who wanted to challenge a performance rating, but nobody came. Two people later told me they were worried others would see them entering my office, which showed me the process needed to be private from the start.

I let anyone ask a manager from another team to review a decision, and suddenly people were sending over every minor disagreement. The reviews piled up and slowed both teams down, so I limited them to decisions affecting pay, shifts, or formal warnings and added a one-week deadline.

target.reason: The action changes decision-review rules and safeguards around work, as well as the process used to address contested decisions.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or revises procedures for raising concerns, requesting reconsideration, and obtaining impartial review.

temporal.reason: The action establishes an ongoing mechanism that individuals can use whenever relevant disputes arise.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager or management system establishes the mechanism, while impartial reviewers outside the immediate team may drive individual reviews.

time_horizon.reason: A new process may become available immediately, but its broader effects on trust, consistency, and perceived fairness usually emerge over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on formal rights and mechanisms for challenging decisions, seeking reconsideration, and obtaining impartial review, making governance and procedural justice the primary fit. Communication-information is secondary because these processes depend on clear channels for raising concerns and conveying decisions, evidence, and outcomes.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It redesigns organizational procedures and channels so concerns, appeals, and impartial reviews are built into the decision environment.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It removes procedural barriers and provides practical means for individuals to challenge decisions or seek reconsideration.

clarifications.for: assigning authority for the initial decision rather than its appeal
routing operational problems upward and specifying the manager’s response
changing formal reporting lines, management layers, or organizational units
setting acceptable risk levels and distributing risk consequences

observations: Employees ask who can review a decision after their manager says it is final.
People raise the same fairness concern through several unrelated channels because there is no clear appeal path.
Similar requests receive different explanations or review steps depending on who handles them.
In 1:1s, employees say they did not raise a concern because the person involved would also decide the outcome.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that people lack a clear, trusted, and impartial way to challenge decisions or unfair treatment.

challenges.what_if: What if people keep challenging decisions because the evidence or measures behind those decisions are inconsistent, so even a clearer appeal path would not make the outcomes feel fair?
What if similar requests are handled differently because people use terms like “fair,” “exception,” or “equal treatment” to mean different things?
What if employees try several channels because hierarchy is filtering their concerns, and they are searching for a way to reach someone who can see the situation firsthand?

categories.description: Changing how collective knowledge is captured, maintained, retrieved, updated, transferred, and deliberately retired.

examples.quote: I started having the on-call engineer add the fix and the warning signs to a shared troubleshooting page after every incident. A month later, the night shift solved a repeat problem without waking anyone up.

I recorded handoff videos before our senior analyst left, but hardly anyone watched them. That showed me people needed searchable steps tied to specific tasks, not two-hour tours of everything she knew.

I told the team to clean out old project files, and they deleted a few notes that were still useful for a customer dispute. I paused the cleanup, restored the files from backup, and required a quick review before anything older was removed.

target.reason: The action changes knowledge-management practices while also shaping the informational context in which work occurs.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes processes and structures for stewarding knowledge and reinforces expectations about their use.

temporal.reason: Capturing, updating, retrieving, transferring, and retiring knowledge require an ongoing system rather than a single intervention.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers usually establish or sponsor the system, while team members collectively contribute, maintain, and use the knowledge.

time_horizon.reason: Benefits emerge over months as knowledge accumulates and become especially valuable over longer periods during turnover, scaling, and organizational change.

domain.reason: Institutional memory primarily concerns how knowledge is documented, kept visible, retrieved, updated, and transferred across the team. It also supports capability development by preserving know-how and enabling learning from prior experience.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It changes the organizational systems, repositories, routines, and cues through which collective knowledge is captured, maintained, retrieved, and retired.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It reduces barriers to effective action by making relevant institutional knowledge accessible, current, transferable, and easier to use.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: It increases organizational members’ knowledge and understanding by preserving and transferring useful information and lessons.

clarifications.for: opening, legitimizing, restricting, or closing a forum for employee voice and dissent
designing or introducing a specific document, diagram, prototype, shared board, or plan
creating or reinforcing shared terminology, labels, metaphors, and concepts
choosing where and how communication happens, including channel-purpose and async norms
translating and cascading strategy while gathering feedback on its interpretation

observations: The same questions are answered repeatedly in meetings or Slack.
Work stalls when the one person who knows a system or process is unavailable.
Team documents contain outdated instructions, broken links, or conflicting versions.
When someone leaves or transfers, coworkers discover that key decisions, contacts, or procedures were never written down.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that important knowledge is not being reliably captured, kept current, found, or transferred.

challenges.what_if: What if work depends on one expert because the system itself is tightly coupled or unusually hard to operate, rather than because knowledge has not been documented?
What if documents decay and handoffs get skipped because capacity is spread too thin for anyone to maintain them, even when people know that work matters?
What if repeated questions and missing records are symptoms of a team carrying too many external commitments to pause, document decisions, or prepare for transitions?

categories.description: Establishing, changing, reinforcing, or relaxing expectations about how people treat one another, communicate, disagree, cooperate, and behave.

examples.quote: I asked everyone to stop interrupting and leave a beat before responding. Meetings felt awkward for a week, but quieter people started speaking up and we made better decisions.

I tried requiring disagreements to stay in the team meeting instead of spilling into side chats. It did not stop the side chats, but it showed me that two people did not feel safe challenging me in front of the group.

I told the team to be more direct with each other, and a few people took that as permission to be blunt about everything. I had to step in, clarify that direct did not mean harsh, and ask them to check how their comments were landing.

target.reason: Behavioral agreements primarily shape relationships and social conditions while also influencing how people communicate and collaborate.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or adjusts shared behavioral rules and reinforces them through communication and modeling.

temporal.reason: These expectations are intended to guide interactions continuously rather than only in a single situation.

locus_of_agency.reason: Behavioral agreements are strongest when jointly developed, although managers may also impose baseline conduct expectations.

time_horizon.reason: Expectations can influence behavior within weeks, but durable changes in interpersonal culture usually emerge over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on shared behavioral expectations governing how team members interact, making culture and norms the strongest fit. Its focus on treatment, disagreement, cooperation, and interpersonal conduct also directly shapes trust and working relationships.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Establishing interpersonal norms changes the social environment by creating shared expectations and cues for communication, cooperation, and disagreement.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Behavioral agreements constrain socially acceptable options by defining conduct that should be avoided or limited.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Clear and supportive norms reduce interpersonal uncertainty and friction, making constructive participation and collaboration easier.

clarifications.for: changing how the team collectively recognizes achievements, milestones, and meaningful occasions
encouraging employees to challenge existing practices, identify problems, and experiment with improvements

clarifications.category: Treatment of Departing Employees / Exit Culture
clarifications.for: setting expectations specifically for how departing employees are treated, discussed, and remembered
establishing peer-to-peer responsibility for feedback, standards, and team effectiveness

observations: People interrupt, talk over, or dismiss one another during meetings.
Disagreements shift into personal remarks, sarcasm, or hostile messages.
Team members complain in side conversations about behavior they do not address in the room.
Different people follow different expectations for response times, meeting conduct, or how to raise concerns.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team lacks clear and consistently reinforced expectations for how members communicate, disagree, and treat one another.

challenges.what_if: What if interruptions, sarcasm, and hostile messages are signs that people are working at an unsustainable intensity, rather than simply lacking behavioral agreements?
What if people talk over one another and avoid direct concerns because rewards favor visible individual wins, speed, or being right over cooperation?
What if disagreements become personal because nobody knows who actually decides, turning meetings into repeated contests for influence?

categories.category: Treatment of Departing Employees / Exit Culture
categories.description: Shaping how people who resign, transfer, are laid off, or are terminated are treated, acknowledged, communicated about, and remembered.

examples.quote: When Maya resigned, I thanked her openly, explained the handoff, and gave the team time to say goodbye. She left on good terms, and two months later she referred a strong candidate to us.

I planned a big send-off for someone transferring to another group, but he looked uncomfortable and left early. Afterward he told me he wanted a quiet exit because the move involved a personal issue I hadn't known about, so I started asking people how they wanted to be acknowledged.

After the layoffs, I kept praising the people who had left, and the team started hearing it as criticism of those who remained. I was surprised by how raw it felt, so I stopped the public comparisons and shared specific memories privately instead.

target.reason: Exit culture primarily changes relational norms and workplace conditions while also shaping the processes used for departures.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes departure practices and norms, then reinforces them through communication and visible treatment of leavers.

temporal.reason: A consistent exit culture is an ongoing norm or system applied across successive departures.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically sets the tone and communication approach while coordinating aspects of the departure directly with the affected person.

time_horizon.reason: Treatment is felt immediately during the departure, while its effects on trust, culture, and reputation can persist for years.

domain.reason: The category centers on shared norms and rituals for treating, acknowledging, and remembering departing employees, while also directly relating to employee departures and offboarding as a talent-management process.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It shapes the social environment and workplace norms around how departures are handled and discussed.

bcw_functions.name: Modelling
bcw_functions.reason: Managers demonstrate respectful and consistent treatment that others can imitate in future transitions.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: How departures are acknowledged and framed influences employees’ emotions, trust, and beliefs about the organization.

clarifications.for: designing team-wide celebrations and recognition rituals for accomplishments or milestones
creating broad participation in finding problems and continuously improving how work gets done
setting ongoing norms for communication, disagreement, cooperation, and interpersonal treatment
making team members accountable to one another for standards and collective performance

observations: Departures are announced late, vaguely, or not at all.
A departing employee loses access before completing planned handoffs or saying goodbye.
Managers or coworkers speak dismissively about people after they resign, transfer, or are terminated.
Departing employees receive noticeably different levels of acknowledgment or support without an explained reason.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that inconsistent or disrespectful treatment of departing employees is damaging trust, continuity, and the team's sense of how people are valued.

challenges.what_if: What if late announcements and abrupt access loss reflect leaders poorly translating legal, security, or organizational pressure while trying to shield the team?
What if departures become chaotic because critical work has no backup owner or prepared successor, making every exit an operational emergency?
What if dismissive comments and uneven acknowledgment come from a shared story that treats leaving as disloyalty, rather than from the exit process itself?

categories.description: Shaping whether feedback, standards, accountability, and collective effectiveness are primarily manager-driven, individually exercised, or maintained between peers.

examples.quote: I asked everyone to flag missed handoffs directly with each other instead of waiting for me. After a few awkward weeks, people started fixing small problems before they reached our team meeting, and our deadlines got more reliable.

I had each person set their own quality bar and report whether they met it. It did not improve the work, but it showed me that everyone had a different idea of what “done” meant, which I would not have seen if I had just pushed harder.

I started having teammates review each other’s mistakes in our weekly meeting. People got way too sharp and one person stopped speaking up, so I paused the group reviews and switched to private, one-on-one feedback until things settled down.

target.reason: The action primarily shapes team norms and relationships around accountability while also affecting how feedback and standards are maintained.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes structures and norms for shared accountability and reinforces them through communication and modeling.

temporal.reason: This is an ongoing cultural pattern rather than a single intervention.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager helps establish the culture, but effective peer accountability increasingly depends on team members maintaining it themselves.

time_horizon.reason: Behavioral changes may emerge over months, while a durable culture of collective responsibility often takes quarters or longer to establish.

domain.reason: The category centers on shared norms for peer feedback, mutual accountability, and collective responsibility, while also defining where authority for enforcing standards resides.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It reshapes the social environment so that feedback, standards, and accountability are maintained through peer norms and interactions rather than relying solely on the manager.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It distributes responsibility and authority among team members, making peer feedback and collective problem-solving easier and less dependent on managerial intervention.

clarifications.for: recognizing accomplishments and milestones through shared celebrations or rituals
building a culture where people routinely propose, test, and adopt improvements to work practices
defining how people should communicate, disagree, cooperate, and behave toward one another

clarifications.category: Treatment of Departing Employees / Exit Culture
clarifications.for: shaping the team's treatment and acknowledgment of people who resign, transfer, are laid off, or are terminated

observations: Team members bring routine performance or behavior concerns to the manager without first speaking to the colleague involved.
A missed commitment is noticed by several peers, but no one addresses it until the manager intervenes.
The same coordination problems recur even though team members discuss them privately afterward.
In meetings, people say that enforcing shared standards is the manager's job.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that team members rely too heavily on the manager and do not hold one another accountable for shared commitments and standards.

challenges.what_if: What if peers do not challenge missed commitments because priorities are unclear, so they cannot tell whether a colleague failed or made a reasonable tradeoff?
What if the manager’s habit of stepping in quickly has taught people that raising an issue upward is safer and faster than resolving it with one another?
What if people avoid peer accountability because productivity is measured as individual output, while time spent protecting collective coordination is ignored or penalized?

categories.description: Changing when, how, and under what circumstances people can access the manager's attention, advice, support, or decision-making authority.

examples.quote: I set aside half an hour every morning when anyone could drop in without booking. People brought me small decisions before they became blockers, and the team moved faster.

I made our one-on-ones optional and told people to book me whenever they needed help. Hardly anyone did, and I learned the newer folks saw booking time as bothering me, which I would not have known otherwise.

I gave everyone my number and said to call whenever they needed a quick decision. I was surprised when routine questions started coming in at night, so I clarified what was truly urgent and set an evening cutoff for everything else.

target.reason: The action changes the conditions and channels through which employees obtain managerial attention, support, and decisions, which can also affect workflow.

manager_mode.reason: The manager typically establishes availability structures such as office hours, response norms, or escalation channels and then personally participates in them.

temporal.reason: Manager availability is generally maintained as an ongoing access arrangement rather than used only once.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager ultimately controls their availability, although effective access norms may be developed with team input.

time_horizon.reason: Changing access can affect support and decision speed within days, while broader improvements in team functioning may emerge over weeks.

domain.reason: The category centers on the manager's own accessibility and availability, while also shaping employees' direct connection to the manager for support, advice, and decisions.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Making the manager’s advice, support, attention, or authority more accessible removes barriers that can prevent employees from acting effectively.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing access times, communication channels, or contact arrangements reshapes the social and organizational environment to make desired behavior easier.

clarifications.for: showing people the desired behavior through your own visible actions
withholding intervention so consequences, accountability, or reorganization can emerge

clarifications.category: Managerial Deep Dives / Direct Engagement with Details
clarifications.for: directly inspecting and engaging with the technical or operational details of work
changing how you solicit feedback, observe operations, and investigate team dynamics

observations: People wait hours or days for the manager to approve routine decisions.
Team members repeatedly ask on Slack when the manager is free.
Questions pile up until the next 1:1 or team meeting.
The same few people regularly get the manager's attention while others rarely speak with them.
Work stops when the manager is in meetings, traveling, or offline.
categories.assumption: The problem is that people cannot get the manager's attention or authority when they need it to move work forward.

challenges.what_if: What if routine decisions keep coming to you because the team has no shared definition of acceptable quality, so people seek approval to avoid getting it wrong? Explore #62 Quality Standards / Quality Reinforcement.

What if people wait for you because repeated managerial rescue has taught them not to exercise their own judgment or experience the consequences of a decision? Explore #29 Deliberate Nonintervention / Allowing Consequences.

What if questions pile up because the team has no clear channel or response norm for different kinds of requests, rather than because you are unavailable? Explore #94 Communication Channels / Media / Async Norms.

categories.description: Structuring vacation and leave policies, encouraging breaks and disconnection, and protecting rest so people can recover.

examples.quote: I started blocking Friday afternoons from meetings and told everyone to sign off early if their work was covered. After a few weeks, people came back on Mondays less worn out, and we still hit our deadlines.
I asked everyone to take a full week off during the summer, but hardly anyone did. It showed me that people were worried about who would cover their work, so encouragement alone was not enough.

I set a rule that nobody should send messages after 6 p.m., and people started saving everything for a flood at 8 the next morning. I loosened the rule so urgent notes could still go through and asked people to schedule the rest for later.

target.reason: The action changes leave rules, availability expectations, and working practices to protect recovery.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes policies and norms while also communicating and modeling that breaks and disconnection are expected.

temporal.reason: Rest and recovery are generally protected through ongoing policies, norms, and routines.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically sets or enforces the framework, while team participation may shape practical coverage and rest norms.

time_horizon.reason: Breaks and time off can improve recovery within days, while sustained protection supports health and performance over quarters or years.

domain.reason: Rest, breaks, and disconnection shape workload, pace, and work cadence, while vacation and leave policies are also core employment and retention practices.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It changes organizational policies, norms, and workflows so taking leave, breaks, and disconnected recovery time is supported by the work environment.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It removes practical and social barriers to rest, such as workload expectations, lack of coverage, or pressure to remain available.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Protected time off and disconnection rules limit work-related demands and contact during designated recovery periods.

clarifications.for: deciding which performance inputs, outputs, outcomes, or feedback signals to track
aligning with other teams on ownership, dependencies, expectations, commitments, or handoffs

observations: Team members leave vacation days unused or repeatedly postpone planned leave.
People send messages and respond to requests during evenings, weekends, or vacations.
Several people say they are tired, have trouble concentrating, or need a break.
People return from leave to a large backlog and immediately work extra hours.
Lunch breaks and time between meetings regularly disappear from calendars.
categories.assumption: The problem is that work practices do not give people enough protected time to disconnect and recover.

challenges.what_if: What if people cannot take real time off because the team has accepted more commitments than its capacity can support, making every absence feel unaffordable? Explore #56 Demand Management / External Commitments.
What if leave creates an immediate backlog because critical work has no backup owners and too much knowledge sits with particular people? Explore #65 Continuity / Redundancy / Succession Design.
What if people stay online because leaders visibly work and respond during evenings and vacations, signaling that disconnection is unsafe despite the formal policy? Explore #2 Behavioral Modeling.

categories.description: Highlighting the broader purpose and impact of the team's effort, for customers, the organization, or the mission, and trying different ways of making it felt.

examples.quote: I brought in a customer to show us how she used the tool during a rough week. The team kept talking about her story afterward, and people started catching small issues they used to wave through.

I started sending a weekly note about how many people our service had reached, but hardly anyone read it. When I asked around, I learned the totals felt too distant; the team wanted to hear what had actually changed for one person.

I put customer thank-you messages on a screen near our desks, and people got so focused on pleasing the loudest customers that they started bumping other work. I cut the display back to a monthly review and added context about who we were trying to help overall.

target.reason: Connecting effort to broader impact primarily changes how people understand and feel about their work while also reinforcing its direction and priorities.

manager_mode.reason: The manager communicates and reinforces meaning rather than directly changing the work or its underlying system.

temporal.reason: Impact highlighting may be an ongoing communication practice or an episodic intervention tied to particular moments.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager commonly initiates the framing, though team members may help identify and reinforce meaningful examples of impact.

time_horizon.reason: A purpose message can affect motivation and perspective within days, while repeated reinforcement can shape commitment over months.

domain.reason: This action makes the team’s broader purpose and impact visible and understandable, while reinforcing shared meaning, mission, and collective identity.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Connecting the team's work to a broader purpose and tangible impact motivates behavior by making the work feel meaningful and emotionally salient.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Explaining how the team's efforts affect customers, the organization, or the mission increases understanding of why the work matters.

clarifications.for: formally communicating organizational matters, strategies, decisions, or expectations
signaling values and priorities through what receives attention or is left unmentioned
carrying the team’s story, standing, and resource needs to external stakeholders

observations: Team members ask why a project matters or who will use the result.
Project updates focus only on tasks, deadlines, and output counts.
People cannot describe what changed for customers or the organization because of their work.
Customer feedback, outcomes, and impact stories are rarely shared with the team.
People describe the work as repetitive, pointless, or disconnected from the mission.
categories.assumption: The problem is that people cannot see or feel how their daily work contributes to a meaningful outcome.

challenges.what_if: What if the work feels pointless because it has been divided into narrow, repetitive tasks that prevent anyone from owning or seeing a meaningful outcome? Explore #7 Work Design / Task Structuring.

What if people cannot describe the impact because the team measures outputs and deadlines but does not collect credible evidence of customer or organizational outcomes? Explore #15 Measurement / Performance Systems.

What if the team understands the mission in general but cannot connect it to current projects because strategy has not been translated into concrete day-to-day choices? Explore #97 Strategy Deployment / Translation / Cascade.

categories.description: Deliberately pushing, sustaining, or pulling back the pace and intensity of work, and deciding how long each mode lasts.

examples.quote: I set a two-week push to clear the backlog, then gave everyone a lighter week afterward. We finished the oldest work without wearing people down for the whole month.

I kept us at a steady, moderate pace instead of rushing before a release, but we still missed the date. It showed me that the real delay was waiting on outside approvals, not how fast the team was working.
I told everyone to slow down after a rough launch, and they pulled back more than I expected. Small tasks started piling up, so I set a minimum daily target until we were moving normally again.

target.reason: Modulating pace primarily changes how work is carried out while also affecting workload conditions and team pressure.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes the cadence and duration of work modes, then communicates when to accelerate, sustain, or ease off.

temporal.reason: Intensity modulation may be embedded in a recurring operating cadence or used episodically for a particular situation.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager commonly sets the expected pace, though effective modulation may incorporate team input about capacity and sustainability.

time_horizon.reason: A pace change affects daily work quickly, while its productivity and well-being effects often become clearer over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: The category centers on setting and adjusting workflow pace, intensity, and duration. It also involves managerial authority over when teams accelerate, sustain effort, or pull back.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Adjusting workload, cadence, and the duration of work modes changes the temporal and organizational environment in which employees perform.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Pulling back or sustaining a manageable pace can reduce overload and make effective, sustainable performance easier.

bcw_functions.name: Coercion
bcw_functions.reason: When managers deliberately push intensity, the heightened demands and time pressure create pressure to increase effort or speed.

clarifications.for: changing meeting participants, facilitation, format, agenda, or interaction flow
shaping work through built-in guardrails, time-boxes, limits, or required procedures

clarifications.category: Unstructured Time / Learning Time / Innovation Time
clarifications.for: giving people protected, unstructured time to pursue learning or experimental ideas

observations: The team is working late or rushing for several weeks without a stated end date.
Errors, rework, or missed handoffs increase during high-pressure periods.
Important deadlines are approaching while work continues at the usual pace.
People treat nearly every request as urgent, regardless of its actual deadline.
After a major push, the team immediately starts another one without a slower period.
categories.assumption: The problem is that the team's current pace and intensity do not match the demands of the work or people's ability to sustain it.

challenges.what_if: What if the sustained rush is not mainly a pacing choice, but the result of accepting too many external commitments and treating them all as fixed? Explore #56 Demand Management / External Commitments.

What if everything feels urgent because the manager gives immediate attention to every new request, unintentionally signaling that interruption matters more than planned work? Explore #4 Informal Signaling / Selective Attention.
What if the team cannot slow down after a push because key work depends on a few people who have no effective backups? Explore #65 Continuity / Redundancy / Succession Design.

categories.description: Setting, defending, or communicating ethical limits on what the team will do, including refusing demands, holding lines, and acting when values conflict.

examples.quote: I refused to let us hide the bad test results from the client, even though sales pushed hard. We showed the full picture, and the client stayed with us because we were straight with them.

I told the team we would not use customer emails for a side campaign, but I waited until the launch meeting to say it. The launch slipped, but the argument revealed that two people had already built the whole plan around data we never had permission to use.

I banned all vendor gifts after an expensive package showed up at the office. People got so nervous that they started refusing coffee during routine site visits, so I clarified that small shared meals were fine and set a dollar limit for everything else.

target.reason: Ethical boundaries establish the values and constraints surrounding the team's work and limit which activities it will undertake.

manager_mode.reason: The manager communicates and models ethical limits, while sometimes directly enforcing them by refusing demands or intervening.

temporal.reason: An ethical stance can be a standing boundary or an episodic response to a specific values conflict.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager is often accountable for drawing and defending the line, although the team's participation can help define and sustain it.

time_horizon.reason: An ethical refusal can constrain action immediately, while consistent adherence shapes trust and culture over quarters or years.

domain.reason: Ethical barriers establish and enforce non-negotiable limits on decisions and actions, while expressing the team’s shared values and expected conduct.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Setting and enforcing ethical limits removes unacceptable courses of action from the team's available options.

bcw_functions.name: Modelling
bcw_functions.reason: Refusing unethical demands and acting consistently during value conflicts demonstrates conduct for team members to emulate.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Communicating and defending the ethical stance shapes beliefs about why particular behaviors are unacceptable or important.

clarifications.category: Sponsorship / Air Cover for Individual Initiatives
clarifications.for: protecting, legitimizing, or amplifying an initiative led by an individual or small group

observations: Team members are asked to hide, soften, or omit information from customers or stakeholders.
People raise concerns that a request could harm users, employees, or the public.
A deadline or revenue target is used to justify bypassing a review, safeguard, or policy.
Different leaders give conflicting instructions about what is acceptable.
People say they are uncomfortable with a decision but do not know whether they can refuse or escalate it.
categories.assumption: The problem is that the team lacks a clear, defended boundary for what it will not do when business demands conflict with ethical responsibilities.

challenges.what_if: What if people bypass safeguards because compensation or material rewards make hitting revenue and deadline targets more valuable than raising concerns? Explore #63 Compensation / Material Incentives.

What if conflicting instructions persist because no one knows which leader has the authority to set limits, approve exceptions, or overrule a risky request? Explore #37 Governance Boundaries / Mandate Levels.

What if people hide or soften information because mistakes and bad news are met with blame, making candor personally risky even when the ethical expectation is understood? Explore #71 Error Acknowledgment / Mistake Response.

categories.description: Designing constraints built into how work unfolds: enabling constraints that open up and guide possibilities (heuristics, guardrails, templates, time-boxes, limits) and governing constraints that restrict or fix behavior (hard limits, mandatory steps).

examples.quote: I gave the support team a simple rule: solve anything under $100 without waiting for approval. Refunds went out faster, and complaints dropped, though we still had a few odd calls to review.

I made every code change go through two reviewers, hoping we would catch more mistakes. Work piled up, but it showed me that only three people knew the oldest part of the system, which I would not have seen otherwise.

I capped our planning meetings at 20 minutes, and people started rushing through real disagreements just to beat the clock. I stretched the limit to 35 minutes and let anyone call for one extra discussion when something felt unresolved.

target.reason: Constraints primarily shape the methods and process of work while also establishing rules and conditions around it.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or modifies structures, guardrails, and rules that guide behavior during work.

temporal.reason: They are generally embedded as ongoing features of the workflow rather than used as isolated interventions.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers can impose constraints directly, although enabling constraints are often more effective when designed or refined with the team.

time_horizon.reason: Constraints affect decisions as soon as they are introduced, with broader workflow effects emerging over subsequent weeks.

domain.reason: These constraints are embedded in workflows and shape how work proceeds, while governing constraints also establish mandatory rules, limits, and permitted discretion.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Embedding guardrails, templates, time-boxes, and mandatory steps changes the work environment so desired behaviors are cued and structured.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Hard limits and governing constraints reduce available options and prevent competing or noncompliant behaviors.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Enabling constraints such as heuristics and templates reduce friction and make effective action easier without prescribing every step.

clarifications.for: redesigning a meeting or organized interaction to improve participation and outcomes
deciding when to accelerate, sustain, or ease the team's work intensity

clarifications.category: Unstructured Time / Learning Time / Innovation Time
clarifications.for: creating dedicated self-directed periods such as learning days, innovation time, or hack weeks

observations: Teams repeatedly debate the same edge cases instead of moving forward.
Similar work is handled differently by different people, with uneven results.
People frequently ask what they are allowed to change or decide on their own.
Projects expand beyond their original scope or miss agreed deadlines.
Critical checks are skipped unless someone remembers to ask for them.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the current workflow lacks clear boundaries, guardrails, or required steps to guide consistent action.

challenges.what_if: What if teams keep debating the same edge cases because past decisions and their rationale are not being captured or found? Explore whether the missing guardrail is actually missing institutional memory.
What if scope keeps expanding and deadlines slip because unfiltered organizational demands repeatedly override whatever boundaries the team sets?
What if people keep asking permission—and skip checks under pressure—because the manager’s past reactions have taught them that independent judgment is risky and speed matters more than diligence?

categories.category: Hiring Process / Hiring Role Definition / Interview Design
categories.description: Designing how a hire is run: defining the role being recruited for, structuring the process, and designing interviews, rubrics, and decision criteria.

examples.quote: I gave every interviewer the same set of questions and a simple list of what a strong answer should include. Our final discussion was much clearer, and we hired someone who has done well so far.

I posted the job as a general operations role, but the people we met were not strong at the planning work we actually needed. It cost us a few weeks, but it showed me that the role needed a much narrower focus before we tried again.

I added a take-home exercise so we could see how candidates handled real work, but several people spent an entire weekend on it and one dropped out. I replaced it with a one-hour exercise during the interview and told everyone exactly how much time to spend.

target.reason: The action primarily designs the methods and criteria used to hire while also defining the content and responsibilities of the role.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates a structured process, interviews, rubrics, and decision rules for hiring.

temporal.reason: The design is commonly created or adapted for a particular vacancy and hiring cycle.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers commonly develop the role and process with interviewers or team members, though they may sometimes define them unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: The design affects recruiting and interviews within weeks, while its fuller impact emerges after the selected person joins the team.

domain.reason: The category centers on hiring and defining roles, which are core people and talent responsibilities. Its secondary focus is designing the hiring workflow, including interview stages, rubrics, and decision criteria.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It changes the hiring environment by introducing structured workflows, interview formats, rubrics, and decision criteria that guide interviewer behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It reduces ambiguity and cognitive burden by clarifying the role and providing tools that make consistent, evidence-based assessment easier.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: It limits unstructured interviewer discretion and reduces reliance on irrelevant or inconsistent criteria.

clarifications.for: changing the ongoing responsibilities or formal expectations of an existing role outside a specific hire
defining which people or functions belong to a team or project group
onboarding selected hires or helping people transition into new team positions
designing awards, prizes, competitions, privileges, or other special recognition mechanisms

observations: Interviewers give conflicting descriptions of what the role requires.
Candidates are asked very different questions depending on who interviews them.
Hiring debriefs rely on general impressions such as “strong” or “not a fit.”
The same role stays open while the team repeatedly changes the candidate profile.
New hires arrive without skills or experience that interviewers assumed someone else had assessed.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the role, evaluation criteria, or hiring process is not defined clearly enough to produce reliable hiring decisions.

challenges.what_if: What if the candidate profile keeps changing because the organization has not translated its strategy into stable choices about what this team needs to become?
What if interviewers keep settling for vague judgments because the compensation on offer cannot attract candidates who meet the stated requirements?
What if the team lacks reliable evidence about which skills actually predict success in the role, so interviewers fall back on impressions and repeatedly revise the profile?

categories.description: Deciding how much to elevate, accommodate, or formally integrate differing work styles, and whether to pair and arrange people directly or help them navigate the overlaps themselves.

examples.quote: I paired our fast sketcher with the person who always caught the small details. They argued over the first draft, but the final version went out earlier and had fewer mistakes.

I let everyone choose their own way of tracking tasks, thinking they could sort out the overlap themselves. Deadlines still slipped, but it showed me the real problem was that nobody knew when someone else was ready for a handoff.

I started rotating people between quiet mornings and group work sessions so both preferences had equal space. The group sessions quickly turned into nonstop meetings, so I cut them back to twice a week and protected the rest of the time.

target.reason: The action primarily adjusts interpersonal arrangements and conditions around collaboration while also shaping how people coordinate their work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager typically creates collaboration arrangements or norms but may also directly pair people or mediate overlaps.

temporal.reason: Integration may take the form of standing collaboration practices or case-by-case adjustments for particular people or situations.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager commonly helps the team establish workable accommodations while sometimes enabling members to navigate differences themselves.

time_horizon.reason: New pairings or accommodations can affect collaboration within weeks, while durable integration and trust often develop over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on integrating different ways of working into collaboration, workflows, and task arrangements. It also involves configuring or pairing people based on their individual styles.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Pairing, arranging, or formally integrating people with different work styles changes the social and workflow environment to support effective collaboration.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Accommodating differences or helping people navigate overlaps removes interpersonal and procedural barriers that could otherwise impede joint work.

clarifications.for: restructuring assignments, deliverables, task scope, or work sequencing
allocating scarce time, energy, expertise, or bandwidth among priorities
adjusting how quickly or simultaneously organizational changes are introduced

observations: Some teammates want to discuss work live while others repeatedly ask to handle it asynchronously.
Handoffs contain either far more or far less detail than the recipient expects.
People regularly complain about interruptions, slow replies, or too many meetings.
Two colleagues repeatedly get stuck over how closely to collaborate or how independently to work.
Team members use different schedules or planning habits, and shared work is missed or delayed at the overlaps.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that differing work styles are colliding without clear agreements or deliberate integration.

challenges.what_if: What if slow replies, sparse handoffs, and demands for fewer meetings are signs that people are overloaded, not that their work styles are incompatible?
What if the need for constant live coordination and detailed handoffs comes from tightly coupled systems rather than personal collaboration preferences?
What if small differences in schedules and communication habits create outsized friction because teammates lack enough familiarity and trust to interpret one another generously?

categories.description: Choosing whether to select, encourage, mandate, or deliberately ignore specific thinking frameworks and tools for decision making, prioritization, and problem solving.

examples.quote: I asked everyone to use the same simple scoring sheet for our big project choices. The debates still got heated, but we picked two projects and actually finished both on time.

I let each team choose its own way to rank customer requests, thinking they knew their work best. The lists clashed badly, but that showed me they had completely different ideas about which customers mattered most—something I wouldn’t have seen with one shared method.

I required a written risk check before every decision, and people started doing them for tiny choices like moving a meeting. It slowed everything down, so I limited the check to decisions that cost real money or were hard to reverse.

target.reason: Selecting or mandating thinking frameworks primarily changes how decisions and problems are handled, while also shaping the rules surrounding that work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes expectations for framework use and communicates which approaches are encouraged, required, or intentionally disregarded.

temporal.reason: A selected or mandated framework usually becomes an ongoing approach to decision making, prioritization, or problem solving.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager often determines whether a framework is selected or mandated, though the team may participate in evaluating and adopting it.

time_horizon.reason: Framework adoption can shape decisions within weeks, but consistent behavioral and performance effects usually emerge over months.

domain.reason: The category centers on adopting thinking frameworks and decision-making methods, making capability development the best fit. The choice to encourage, require, or ignore them adds a governance dimension involving mandates and decision rights.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Selecting or embedding common thinking frameworks changes the decision-making environment by introducing shared structures, prompts, and routines.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Mandating particular frameworks limits the range of acceptable approaches and reduces reliance on competing decision-making methods.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Providing or encouraging suitable frameworks can reduce cognitive friction and make effective prioritization, problem solving, and decision making easier.

clarifications.for: importing a named management philosophy such as Lean, Agile, or sociocracy as an overall operating approach

clarifications.category: Mentorship Design / Buddy Systems / Peer Guidance
clarifications.for: matching mentors, buddies, or peers and defining how their guidance relationships are supported

observations: Teams use different criteria to prioritize similar requests.
Decision meetings wander between options without a shared way to compare them.
Decisions are repeatedly reopened because the reasoning was not recorded or structured.
People invoke different frameworks in the same discussion and reach conflicting conclusions.
Team members ask for a clearer method to analyze tradeoffs or solve recurring problems.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that people lack a shared or appropriately chosen method for thinking through decisions, priorities, or problems.

challenges.what_if: What if people use different prioritization criteria because the performance measures reward conflicting outcomes, not because they lack a shared thinking method?
What if decisions are repeatedly reopened because no one is sure whose decision is final, regardless of how well the reasoning is structured?
What if tradeoff discussions wander because the team has only filtered or secondhand information about customer needs, leaving each person to fill the gaps differently?

categories.description: Reinforcing norms by showing people what others do and approve of, through peer comparisons, benchmarks, and visible exemplars.

examples.quote: I showed the team how the other shift handled handoffs and shared a few comments from people who liked the change. We copied their checklist, and our missed details dropped within a month.

I posted the response times from each branch, thinking the slower ones would follow the faster ones. Nothing changed, but it revealed that the quickest branch had fewer approval steps, which I would not have known from the numbers alone.

I put up a weekly board showing who closed the most support tickets. People rushed to stay near the top, and the harder cases started getting ignored, so I took the board down and began sharing examples of careful work instead.

target.reason: Social comparisons shape the team's normative environment and thereby influence how people perform their work.

manager_mode.reason: The manager communicates what is normal or approved, sometimes embedding that message in benchmarks, dashboards, or recognition practices.

temporal.reason: Comparisons may be used as one-time prompts or maintained as recurring benchmarks and visible exemplars.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically chooses and presents the comparison, although team members collectively supply and validate the norms being highlighted.

time_horizon.reason: People can recognize the normative signal immediately, while meaningful behavioral alignment typically emerges over the following weeks.

domain.reason: The action shapes shared expectations by making peer behavior and approval salient; its supporting mechanism is communicating visible comparisons, benchmarks, and exemplars.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Peer comparisons and approval cues motivate behavior by making social norms salient and shaping beliefs about what is expected or desirable.

bcw_functions.name: Modelling
bcw_functions.reason: Visible exemplars and examples of peers' behavior provide patterns that people can imitate.

clarifications.for: directly praising, rewarding, challenging, or discouraging an individual's behavior in public
shaping shared identity through narratives about the team's origins and history
changing how the team acknowledges, owns, discusses, and corrects mistakes

observations: People say “nobody does that” even though several peers already do it consistently.
A desired behavior appears in one team but is rarely copied by neighboring teams.
Employees ask to see examples of what good performance looks like.
The same few visible people ignore a norm, and others begin following their example.
Adoption remains low even after the expected behavior has been communicated several times.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that people do not see the desired behavior as common, approved, or visibly practiced by relevant peers.

challenges.what_if: What if people understand that the behavior is expected but the available tools make it slow, awkward, or easy to forget?
What if employees copy the visible noncompliance because the material incentives still reward the old behavior more strongly than peer examples reward the new one?
What if adoption remains low because this is one change among too many, and people lack the capacity to absorb another expectation even when peers model it?

categories.description: Deciding the method for introducing a change itself: pilots, experiments, phased rollouts, opt-in adoption, or top-down mandates.

examples.quote: I tested the new handoff process with one small team before rolling it out elsewhere. They caught a few rough spots, and the next group picked it up with a lot less confusion.
I made the new scheduling tool optional, but hardly anyone used it. That showed me the old tool was tied into two daily tasks I hadn’t known about, so I stopped pushing and fixed those gaps first.

I told everyone we were switching to the new approval process on Monday, and people rushed to clear weeks of requests before the deadline. The backlog landed on two reviewers, so I extended the cutoff and moved teams over in smaller batches.

target.reason: The action changes the conditions and process by which a new practice or system is introduced and adopted.

manager_mode.reason: The manager structures the adoption mechanism and communicates whether participation is experimental, optional, phased, or mandatory.

temporal.reason: The approach is generally selected for the introduction of a particular change rather than maintained as an ongoing system.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically selects the introduction approach, though pilots, experiments, and opt-in adoption can involve team participation and feedback.

time_horizon.reason: Initial effects appear within weeks as adoption begins, while broader uptake and learning often unfold over several months.

domain.reason: The category centers on deciding whether change is mandated or voluntary and who controls adoption, making governance the primary fit. Pilots, experiments, and phased rollouts also concern the operational sequencing and delivery of change.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Pilots, phased rollouts, and implementation structures alter the organizational environment in which the new behaviour occurs.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Testing and staging a change can identify barriers, reduce implementation friction, and make adoption easier.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Top-down mandates and non-optional rollouts limit the choice to continue competing or legacy behaviours.

clarifications.for: establishing enduring decision rights and mandate levels across the organization
deciding whether a specific departure from an existing rule or process is permissible

clarifications.category: Formal Policies / Handbooks / Codes of Conduct
clarifications.for: codifying a change as a formal policy, handbook provision, or code of conduct

observations: A new process was announced to the whole team at once, and several people immediately raised practical issues.
Different teams are adopting the change in different ways, with uneven results.
People keep asking whether the new approach is optional, temporary, or required.
The team is delaying adoption while waiting to see whether the change works elsewhere.
A previous rollout had to be reversed after disrupting day-to-day work.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is the way changes are introduced does not provide the right balance of learning, risk control, clarity, and commitment.

challenges.what_if: What if the uneven adoption and failed rollout are exposing technical dependencies or local system constraints, rather than a problem with how the change was introduced?
What if people are unsure whether the change is optional because leaders have not agreed who has the authority to mandate it or allow exceptions?
What if the broad launch was rushed by organizational pressure that reached the team without enough filtering, forcing a reversal when operational problems surfaced?

categories.category: Unstructured Time / Learning Time / Innovation Time
categories.description: Setting aside unstructured, self-directed time for learning, exploration, and innovation, such as hack weeks, learning days, or a percentage of time.

examples.quote: I gave everyone one Friday afternoon a month to chase any idea they were curious about. One engineer built a small tool that cut our weekly reporting work nearly in half.

I tried a week where people could explore whatever they wanted, but most kept doing their regular work. It showed me they did not believe I would really protect the time, which I would not have known if we had not tried it.

I let the team spend ten percent of each week learning or experimenting, and people got so excited that a few deadlines started slipping. I scaled it back to one shared afternoon every other week and asked everyone to wrap up urgent work first.

target.reason: The action changes how time is allocated and creates conditions for self-directed learning, exploration, and innovation.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates a time-allocation structure and then deliberately gives people latitude over how to use it.

temporal.reason: It can be a recurring standing allocation, such as a percentage of work time, or an episodic event, such as a hack week.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager enables the time, while team members largely choose and pursue their own learning or innovation activities.

time_horizon.reason: Exploration may produce early ideas within weeks, but meaningful capability or innovation outcomes usually emerge over months.

domain.reason: This action redesigns work schedules and capacity by reserving dedicated time for self-directed exploration, while also supporting skill development, learning, and experimentation.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Protected self-directed time removes workload and scheduling barriers that would otherwise prevent learning, experimentation, and innovation.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Formally changing the work schedule through hack weeks, learning days, or allocated percentages creates an environment that supports exploration.

clarifications.for: structuring the format, facilitation, participants, or sequence of a meeting
modulating the team's overall work speed and intensity over a defined period
using heuristics, guardrails, templates, time-boxes, or hard rules to shape how work unfolds

observations: Team members say they have no time to learn tools or skills outside their immediate tasks.
Improvement ideas are repeatedly added to a backlog but never explored.
People use the same methods despite regularly pointing out their limitations.
Hack days or learning activities are routinely canceled when delivery work increases.
Employees pursue experiments informally after hours rather than during the workday.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is people lack protected time to learn, explore ideas, and test improvements beyond immediate delivery work.

challenges.what_if: What if learning and experimentation keep losing out because the organization defines productivity only as immediate delivery, making exploratory work look unproductive?
What if there is no room for improvement work because the team has accepted more external commitments than it can reliably fulfill?
What if canceled learning days and after-hours experiments show that the manager’s everyday attention signals that delivery always matters more, regardless of what is formally encouraged?

categories.description: Personally stepping into a specific conflict between two or more people to mediate, facilitate, arbitrate, or broker a resolution.

examples.quote: I sat down with two leads who kept fighting over who owned the release. I had each one spell out what they needed, then helped them split the decisions between them. The next release was bumpy, but they stopped blocking each other.

I brought two designers together and asked them to talk through months of sniping. They stayed polite in the room and went right back to it afterward. I learned the argument was really about one of them feeling shut out of client meetings, which neither had mentioned before.

I stepped in when three technicians were blaming each other for a bad repair and made the final call on who would handle each part going forward. They took my call as proof that one person was at fault and started freezing him out. I met with them again, corrected that reading, and narrowed my decision to the work split instead of who was to blame.

target.reason: The intervention primarily changes interpersonal relationships and the conditions for working together.

manager_mode.reason: The manager personally enters the conflict to mediate, facilitate, arbitrate, or broker an agreement.

temporal.reason: The action is undertaken in response to a specific conflict rather than maintained as a standing system.

locus_of_agency.reason: Mediation usually depends on the manager and participants jointly reaching resolution, though arbitration may involve a unilateral managerial decision.

time_horizon.reason: The intervention can quickly reduce active tension, while a stable resolution may take several weeks to establish.

domain.reason: Mediation primarily repairs interpersonal trust and working relationships, while arbitration or brokering a resolution also involves decision authority, fairness, and agreed rules for resolving disputes.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Managerial intervention changes the immediate social environment by introducing a neutral third party and a structured process for resolving the conflict.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Mediation removes interpersonal and communication barriers that prevent the parties from reaching agreement and working together effectively.

clarifications.for: strengthening everyday relationships through informal, non-work interaction
mobilizing organizational allies to support the team's initiatives or resource needs
using skip-level meetings to hear directly from people several layers away

observations: Two colleagues repeatedly talk over or challenge each other in meetings.
A disagreement continues through long message threads without reaching a decision.
Team members avoid putting the same two people on shared work.
One or both parties complain about the other in separate 1:1s but do not speak directly together.
Work requiring cooperation between the parties has stalled or been handed to someone else.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is the people involved cannot resolve a specific conflict without a neutral third party guiding or deciding the way forward.

challenges.what_if: What if the recurring disagreement is not mainly interpersonal, but a result of both people believing they have the right to make the same decision?
What if the two colleagues are being rewarded for competing outcomes, making conflict rational even if their relationship is workable?
What if they keep challenging each other because the team has no shared definition of acceptable quality, so each person is defending a different standard?

categories.description: Choosing and shaping the channels and media people use and the norms around them, such as synchronous versus asynchronous, written versus verbal, and which channel suits which purpose.

examples.quote: I moved routine project updates out of meetings and asked everyone to post a short written note by Thursday. The Friday meeting got shorter, and we spent it sorting out the two issues that actually needed a live discussion.

I tried handling a tense product decision entirely in a group chat, but people kept talking past each other. It showed me that written messages were fine for sharing facts, but I couldn't hear how worried two people were until I called them.

I told the team to use our urgent chat room whenever they were blocked, and suddenly every small question landed there with an alert. I muted the noise by limiting it to problems that stopped work completely and moved everything else to a daily question thread.

target.reason: Channel choices and communication norms primarily shape how work is coordinated while also influencing the team's operating context.

manager_mode.reason: The manager establishes a communication structure and reinforces it by explaining and modeling appropriate channel use.

temporal.reason: Channel and media norms usually operate as ongoing rules or conventions for everyday collaboration.

locus_of_agency.reason: Effective communication norms are commonly shaped with team input because members must collectively adopt and sustain them.

time_horizon.reason: New channel guidance can affect communication immediately, while consistent behavioral adoption usually develops over several weeks.

domain.reason: The category primarily concerns how information flows through different channels and media, including matching channels to purpose. Its secondary focus is establishing shared norms and expectations for synchronous, asynchronous, written, and verbal communication.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: It reshapes the digital and social communication environment by establishing which media, timing patterns, and channel norms support different purposes.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: It reduces communication barriers and coordination friction by making interactions more accessible, appropriate, and manageable.

clarifications.for: creating a dedicated forum where people can safely voice ideas, concerns, frustrations, or dissent
introducing, changing, encouraging, or retiring a work artifact such as a plan or shared board
standardizing the words, labels, metaphors, or concepts used to discuss the work
preserving institutional memory through deliberate capture, maintenance, retrieval, transfer, and retirement
cascading strategy and showing how team work connects to organizational direction

observations: Important decisions are scattered across meetings, direct messages, email, and chat threads.
People regularly say they missed an update or did not know where to find it.
Meetings are used mainly to read out information that could have been shared in writing.
Urgent requests and routine updates arrive through the same channels.
Team members expect immediate replies to messages regardless of time zone or working hours.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is unclear or poorly matched communication channels and response norms are causing information loss, interruptions, and unnecessary meetings.

challenges.what_if: What if decisions are scattered across channels because nobody is clear who can decide, approve, or close a discussion?
What if channel proliferation reflects fragmented reporting lines and organizational silos, with each group maintaining its own communication system?
What if everything arrives as urgent and demands an immediate response because weak planning practices keep turning foreseeable work into last-minute surprises?

categories.description: Designing or adapting career ladders, level definitions, and the criteria and processes for advancement.

examples.quote: I rewrote the level descriptions with examples of what the work actually looked like on our team. People had clearer talks with their managers, and two promotions went through with far less back-and-forth.

I tried using one promotion checklist for every role, but it fell apart for our support team. That showed me their strongest work was being missed because the checklist leaned too heavily on shipping new things.

I opened promotion requests to anyone who thought they were ready, and suddenly almost half the team applied. I paused the round, added a short readiness conversation first, and reopened it once people understood the bar better.

target.reason: Career ladders and promotion processes primarily change the rules and conditions surrounding work while also shaping individual development and advancement.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or modifies a formal advancement system and communicates what capabilities and outcomes the organization values.

temporal.reason: The architecture establishes an ongoing framework used repeatedly for development, evaluation, and advancement.

locus_of_agency.reason: A manager can design or adapt the framework, but organization-wide standards are often substantially shaped by HR and senior leadership outside the team.

time_horizon.reason: The framework can influence development and promotion decisions within months, while its broader effects on careers and organizational capability unfold over quarters or years.

domain.reason: Career ladders, role levels, and promotion criteria are core talent and career-management structures. The advancement process also involves governance through decision rights, consistent rules, transparency, and fairness.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Establishing career ladders, level definitions, and advancement processes changes the organizational environment that guides employee behavior.

bcw_functions.name: Incentivisation
bcw_functions.reason: Linking defined behaviors and achievements to promotion creates a valued positive consequence that reinforces those behaviors.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Clear criteria increase employees’ understanding of what performance and capabilities are required for advancement.

clarifications.for: choosing the standing balance between filling roles through internal promotion and external hiring
changing the system used to assess, document, discuss, and calibrate individual performance
determining which work should remain internal and which should be assigned to external providers or contingent staff
ensuring critical-role coverage through backups, knowledge sharing, redundancy, and succession preparation

observations: Employees ask what they need to demonstrate to reach the next level and receive different answers.
Promotion discussions rely on broad statements such as "show more leadership" without concrete examples.
People doing similar work hold different titles or levels.
Managers struggle to explain why one person was promoted and another was not.
Employees see no clear path for advancement without becoming a people manager.
