categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is unclear, inconsistent, or incomplete definitions of levels and promotion requirements are making career growth difficult to understand and apply fairly.

challenges.what_if: What if inconsistent titles and promotions are being used to solve pay problems or retain people, rather than reflecting genuine uncertainty about levels?
What if employees cannot advance as individual contributors because the organizational structure only creates higher-level roles through management positions?
What if managers give different definitions of leadership because the organization lacks a coherent management philosophy, not because the career ladder itself is unclear?

categories.category: Mentorship Design / Buddy Systems / Peer Guidance
categories.description: Designing mentorship approaches and arranging who guides whom, including formal programs, informal pairings, buddy systems, peer mentoring, and reverse mentoring, and deciding how they are matched and supported.

examples.quote: I paired each new starter with someone doing the same job on a different project. They met twice a week for the first month, and the new people started asking for help sooner instead of quietly getting stuck.

I matched people based on the skills they wanted to learn, but most pairs stopped meeting after a few weeks. It showed me that schedule overlap and actually liking the other person mattered more than a perfect match on paper.

I asked junior staff to guide senior managers on how they used our tools, and a few managers started sending them every small tech question. The junior staff got swamped, so I limited the sessions to once a month and gave each pair a short list of topics.

target.reason: Mentorship systems primarily change guidance relationships and support structures, with the secondary aim of developing participants' skills and capabilities.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates the matching and support structure and may also personally arrange, monitor, or facilitate individual pairings.

temporal.reason: Mentorship and buddy approaches are generally ongoing structures maintained over a meaningful period.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager commonly establishes or coordinates the approach while team members provide the actual peer guidance, though matching may sometimes be decided unilaterally.

time_horizon.reason: Developmental and relationship benefits usually emerge over months, while onboarding help and practical guidance can appear within weeks.

domain.reason: Mentorship, buddy systems, and peer guidance primarily build skills and knowledge through supported learning relationships. Their design also depends on creating effective interpersonal connections and trust between mentors, buddies, and mentees.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Establishing mentor, buddy, or peer-guidance relationships changes the social environment by embedding accessible sources of guidance and support.

bcw_functions.name: Modelling
bcw_functions.reason: Mentors and peers demonstrate effective behaviours, approaches, and professional norms that others can observe and imitate.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Ongoing guidance and support help people overcome practical, social, or confidence-related barriers to performing desired behaviours.

clarifications.for: adopting a whole management school or philosophy from another organization
deciding whether to encourage, require, or ignore particular thinking and decision-making frameworks

observations: New hires repeatedly ask basic process questions because they do not know whom to approach.
A small number of experienced employees receive most requests for help.
People say they are unsure how to learn skills that are not covered in formal training.
Employees work through similar problems alone instead of seeking advice from peers.
Existing mentor pairings rarely meet or stop meeting after the first few sessions.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that people lack reliable access to experienced peers who can provide practical guidance and support.

challenges.what_if: What if people know whom to ask, but experienced employees have no capacity for guidance and delivery work always crowds out mentor meetings?
What if people work through problems alone because exposing uncertainty or asking basic questions feels unsafe, not because experienced peers are unavailable?
What if mentoring fades because helping peers is treated as nonproductive work and remains invisible in performance signals?

categories.description: Deciding how strategy is translated into team-level choices and communicated down, up, and out, including how it is cascaded, interpreted, negotiated, and fed back, and how well the team can see how its work connects to it.

examples.quote: I took the company’s three priorities and had the team map each project to one of them. We dropped two projects that did not fit, and people got much clearer about why the remaining work mattered.

I sent our leads a slide deck and asked them to explain the new direction to their teams. It did not land—each lead told a different story—but that showed me which parts were still open to interpretation, so we worked through those together.

I told the team we were shifting hard toward customer retention, and they unexpectedly paused almost every piece of new-customer work. I clarified that the shift was not a full stop, then reviewed the paused work with them and restarted the pieces we still needed.

target.reason: Strategy deployment primarily shapes team direction, priorities, and choices while also creating the communication and feedback context connecting the team to the wider organization.

manager_mode.reason: Managers establish mechanisms for translating and feeding back strategy and communicate how team work connects to strategic goals.

temporal.reason: Effective strategy translation is usually an ongoing cascade and feedback system rather than a single communication event.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager and team jointly interpret and operationalize strategy, while organizational leaders and stakeholders outside the team often set or reshape it.

time_horizon.reason: Strategic alignment typically affects outcomes over months, although clearer priorities and choices can influence team behavior within weeks.

domain.reason: The category centers on how strategy and context flow across levels and become visible and understandable to the team. It also concerns who interprets, negotiates, and converts strategy into team-level decisions.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Translating and cascading strategy increases understanding of priorities, rationale, and how team activities connect to organizational goals.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Converting high-level strategy into actionable team choices and feedback channels reduces ambiguity and makes aligned action easier.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Framing the strategy in locally meaningful terms can strengthen commitment and motivation to pursue it.

clarifications.for: establishing a channel for people to surface concerns, needs, ideas, frustrations, or dissent
creating or revising a tangible artifact such as a roadmap, diagram, prototype, board, or plan
aligning the team on common vocabulary, names, labels, metaphors, or concepts
capturing and maintaining knowledge so it remains retrievable and transferable over time
setting communication-channel choices and norms for synchronous, asynchronous, written, or verbal exchange

observations: Team members give different answers when asked about the organization’s top priorities.
Current projects continue unchanged after leaders announce a new strategy.
Planning meetings include repeated questions about how proposed work supports company goals.
Different teams interpret the same strategic priority in conflicting ways.
Employees say they hear strategic announcements but do not know what decisions they should make differently.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the organization’s strategy has not been translated into clear, shared choices for the team’s day-to-day work.

challenges.what_if: What if old metrics still reward old priorities, so teams are acting rationally when their projects remain unchanged after a new strategy is announced?
What if teams understand the new strategy but cannot change course because existing external commitments have not been reduced or renegotiated?
What if conflicting interpretations persist because no one has clear authority to resolve tradeoffs between leadership mandates, team priorities, and local decisions?

categories.category: Formal Policies / Handbooks / Codes of Conduct
categories.description: Creating, adapting, interpreting, communicating, enforcing, or retiring formal written rules, policies, handbooks, and codes of conduct, and deciding how literally they apply.

examples.quote: I rewrote our travel rule to spell out what needed approval and walked the team through a few real examples. The back-and-forth on expense claims dropped, though we still had a couple of odd cases to sort out.

I tried enforcing the same late-arrival rule on every shift, and it fell apart within a week. It showed me that the opening crew depended on a bus that often arrived late, which I would not have known from the schedule alone.

I added a written rule about rude messages after a few nasty team chats, and people suddenly reported every blunt comment. I clarified that the rule was for personal attacks, not ordinary disagreements, and reviewed the first few reports myself until things settled down.

target.reason: Formal policies primarily shape the rules and conditions surrounding work, while often prescribing how work and conduct should be carried out.

manager_mode.reason: Creating, adapting, or retiring written rules changes the governing system, while communicating and interpreting them signals expected behavior.

temporal.reason: Policies generally remain in force as ongoing rules even though their creation, enforcement, or retirement may involve discrete actions.

locus_of_agency.reason: Managers often decide how to interpret and apply rules within their authority, while organization-wide policies may be driven by executives, HR, legal, or regulators.

time_horizon.reason: Formal rules can alter expectations within weeks, while consistent behavioral and cultural effects typically develop over months.

domain.reason: Formal policies and codes chiefly establish mandated rules, decision boundaries, enforcement, exceptions, and interpretation. Their documentation and communication also determine how clearly those rules are understood and applied.

bcw_functions.name: Restriction
bcw_functions.reason: Formal policies and codes constrain behavioural options by defining required, permitted, and prohibited conduct.

bcw_functions.name: Education
bcw_functions.reason: Communicating and interpreting written rules increases employees’ understanding of expected behaviour and organizational standards.

bcw_functions.name: Coercion
bcw_functions.reason: Enforcing policies creates pressure to comply through anticipated disciplinary or other negative consequences.

clarifications.for: determining which matters leadership mandates and which teams or individuals control
defining or approving legitimate exceptions to an existing written policy
deciding how to launch a new policy or change through pilots, phases, opt-in adoption, or a mandate

observations: Employees ask for written guidance on how to handle the same situation repeatedly.
Similar cases receive different decisions depending on which manager handles them.
People refer to outdated documents or different versions of the same policy.
A written rule is routinely ignored, worked around, or enforced only for some employees.
Managers disagree publicly about what a policy requires or how strictly it should apply.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that formal expectations are missing, unclear, outdated, inconsistently interpreted, or inconsistently enforced.

challenges.what_if: What if the written policy is clear, but leaders visibly bend it themselves, teaching employees that the real rules come from behavior rather than the handbook?
What if managers work around or selectively enforce the policy because current targets and performance signals make compliance costly?
What if outdated versions and conflicting interpretations are symptoms of repeated changes arriving faster than people can absorb them, rather than a problem with the policy itself?

categories.description: Changing how the team plans, estimates, forecasts, and commits to work, including the horizons, methods, and confidence levels used.

examples.quote: I stopped asking for one firm delivery date six months out and had the team give a likely range instead. We updated the range every two weeks, and our partners finally had enough warning to adjust their own schedules.

I tried estimating every task in hours before we started the next batch of work. It took too long and still did not make our dates more accurate, but it showed me that waiting on outside teams was the real source of delay.

I asked everyone to commit only to work they were very sure they could finish that week. People got so cautious that we took on far less than we could handle, so I lowered the confidence bar and added a small stretch list.

target.reason: The action primarily changes planning, estimation, forecasting, and commitment methods, while potentially affecting which work the team prioritizes.

manager_mode.reason: The manager creates or modifies recurring processes, methods, horizons, and rules for planning and forecasting.

temporal.reason: The changes typically establish ongoing practices used across repeated planning and commitment cycles.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically shapes these practices with the team because their effectiveness depends on collective participation and adoption.

time_horizon.reason: Effects can appear within the next few planning cycles, while forecast quality and commitment reliability often improve over several months.

domain.reason: Planning, estimating, forecasting, and committing primarily shape how work is organized, prioritized, paced, and delivered. The secondary angle is how expectations, uncertainty, confidence levels, and future workload are communicated to stakeholders.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Changing planning horizons, estimation methods, and commitment routines restructures the team's process environment and introduces new cues and workflows for managing work.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: More realistic forecasts and confidence-based commitments reduce uncertainty and coordination barriers, making effective delivery easier.

clarifications.for: redesigning the workflow steps and handoffs used to execute work
introducing, encouraging, replacing, or deprecating a specific working practice
changing the schedule, frequency, duration, or synchronization of recurring activities
changing what productivity means or how it is measured and discussed
setting quality standards or reinforcing quality through reviews and feedback

observations: The team repeatedly misses promised dates or changes them at the last minute.
Estimates are presented as firm commitments even when major unknowns remain.
Planned work regularly exceeds the team’s available capacity.
Forecasts change significantly from one planning meeting to the next without an explanation.
Team members spend substantial time creating detailed plans that quickly become obsolete.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that the team’s planning, estimation, or commitment practices do not reflect actual capacity and uncertainty.

challenges.what_if: What if estimates are unstable because technical dependencies and system boundaries make the work genuinely unpredictable, not because the team plans poorly?
What if firm commitments and last-minute changes are responses to unfiltered senior pressure that reaches the team without enough translation or protection?
What if plans become obsolete because the team keeps accepting new external requests and shifting commitments, not because its forecasting method is weak?

categories.description: Deliberately working to retain specific people or groups, through stay conversations, understanding what keeps them, addressing flight risks, and acting before they decide to leave.

examples.quote: I sat down with one of our strongest engineers and asked what was making her look around. She said the constant on-call load was wearing her down, so I changed the rotation and she decided to stay.

I offered a flexible schedule to a supervisor I thought was burned out, but he still left. Our conversation showed me the real issue was that he wanted to lead a larger team, which I would not have known otherwise.

I gave two hard-to-replace analysts extra pay after they told me recruiters were calling. Word got around, and several others assumed they needed outside offers to be valued, so I stopped making one-off deals and met with the team to explain how pay decisions were made.

target.reason: Retention efforts primarily improve conditions, relationships, and support around the work while also addressing an individual's motivations and needs.

manager_mode.reason: The manager directly holds conversations and addresses concerns, sometimes creating broader practices or conditions to reduce flight risk.

temporal.reason: Retention can be an ongoing management practice or an episodic intervention for a particular flight risk.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager typically works with an individual to understand and address retention needs, though group-focused efforts may involve the wider team.

time_horizon.reason: Employees may quickly feel heard or supported, while durable improvements in retention usually emerge over several months.

domain.reason: Retention, flight-risk management, and preventing departures are core people-talent concerns. Stay conversations also depend on trust and direct relationship-building to understand what employees value and what might cause them to leave.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Stay conversations identify and address individual barriers, unmet needs, and flight risks so remaining with the organization becomes more feasible and attractive.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Managers act on feedback by adjusting work conditions, roles, relationships, or supports that influence an employee’s decision to stay.

bcw_functions.name: Persuasion
bcw_functions.reason: Demonstrating that the employee is valued and framing future opportunities can strengthen commitment and motivation to remain.

clarifications.for: altering team membership through hiring, removal, transfers, or replacement
confronting performance or behavioral problems with clear expectations and corrective consequences
determining who should receive stretch work, visibility, advancement opportunities, or career sponsorship

observations: A valued employee says in a 1:1 that they are considering other opportunities.
Several people in the same role or group have left within a short period.
Employees ask about promotion, pay, flexibility, or workload but receive no clear follow-up.
A previously engaged employee stops volunteering ideas, withdraws from discussions, or declines future assignments.
Exit interviews repeatedly cite issues that current employees are also raising.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that valued employees have unmet needs or unresolved concerns that may cause them to leave unless addressed early.

challenges.what_if: What if withdrawal and clustered departures are symptoms of sustained work without enough recovery, so individual stay conversations would only address the consequence?
What if employees have stopped volunteering ideas because they have learned that raising concerns changes nothing, not because they are preparing to leave?
What if questions about pay, promotion, and flexibility point to decisions that feel arbitrary and cannot be challenged through a trusted process, rather than a lack of retention outreach?

categories.description: Connecting directly with people two or more levels away in the hierarchy, through skip-level meetings, open access, and conversations that bypass the usual chain.

examples.quote: I met monthly with small groups of people two levels below me, without their managers in the room. They raised a recurring handoff problem I had never heard about, and we fixed it before the next release.

I set up open office hours, but almost nobody came. I learned that people worried their managers would see a visit as going around them, so the silence told me the access did not feel as open as I thought.

I started messaging junior team members directly when I had questions, and they treated every note like an urgent order. I was surprised by how much work my casual questions created, so I cut back and began saying clearly when no action was needed.

target.reason: Skip-level engagement changes communication channels and hierarchical relationships while also surfacing information that can influence priorities and direction.

manager_mode.reason: The manager personally connects with people across levels and may establish recurring meetings or open-access mechanisms to support those connections.

temporal.reason: It may be a standing access practice or an occasional conversation prompted by a particular need.

locus_of_agency.reason: The connection depends on interaction between the manager and a person at another level, although the manager typically initiates and structures access.

time_horizon.reason: Information and connection can improve within days, while trust and broader cross-level communication benefits usually develop over weeks.

domain.reason: The category primarily builds direct cross-level relationships, trust, and access between leaders and employees beyond their immediate reporting lines. It also creates an information channel that bypasses the usual hierarchy, improving upward and downward visibility.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Creates direct cross-level communication channels that alter the social environment and reduce reliance on the formal hierarchy.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Removes hierarchical and access barriers, making it easier for employees to share information, raise concerns, and engage senior leaders.

clarifications.for: helping team members develop rapport through informal social connection
building a coalition of stakeholders to advance the team's interests across the organization
stepping into a particular dispute to facilitate or broker a resolution

observations: Frontline employees say they rarely hear directly from senior leaders.
Questions or concerns change as they move up through management layers.
Senior leaders are surprised by issues that have been discussed for weeks within frontline teams.
Employees avoid raising topics when their direct manager is in the room.
Skip-level employees ask for more opportunities to share feedback or understand leadership decisions.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is that hierarchy is filtering information and preventing senior leaders and employees from understanding each other directly.

challenges.what_if: What if employees are not being filtered by hierarchy, but are self-censoring because performance reviews and career consequences seem to reward agreement over candor?

What if the disconnect comes from strategy being poorly translated, so frontline teams cannot make sense of leadership decisions and senior leaders cannot recognize operational concerns in strategic terms?
What if employees hold back because they do not trust that concerns will be handled impartially or without retaliation, regardless of whether a senior leader is present?

categories.description: Working with the team as a whole to improve how it works together, through team coaching, facilitated team processes, teamwork retrospectives, launches and resets, and working through group dynamics.

examples.quote: I started a short weekly look-back where everyone named one thing that helped and one thing that got in the way. After a few weeks, handoffs got smoother and people brought up small problems before they turned into fights.

I ran a session to agree on how we would make decisions, but the new rules fell apart within days. It showed me that the real issue was not the rules—it was that two people did not trust each other enough to share unfinished work.

I asked everyone to put recurring frustrations on the board during a team reset, and the list got personal fast. I stopped the discussion, removed names from the examples, and had us come back the next day with a tighter focus on behaviors we could actually change.

target.reason: Team coaching primarily improves collective methods and practices while also addressing relationships, norms, and group dynamics.

manager_mode.reason: The manager directly coaches or facilitates the team and may also establish recurring processes such as retrospectives.

temporal.reason: It includes episodic launches and resets as well as standing practices such as recurring retrospectives.

locus_of_agency.reason: The manager facilitates improvement collaboratively, while the team often diagnoses issues and owns the resulting changes.

time_horizon.reason: Process improvements may become noticeable within weeks, while deeper shifts in norms and group dynamics often take months.

domain.reason: Team coaching and facilitated retrospectives build the team’s collective ability to collaborate and improve. Launches, resets, and work on group dynamics also shape shared expectations and norms for how members work together.

bcw_functions.name: Training
bcw_functions.reason: Team coaching and facilitated practice build the team’s skills in communication, coordination, reflection, and collaborative problem-solving.

bcw_functions.name: Enablement
bcw_functions.reason: Facilitation helps teams identify and overcome relational, procedural, and group-dynamic barriers that impede effective teamwork.

bcw_functions.name: Environmental Restructuring
bcw_functions.reason: Launches, resets, and retrospectives reshape the team’s social environment by establishing clearer norms, routines, roles, and interaction patterns.

clarifications.for: addressing one individual's development, motivation, or performance through coaching
developing specific individual or collective capabilities through structured learning
benchmarking the team against practices used by other organizations

observations: The same disagreements resurface across multiple team meetings without resolution.
A few people dominate discussions while others rarely speak.
Team members leave meetings with different understandings of what was decided or who owns the next step.
People complain about one another after meetings instead of raising concerns with the group.
Handoffs, decisions, or working agreements repeatedly break down across the team.
categories.assumption: If you choose this intervention, you are betting that the problem is how the team works together as a group, rather than the skills or performance of any one individual.

challenges.what_if: What if individual productivity measures reward visible airtime, personal output, and local wins, making domination, weak handoffs, and private blame rational behaviors?
What if recurring disputes and broken handoffs reflect technical system boundaries that create ambiguous ownership and dependencies no amount of team facilitation can remove?
What if people keep revisiting decisions because they are working from different definitions of acceptable quality, not because they lack the ability to work through disagreements?
